brief: Bright start-button fanfare blip with flash feel; knobs: waveform (square|pulse12|saw), pitch, flourish 0..1, sparkle 0..1, tempo rate, tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: sparkle

flaws: At 1.18 s the sound is too long for a start-button blip. The brief implies a short, snappy fanfare, but the final held note takes up about half the length and sits at a flat, sustained plateau.

The envelope has no punch. The held note is a block of near-constant amplitude with a slow decay, so it reads as a sustained tone, not a flash or sparkle. Even the no-tail version (0.72 s) is a flat slab with a hard cutoff.
The flourish is only a few quiet, soft-attack grace notes, and they are very low in level compared with the main note. They read as a weak pre-roll, not a bright arpeggio.

Range extremes are not equivalent. At minimum settings the flourish is slow and the centroid is low (1873 Hz), so it is not bright. At maximum settings the flourish becomes a dense, quiet smear and 20% of the render is silence, with the main note starting late.
The long fade-out tail, with the waveform dwindling to near-nothing over the last 0.3 s, is wasteful for a UI sound. The tail toggle should be a short/long choice, and its default should be off.
The pulse12 waveform has a much lower RMS (0.136) than the others, so loudness is inconsistent between waveform choices.
grades.lesson: For short UI or game feedback sounds, shape the envelope to the brief (fast attack, brief body, quick decay) and keep the total length tight. Don't let one sustained note dominate the duration. Make sure the ornamental parts (flourishes, sparkle) are audible and balanced against the main note at both ends of their range.

flaws: The default has a rising arpeggio of 3-4 stepped notes ending on a longer accented note. This reads as a chiptune start jingle, but it runs about 0.48 s, so it is slightly long for a blip.
The sparkle layer shows up as faint falling or rising diagonal lines after the final note. It is subtle at defaults, so the 'flash' feel is weak.
The tail knob is a toggle, but 'long' is only 0.79 s and 'short' changes the note pattern as well as the decay, so it is not a clean tail control.
At max range the descending sparkle line and the denser note run make the sound busier and less like a blip, though it still holds together and is not broken.
grades.lesson: Make each knob change only the one property it names, and check that the extremes keep the sound's core identity. Toggles like a tail switch should not also alter the note timing or pattern.

flaws: The default render opens with two isolated clacks and then a dense burst, so the start of the take sounds like a different event than the rest.
Both seeds change the arrangement a lot. Seed 2 is a sparse series of clusters, while Seed 3 is a near-continuous roll. They read as different gestures, not as two takes of one mash.
The minimum extreme is only three isolated clicks with 85% silence. It is usable as a single-click mode but no longer sounds like a mash.
The maximum extreme is a dense, wash-like noise bed with a flat spectrogram and no discernible individual clacks, which sounds more like static or rain than buttons.
The room tail toggle adds only a faint low smear, so the effect is subtle and does not clearly change the perceived space.

brief: Rhythmic run of blacksmith hammer blows on hot iron. Knobs: hammer weight (light/heavy), tempo rate, force 0..1, irregularity 0..1, metal ring 0..1, tail toggle.

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 2.32); takes should stay the same sound
knobs with a subtle effect: force

flaws: Every blow looks identical in shape: a sharp transient with a fixed exponential decay, so it sounds machine-gunned and not like a smith working. The default is very regular and force barely varies between hits.
The heavy hammer looks mostly like a lower-pitched copy of the light one. It has no longer ring or thud body, so it reads as a pitch shift.
Minimum ranges give three sparse hits with 56% silence. That is a slow, thin result, not a rhythmic run, and the gaps are long.
With the tail off, the spectrogram shows ring-like horizontal lines, so the tail toggle seems to remove the noisy decay and leave a purer tone. The result is more synthetic, not simply drier.
The maximum setting stacks blows tightly so tails overlap into a dense wash and the individual strikes blur.
grades.lesson: For repeated-hit sounds, build per-hit variation into the model (amplitude, timing, spectral tilt, ring decay), not just a global seed or irregularity knob. Make sure categorical choices such as weight change the body of the sound, not only its pitch.

brief: Single isolated keystroke with press and release; knobs: switch type (membrane/mechanical/laptop), key size (letter/space/enter), force 0..1, rattle 0..1, pitch, room tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: rattle

flaws: The press and release are nearly equal in level and look alike, so the release reads as a second keystroke rather than a softer, higher key-up click. Real key-ups are noticeably quieter and thinner.
The 'mechanical' switch type was not shown in the renders, so I could not check that it reads as a distinct clicky switch.

The room tail adds a 0.62 s wash and raises the centroid to about 2.4 kHz. It sounds like a reverb layer rather than a natural room decay, and the default 0.27 s is short enough that it may feel abrupt.
The membrane and laptop types differ mainly in level and brightness, with the same decay structure. Laptop looks like a weak, thin version of the same click.
grades.lesson: When a sound has two linked events (such as press and release, or strike and rebound), give the second event its own level, spectrum and decay so it reads as a different physical action. Don't copy the first event at a similar level.

brief: Hammer strike on a blacksmith's anvil. Knobs: anvil size (small/medium/large), force 0..1, ring amount 0..1, dampening 0..1, pitch, ring-tail toggle.

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: force

flaws: The defaults have a sharp transient followed by a long decaying tail with discrete ringing partials in the spectrogram, which reads as a struck metal object. However, the low-frequency energy at the bottom is strong and sustained, so it sounds more like a bell or gong than a hard steel anvil, which would be brighter and more clangy.

The beating or amplitude modulation in the tail is a nice touch, but the spectrum looks like a few pure sine partials with little broadband impact noise at the strike. The hammer contact may sound synthetic and lack a real metallic 'clank'.

The size knob changes the length a lot (0.97 s to 2.64 s), so large is probably too long for a single anvil hit and small is a different pitch rather than just a different mass. This is acceptable but a bit coarse.

The 'all ranges at minimum' render is 1.94 s with a low centroid, and the 'all at maximum' render is only 0.44 s. The ranges seem to be inverted or mixed, because the dampening knob dominates length, so the extremes are not intuitive. The maximum case also looks like a duller thud with a smeared block of energy, and the stray vertical bars suggest some artefacts.
The tail toggle only changes the length from 1.64 s to 0.54 s, and the spectrogram suggests the pitch character changes with it. It should only remove the ring.
grades.lesson: When several knobs affect the same property (such as decay length), check that their extremes combine into sensible, predictable results, and make sure toggles change only the one thing they are named for.

brief: Burst of continuous typing on a desk keyboard; knobs: switch type (membrane/mechanical/laptop), typing rate, intensity 0..1, spacebar-and-enter amount 0..1, desk resonance 0..1, room tail toggle

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 2.41); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: The default has about 45% silence from long pauses between bursts, so it reads as a few clusters rather than continuous typing. The brief asks for a 'burst of continuous typing'.
The minimum-range render is sparse and very bright (centroid 3474 Hz, 74% silence). It reads as thin ticks rather than typing, though it is not broken.
The default and laptop renders both end with isolated single keystrokes and silence, so the tail feels abrupt without the room toggle.

Individual keystrokes look quite uniform, with few clear down/up click pairs. This makes the mechanical and membrane types less distinct than they could be, though the membrane type is clearly lower (429 Hz centroid).
grades.lesson: When the brief says 'continuous' activity, make the default event density steady and have pauses be an explicit, optional knob. Otherwise random gaps dominate the timeline and the sound reads as separate clusters.

brief: Analogue bass-drum one-shot; knobs: circuit (808|909|606), decay 0..1, pitch-sweep 0..1, click 0..1, tune 30-80 Hz, tail toggle

errors: knobs with no audible effect: click

flaws: The default 808 kick has a centroid of 75 Hz and the spectrogram shows almost no visible pitch-drop line. The sweep is subtle, so it reads more as a sustained sub sine than a punchy kick.
Seeds 1-3 look nearly identical (same envelope, same centroid of 75-76 Hz). The variation is too small to be useful as separate takes, though it is not unrelated.

At minimum range the kick is a long, flat sub-tone with a weak transient. At maximum range the envelope gets lumpy and the tail runs to 1.8 s. Both extremes feel less like a tight kick than the defaults do.
The 606 preset has 17% silence and a very short body. The click shows as a detached blob in the spectrogram, so it looks slightly separated from the body rather than integrated.
The 909 and 606 are distinguishable mainly by length and a slightly higher centroid, not by the character those circuits are known for (e.g. 909 punch, 606 snap).
grades.lesson: Make the defining gesture of a sound (e.g. a kick's pitch drop) clearly visible in the spectrogram at default settings, and make per-seed variation large enough to see in the render, not just in the numbers.

brief: Hazard-light ticking at doubled cadence; knobs: relay type (mechanical/digital), brightness 0..1, dashboard resonance 0..1, rate, tail toggle

errors: knob dashboard: 77% of the buffer is silent
knob rate: 77% of the buffer is silent
random combination 3: 71% of the buffer is silent
warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: tail
knobs with a subtle effect: tail

flaws: The default shows about 10 evenly spaced ticks in 2 s with nothing to mark the tick-tock pairing, so it reads as a plain metronome, not the doubled cadence of a hazard relay.
The ticks are very regular in level and timing, so a human-feel jitter is missing. The two seeds differ mainly in small amplitude changes.
At the maximum extreme the ticks smear into a continuous buzz, with a strong low band that dominates, and the individual relay clicks are lost.
The mechanical and digital relays differ mostly in spectral tint, not in the physical character of the click, such as the contact bounce and the solenoid thunk.
The tail toggle adds a decay resonance that is barely audible in the waveform. The 2 s file ends with a lingering noise floor, not a clean loop point.
grades.lesson: Make each variant differ in physical character and not only in spectral tint, keep the defining rhythmic or structural feature of the brief clearly visible at defaults, and check that the extreme settings still read as discrete events instead of blurring into a continuous texture.

brief: Mouse button click, single or double; knobs: mouse build (cheap plastic/gaming/silent), click count (single/double), sharpness 0..1, release level 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The 'silent' build has a lower centroid (533 Hz) and a higher RMS (0.14) than the others, so it reads as a dull thud and not a quiet click. It is louder than the cheap and gaming builds, which is backwards for a build called silent.
The default is already a down-click plus a release click about 0.1 s later, so the 'single' count is really two events. The gap is long for a mouse button, so the release reads as a second click.

With the tail off, the energy stays in the lower bands and the release click is noticeably weaker. This is acceptable, but the tail toggle changes the character more than a reverb or room tail should.
The spectrogram has coarse time resolution and shows blocky banding, so the click's high-frequency snap is hard to confirm. The 0.23 s length and the transient shape fit a mouse click.
grades.lesson: Make each preset's loudness and spectrum match what its name promises (e.g. 'silent' should be quieter), and check that any 'single' or 'one-shot' option does not already contain several events.

brief: Turn-signal relay tick-tock pair; knobs: relay type (mechanical/digital), click sharpness 0..1, tock body 0..1, rate in Hz, cabin reverb tail toggle

errors: defaults: 75% of the buffer is silent
knob relay: 80% of the buffer is silent
knob sharpness: 74% of the buffer is silent
knob sharpness: 77% of the buffer is silent
knob body: 82% of the buffer is silent
knob body: 75% of the buffer is silent
knob rate: 83% of the buffer is silent
seed 2: 75% of the buffer is silent

seed 4: 75% of the buffer is silent

random combination 3: 79% of the buffer is silent

flaws: The digital relay type is a pure decaying sine tone and reads as a synth beep rather than a relay. It has no click transient, and its tick and tock are very different in level.
The render is a single tick-tock pair at 0.43 s. At very low rate settings the silence share rises to 60%, so the loop may not read as a steady blinker.
The mechanical default's tock is much longer and louder than the tick, with a ringing tail that looks a bit like a resonant thud. The seeds differ mainly in the high-frequency partials.
Rate is the only timing control. There is no tick/tock level or pitch-ratio knob beyond the single 'tock body' control.
grades.lesson: When a sound has several variants (e.g. mechanical vs digital), check each variant against the real thing on its own. Give every variant the same essential transient and character, not just a different tone.

brief: Analogue snare blending tuned oscillators and noise; knobs: circuit (808|909|linn), tone-mix 0..1, snappy 0..1, decay 0..1, pitch 150-300 Hz, tail toggle

flaws: Defaults decay to near-silence by about 0.25 s, so about 28% of the render is a dead tail. The snare reads a bit short and dry, with little of the body or snap-tail shimmer a real 909 or 808 has.

The spectrogram shows a bright red band at the very bottom (about 150-200 Hz) that is strong and sustained, with relatively weak mid and high noise energy. The noise (snare wires) component looks thin for a snare, and the tonal part dominates.

The circuit options are only subtly different (centroid 2031 vs 1490 vs 1780 Hz), and the 909 option is not clearly distinct from the 808 in the picture. Linn has a longer, more even decay, which is the clearest difference.
Range extremes mainly change length and brightness (0.33 s vs 0.50 s). The minimum setting is a very short, tick-like hit, which is borderline as a usable snare.
The tail=false render is shorter and brighter, but it loses the low tone almost entirely, so the toggle changes the character more than just the tail.
grades.lesson: Make the options of a categorical knob (such as a circuit or model choice) differ audibly in spectrum and envelope, and check on the spectrogram that the noise and tone layers each contribute where the real instrument has energy, not just in one band.

brief: Notched mouse scroll wheel spin; knobs: wheel type (notched/free-spin), scroll rate, detent clarity 0..1, spin length 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: At default the notched wheel is a dense train of clicks with near-constant amplitude, then a short tail. A real flick decelerates, with click spacing widening as the wheel slows. Here the spacing looks roughly uniform, so it reads more like a ratchet or buzz than a coasting wheel.
The free-spin preset is a smooth, decaying tonal wash with no visible clicks. It is a sensible alternative but sounds more like a bearing hum than a mouse wheel, and it is long for a mouse scroll.

The minimum range gives a short, sparse burst of about 9 clicks that look a bit uneven, and the maximum is a dense wall of clicks. They are all recognisably the same kind of sound, but the maximum comes close to merging into a buzz.
The tail toggle only changes the decay at the end and adds a little silence. It is a minor control that does not change the sound much.
Click amplitudes look fairly uniform, with little per-click randomness, which makes the train feel mechanical.
grades.lesson: For any repeating-event sound (clicks, steps, ticks), model the physical process that governs timing and energy, such as deceleration, per-event amplitude jitter and spacing drift. A uniform pulse train reads as a machine, not as the real object.

brief: Driver door shut with solid seal thunk; knobs: door size (compact/sedan/SUV), force 0..1, seal suction 0..1, latch click level 0..1, cabin tail toggle

flaws: The latch click is barely visible in the spectrograms. Nearly all energy sits below about 500 Hz, so the metallic latch snap that makes a door read as a car door looks weak or missing.
The SUV size has more silence (39%) and a shorter-looking visible body than the sedan default, so the decay reads as a thinner thunk rather than a bigger door.
The cabin tail toggle shortens the sound to 0.50 s but still leaves a long flat low-level trailing line. The 'off' state is not much more distinct than a trimmed version of the default.
The seeds look like the same event, but the visible detail differs mainly in how the decay is filled in. The attack structure is the same across takes, so the variation is modest.
grades.lesson: Make sure each named layer (such as a latch click or seal suction) leaves a distinct, visible signature in a different frequency band. Otherwise it blends into the main body, and the knob controlling it changes level without changing character.

brief: Hot iron plunged into a water trough. Knobs: blade size (dagger/sword/horseshoe), heat 0..1, bubble amount 0..1, splash 0..1, steam-tail toggle.

flaws: The broadband hiss is a noise burst with a decay, and the spectrogram looks like a generic white-noise wash. A real quench has a sustained, slightly modulated steam hiss with a more obvious initial plunge and splash.
The bubbles appear as thin falling streaks that are sparse and sit mostly in the second half. They read as isolated pings, not a dense bubbling cluster, and they stay weak at the default setting.
The 3 s default is long for a quench, and the tail is a smooth fade of about 22% near-silence. It is acceptable but a little drawn out.
Blade size mostly changes the bubble pattern and a little of the centroid. The three blade settings look quite similar, so the difference is subtle.
With tail=false the sound is 1.23 s, mostly noise followed by a few bubbles, and it ends fairly abruptly. It still reads as a quench, but it is a much thinner version of the sound.
The minimum-range render has no bubbles and is just a decaying noise burst, which loses the identity of the sound.
grades.lesson: Make each feature that defines the sound (here, bubbles) audible at its low extremes and in every discrete option, so that the sound is still recognisable when the knobs are pushed to their limits.

brief: Inner handle pull, latch release and seal peel; knobs: handle material (plastic/chrome), pull speed 0..1, seal peel amount 0..1, hinge creak 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The latch click is a sharp transient and reads correctly, but the seal peel is a diffuse noise bed that sounds more like a generic rustle than a rubber seal releasing.
At maximum settings the click is no longer a distinct latch event. It moves earlier and the sound turns into a broad noisy swell, which weakens the sequence of handle, latch, then seal.
Plastic and chrome differ only slightly (centroid 1754 vs 1964 Hz), so the material switch is a subtle change rather than a clear one.
Disabling the tail leaves a hard gate cut at about 0.9 s, with 30% silence and abrupt chopped segments. A designer would hear this as an artifact.
The pull-speed range and the hinge creak are hard to read in the spectrograms. The creak shows as faint horizontal lines and is easily lost under the peel noise.
grades.lesson: Make each knob audibly and visibly shape one distinct event in the sound, and keep the main transient identifiable at every extreme. Where a toggle removes a tail, fade it out rather than gating it.

brief: Short woody rimshot ping; knobs: circuit (808|909|cr78), brightness 0..1, decay 0..1, pitch 400-1800 Hz, tail toggle

flaws: The default render is a short, sharp transient with a quick decay, which fits a rimshot. The energy sits in a few narrow horizontal spectral lines (a tonal ping) with little noise or crack. It reads as a clean synthetic click-ping rather than a woody rimshot.

The circuit variants (808, 909, CR-78) look and measure nearly alike. 808 and 909 have almost the same centroid (1129 vs 1126 Hz) and differ mainly in length, so the choice knob adds little character.

At the maximum range the sound turns into a longer, ringing, bright tone (0.31 s, centroid 2908 Hz). It sounds more like a tuned blip or woodblock than a rimshot, and the maximum is clearly different from the default.
At the minimum range the sound is very short and dull (0.10 s, centroid 412 Hz) and carries little energy. It is usable as a thud but loses the ping.
The tail toggle works and adds a plausible room or ring-out. The tail looks slightly blotchy, with irregular energy patches rather than a smooth decay.
The two seeds look like takes of the same sound, with the same shape and slightly different peaks and detail. The variation is subtle but appropriate.
grades.lesson: When a sound has selectable variants (such as machine models), make each one differ audibly in spectrum and envelope, not only in length, and check the spectrogram to confirm the variants are distinct.

brief: Single floorboard creak under a footstep; knobs: wood (pine|oak|rotten), stress 0..1, groan length 0..1, pitch, room tail toggle

flaws: Defaults read as a thump or knock with a ringing tail, not a creak. The waveform opens on a hard, dense low transient and the spectrogram is dominated by a low band at the bottom (centroid 366 Hz). A creak should show a sustained, wandering stick-slip tone with a pitch contour and a pulsed texture, and none is visible.

Creak character is absent. There is no rising or falling friction line and no pulse train of micro-slips. The only spectral features are a few thin horizontal lines that look like fixed resonances, with a single decaying burst, so the brief's 'groan' is not heard as such.
The 'wood = rotten' render shows sparse, isolated ticks over a low rumble, which looks like random clicks rather than a creak. 'Pine' shows two decaying thumps, which looks like a double knock.

'room = false' gives two separate bursts with a clear gap, the second one a smooth swelling blob. This reads as two unrelated events rather than one board creaking. Its 40% silence suggests the creak is fragmented.

Minimum settings are very low (centroid 178 Hz) and read as a dull low thud. Maximum settings give a double thump with a long tail. Neither reads as the same sound as the defaults, so the range is inconsistent.
Seeds change where the secondary bursts fall, but all share the same dominant thump onset. The sound is consistent, but variation is mostly where the second event lands, and it is a thump either way.

Knobs are mostly sensible (wood type, stress, groan length, pitch, room tail), but the 'groan length' range seems to add decaying thumps rather than extend a sustained creak, so the knob does not do what its name promises.
grades.lesson: Model the defining mechanism of the sound (here sustained stick-slip friction with a pitch contour) rather than a generic impact-plus-decay. Then check in the spectrogram that its signature feature, such as a moving tonal line, is visible at defaults.

flaws: Default render reads as a smooth, sustained 1.7 s noise swell with a symmetric fade-in and fade-out. A real floorboard creak is a stick-slip sequence of irregular pulses with a pitch that glides. The dense, even waveform sounds more like a bowed or rubbed tone than wood.

The spectrogram shows static horizontal bands at roughly constant frequency, with no visible pitch glide and no discrete stick-slip pulses. This is the biggest realism gap, because the groan is the defining character of a creak.
The brief says a creak under a footstep, but there is no weight-onset thump or transient at the start. The sound begins as a soft swell, so it has no footstep context.

The pine and oak defaults are near-identical in shape, with only a small change in centroid. Rotten is the only choice that differs clearly. Rotten shows the right irregular, pulsed creaking, which suggests the default should have that kind of pulsing.
The room = false render is a symmetric, blunt-ending blob about 1.16 s long, with an abrupt cutoff at the end and no natural decay. That sounds unfinished.
The minimum-range render turns into a short, cracky burst with a noise lead-in, which reads as a snap or crack rather than a creak, so the extremes do not stay the same kind of sound.
The seeds share one envelope shape but differ little in detail. They are acceptable, but the sustained-tone character is the same in all of them.
grades.lesson: Before polishing knobs, check that the sound's defining micro-structure (here irregular stick-slip pulses with a gliding pitch) is visible in the spectrogram at defaults. A smooth, symmetric envelope over static spectral bands will read as the wrong sound however well the knobs work.

flaws: Default render reads as a dense, noisy burst with a smooth swell and decay, closer to a rumble or rough friction wash than a floorboard creak. There is no clear pitched groan contour (a gliding resonance) in the spectrogram.

Energy is concentrated below about 1 kHz with a centroid near 530 Hz. A creak should show stick-slip pulses and a resonant formant that moves. Here the spectrum is mostly a low smear with weak upper structure.
The footstep is missing. The brief says a creak under a footstep, but there is no initial thump or weight-shift transient at the start.
The pine and default renders look almost the same (centroid 533 vs 614 Hz, similar envelope), so the wood choice barely changes the character. Only rotten is clearly different, with discrete pulses.
Range extremes drift from the sound. The minimum is a short, low decaying thud, not a creak. The maximum is a long, dense, uniform block of noise at 2.35 s.
With room tail off, the sound ends abruptly at the cutoff (1.40 s, 31% silence) instead of decaying naturally.
The seeds share the same overall envelope but differ a lot in the character of the fine pulses, so they read as loosely related rather than as two takes of one creak.
grades.lesson: Build the sound's defining feature explicitly, such as a gliding resonance with stick-slip pulses, plus any event named in the brief, such as the footstep impact. Do not rely on shaped noise with an envelope. Then check that the spectrogram shows that feature at defaults and at the extremes of every knob.

brief: Aggressive door slam shaking the cabin; knobs: door size (compact/sedan/SUV), force 0..1, panel rattle 0..1, low-end weight 0..1, pitch, boom tail toggle

flaws: The waveform is a sharp transient with a ~0.5 s decaying low rumble, which fits a car door slam. But the spectrogram shows energy almost entirely below ~300 Hz (centroid ~198 Hz). That makes it read as a muffled thud with little metallic latch click or panel crack, so it is less aggressive than the brief asks for.

Door size compact/sedan/SUV barely changes the spectrum: the centroid is 193 Hz for compact and 198 Hz for SUV, and the differences are mostly level. A designer would expect an audible size change in pitch or body, not just loudness.
The range extremes at min and max look almost the same, with centroids of 171 and 234 Hz. The knobs produce subtle changes, so the range is narrow.

Turning the boom tail off gives a clean sinusoidal ringing decay, like a pure tone. It sounds synthetic and tonal, unlike the noisy default, and it shortens the sound to 0.8 s. The toggle is a bit of a gimmick as built.
The 17% silence is the tail's quiet end, which is acceptable for a one-shot, but the hit has little distinct latch or rattle detail in the high frequencies.
grades.lesson: Make each categorical or range knob change the spectral character (pitch, brightness, decay), not just the level. Also check that the 'off' state of a toggle still sounds like the same kind of sound, not a different synthesis path.

brief: Larger swell bursting over a breakwater; knobs: size (small|medium|storm), impact 0..1, foam hiss 0..1, rumble 0..1, tail toggle

errors: knob rumble: build failed: interrupted

flaws: The envelope is a symmetric spindle: a slow rise to a peak at about 0.8 s, then a long decay. A wave bursting over a breakwater should have a fast impact onset, a roaring foam burst, then a hissy drain-off. The slow swell reads as a gentle surge or a fade-in/out, not a crash.

The spectrogram is a flat, uniform band of mid-high noise with no visible low-end rumble and no spectral evolution. The bright foam hiss never separates from the low thump, and the sound does not darken as it decays. It reads as generic shaped noise.

The size knob changes only the length and the level slightly. Small, medium and storm have the same centroid (about 2100 Hz) and the same shape, so storm sounds like a longer small rather than a bigger, heavier wave. Larger water should have more low-frequency weight and a stronger impact.

The all-min and all-max extremes look nearly identical to the default. The impact, foam and rumble knobs have little visible effect on the picture, so the range is narrow and the controls feel cosmetic.
The tail toggle only trims the end (2.55 s vs 3.30 s, silence 26%). That is a lazy way to shorten the sound, and the cut-off tail looks truncated rather than naturally decaying.

Seeds 2 and 3 share the same spindle shape but differ in where the peak falls and in how pronounced the secondary bumps are. That is acceptable variation, but it cannot make up for the wrong core envelope.
grades.lesson: Before building, sketch the characteristic envelope and spectral evolution of the real event (for a crash: instant transient, then a bright burst, then a darkening decay). Make the main knobs, such as size, change the spectrum and the envelope shape as well as the duration and level.

flaws: Every render has the same envelope: a sharp transient at t≈0 followed by a smooth exponential decay. It reads as a single explosion or thump with a noise tail, not a wave swelling and bursting over a breakwater. There is no build-up and no secondary wash or drain-off.
The brief says 'swell bursting', but the waveform shows no swell rise. The peak is at the very start, so the attack is too abrupt and the sound lacks the characteristic ramp into impact.

The spectrogram energy is concentrated in a low-frequency band at the bottom and is mostly flat noise above it. The foam hiss is not visible as a distinct, evolving high-frequency component, so the sound lacks the sizzling bubble decay of real surf.

Size extremes change only the length and brightness slightly (2.6 s / 3.3 s / 3.9 s, centroid 1808 / 1500 / 1321 Hz). Small and storm read as the same sound at different durations rather than different-scale events. Storm does not feel notably bigger or heavier.

Minimum ranges give a bright, thin, dull decay (centroid 1991 Hz) and maximum ranges give a denser burst. The two extremes are clearly different, but neither adds structure: no multiple impacts, no layered wash.

Defaults carry 24% silence-flagged samples, and the tail looks like a smooth fade-out of low-level noise. This is tail-end dead air rather than a convincing receding wash, and the tail toggle just truncates it.
The seeds share the same shape with small detail changes. That is acceptable, but the shape itself is too generic to give variety between takes.

Knobs are reasonable in name (impact, foam, rumble) but they mostly rescale one envelope instead of controlling separate layers. There is no control over swell build time, wash length or spray timing.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes a multi-stage event (build-up, impact, wash, drain), give each stage its own visible envelope and spectral layer, and make size change the structure and timing, not just the duration and brightness of one decaying noise burst.

flaws: The envelope reads as a symmetric spindle, with a swell building and then decaying evenly. A wave bursting over a breakwater should swell and then hit with a sharp impact, followed by a long foamy wash. The defaults do not show this impact-then-wash shape.

The spectrogram energy sits mostly in the low-to-mid band and fades to near nothing in the upper half. Foam hiss should show up as sustained broadband high-frequency content, but it barely appears at the defaults (centroid 1632 Hz).
The impact is not distinct. The peak is a ragged cluster of spikes in the waveform rather than a single thump, and there is no visible low-frequency boom with a pitch drop.
Size changes mostly duration and loudness. Small, medium and storm have the same shape and the same centroid, so storm does not sound like a bigger body of water.
The tail toggle only trims about 0.5 s and does not change the character. 'Tail = false' still has a decaying body, so the knob has little effect.
The 12% silence at the defaults suggests a gap or a fade to near-silence at the end, which gives a thin, abrupt wash instead of a natural recession of water.
Every range at minimum drops the rms to 0.079 and shifts the centroid up to 2112 Hz, which reads as thinner and brighter rather than as a gentler version of the same crash.
grades.lesson: Build the signature temporal shape of the event (for example, a sharp attack followed by a long, textured decay) into the defaults, and check that each knob changes a distinct feature of the spectrogram rather than only the length or level.

brief: Belt release and webbing retracting into spool ending in a thud; knobs: retract speed 0..1, webbing friction 0..1, end-stop thud 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The retract phase is a broadband noise swell with a faint rising and falling arc. It reads more as a generic whoosh than a ratcheting spool. There are no visible ratchet or click pulses, which are the signature of a real retractor.

The end-stop thud is short and mostly low-frequency. It is clear in the picture but lightly weighted, and it sits slightly detached from the retract after a dip. A real belt snaps home with a plastic or metal clack, and here the top end of that hit is limited.
At the minimum range settings the sound becomes quiet and dull (peak 0.43, centroid 468 Hz). The retract is flattened into a near-constant band, so it reads as a different, muffled sound.
The tail toggle only trims the decay. Its effect is small, so it is a marginal control compared with a knob for ratchet density or spool size.
grades.lesson: Include the defining micro-structure of the real source, such as ratchet clicks, pulses or resonances, rather than only a noise envelope with the right length and spectrum. Check that each range extreme keeps that structure audible, not just that it stays non-silent.

brief: Closed hi-hat from six square oscillators through bandpass; knobs: metal (thin|bright|dark), decay 0..1, tone 0..1, accent 0..1, tail toggle

errors: knob decay: 74% of the buffer is silent

flaws: The spectrograms show energy in sparse horizontal lines, which suggests discrete square-oscillator partials. At defaults the high-frequency noise-like sizzle is weak, so it may sound pitched or metallic-ringy rather than like a real hat.
Defaults decay slowly for a closed hat (about 0.11 s with a smooth exponential tail, and 0.15 s for dark). Closed hats usually have a tighter, more abrupt gate.
The 'dark' variant has strong low-mid lines near 2-3 kHz and reads more like a clank or tom-ish tick than a hat.
The 'tail' toggle makes the sound longer (0.24 s), which moves it toward a half-open hat and blurs the 'closed' identity.
The accent knob is not clearly distinguishable in the renders, and the 'thin' variant is very short at 0.08 s and borders on a click.
grades.lesson: When synthesizing from a few discrete oscillators, add noise or modulation so the spectrum fills in rather than showing isolated lines. Check that each preset and toggle stays within the identity of the named sound, not just that it sounds different.

brief: Bright cracking snare with gated noise tail; knobs: size (tight|room|hall), crack 0..1, gate-length 0..1, saturation 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Waveform is a long, dense, sustained wash with a slow decay across 0.26-0.46 s. It has no sharp transient and no visible body-to-noise split, so it reads as a noise burst rather than a snare.

The spectrogram shows a flat, broadband smear with a single low red line near the bottom, which looks like a static tone or a weak pitch drop. There is no clear snare body (about 180-250 Hz) with a fast decay, and no bright crack in the first few ms.

The 'gated' tail is not convincing. At the max setting it is a hard step: full-level noise that cuts abruptly to a low-level tail at about 0.3 s. That reads as a clunky level drop, not a gate. The default tail is just a slow exponential decay with no gate character.

The size options (tight/room/hall) differ only by a bit of length (0.26/0.36/0.46 s) and a small centroid shift. They do not change the character, and 'hall' gets a long dull decay instead of a distinct room or reverb. The result is three near-identical takes.

Minimum range is a gentle decaying buzz with no real crack, and the max is a sustained slab with RMS 0.405. These extremes sound like different, partly wrong sounds rather than a tighter or looser snare.
Toggling tail=false just trims the length and leaves the body. The 'tail' control does not give a clean gated-noise vs dry-body contrast.
The three seeds are almost identical in envelope, length and centroid. Only the fine speckle differs, so there is barely any variation between takes.
grades.lesson: Check that the waveform envelope shows the signature shape of the named sound (for a snare, a sharp transient followed by a quick body decay and a separate noise tail) at defaults and at extremes. Make discrete options like size change the character, not only the length, and make a 'gate' produce a clean, deliberate cutoff rather than a step or a plain decay.

flaws: Defaults do not read as a snare. The envelope is a slow, roughly linear decay over 0.31 s with no sharp transient and no body/crack separation. It looks like a decaying noise burst.
The 'gated noise tail' is not visible. The envelope has no hard cut. Every render fades smoothly with a lingering low-level tail, so it does not sound gated.

The spectrogram is a broadband smear with no snare structure. There is no tonal body around 180-250 Hz with a pitch drop and no distinct snare-wire noise band. The only clear feature is a thin low red line at the bottom.
The waveform is very dense and has a high RMS (0.30 against a 0.9 peak), so it is heavily saturated or compressed. The punch is lost, and the result is a buzzy burst.

The size knob changes length by only 0.27 s to 0.35 s, which is barely different. 'Tight', 'room' and 'hall' do not read as different spaces. A hall snare at 0.35 s is not plausible. The max range render looks like a flat block of noise that ends abruptly at 0.40 s.
The tail toggle makes almost no visible difference (0.31 s in both renders, similar envelope), so it is a weak control.
The centroid of about 3.4 kHz is acceptable for 'bright', but the energy is spread flat across the spectrum. This sounds like white noise rather than a crack.
grades.lesson: Check that the signature feature in the brief (here the gate, and the body-plus-crack structure) is visible in the default render's envelope and spectrogram. Make each knob, especially size and toggles, produce a clearly different render, not a small tweak.

flaws: Waveform has no sharp transient: the envelope is a slow linear decay over about 0.29 s, so it reads as a decaying noise burst rather than a snare crack with a fast attack and body.

There is no visible tonal body or pitch drop. The spectrogram is flat broadband noise with only a thin red line at the very bottom, so there is no drum shell resonance and the result sounds like a noise hit, not a snare.

The brief says 'gated noise tail', but the tail just decays gradually into the end. There is no distinct crack followed by a hard gate cut, so the gate character is missing, and the 'tail=false' render looks almost the same as the default.

The size options (tight/room/hall) mostly change the length (0.22 s to 0.42 s) and give a noisy sustained plateau. They do not suggest a different room or reverb, and hall looks like a longer gated noise burst.

The spectral content stays similar and flat across settings, with a centroid around 2.5-3.4 kHz. The crack knob and the extremes do not make the sound clearly different in timbre. The minimum extreme ends in a low-level wobble or DC-like artifact.
grades.lesson: Check that the picture shows the defining structure of the named sound (a sharp attack, a tonal body with a pitch drop, a distinct gated tail) rather than a generic noise burst with a decay, and make the knobs change those features, not just the duration.

brief: Seatbelt tongue clicking into buckle; knobs: buckle material (plastic/metal), insertion speed 0..1, click brightness 0..1, webbing rustle 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The default has a long pre-roll of noisy scrape/rustle (about 0.3 s) before the click, and the spectrogram shows it as a broad smear. A real buckle insertion is a short slide followed by a sharp click, so the lead-in reads as a wash and makes the sound feel padded.

The main click is a single impact with a ringing tail of discrete low-to-mid tonal lines. It sounds like a generic struck object more than a latching two-part plastic click (a click plus a secondary snap or clack). The metal variant is a clean ring that reads as a small bell or ping, not a buckle.

The 1.1 s default length with about 32% silence is too long for a seatbelt click. The tail trails off into near-nothing for roughly 0.4 s, which makes the file look larger than it is and gives the designer dead air to trim.

Every range at its minimum shifts the click later and shortens the lead-in, and the tail=false render is stranded with the click at the very end of a 0.59 s file, so the sound is almost all pre-click rustle. The result barely reads as a click event. Timing of the click within the file also changes with the knobs, which is awkward to place in a scene.
Material = metal changes mostly the ringing partials, which is a reasonable difference, but the default plastic version is still too resonant to read as plastic.
Webbing rustle has no distinct identity: it sits as a noisy pre-click smear rather than a separate cloth texture, so it is hard to tell it from the insertion scrape.
grades.lesson: Anchor the key transient at a fixed, short offset from the file start and keep optional layers from moving it or padding the file; trim dead lead-in and trailing silence so the sound is tight, and make each layer (scrape, click, rustle) spectrally distinct so the knobs read as separate elements.

flaws: The pre-click rustle/insertion scrape is a diffuse, low-level noise bed. It reads as generic hiss more than webbing or tongue sliding, so the lead-in is weak.
The default plastic render has two transients (the click and a second, slightly smaller one) that look nearly the same. The two-stage latch is plausible, but the second hit looks a bit like an echo.

grades.lesson: When a sound is made from a modulated noise bed, add distinct per-event detail (a pitched or filtered transient, a liquid or resonant component) and check that the material or choice knob changes the resonant character, not only the brightness and level.

brief: Photocopier lid close and scan-bar sweep with light hum; knobs: copier size (compact/full), sweep speed rate, lid slam 0..1, motor hum 0..1, carriage return amount 0..1, tail toggle

grades.lesson: Check that the amplitude envelope matches the physical gesture, not just the spectrum. A slow, sustained gesture such as a creak, groan or swell needs a gradual onset and a stick-slip texture, so do not start it with a full-scale transient that turns it into an impact.

flaws: The waveform is a burst-like amplitude blob, not a groan. A creaking stair should show sustained, pitch-modulated stick-slip resonance with a slow rise and a tonal contour. The spectrogram shows mostly low-band energy with scattered noisy specks and only faint short streaks, so it reads as a generic rumble or noise burst.
The onset is a sharp transient spike at the start, followed by a lumpy second swell. That suggests an impact plus a noise burst, not a tread slowly taking weight, and the 'groan' character is weak.
Energy sits in a low band at the bottom, with a centroid around 1 kHz. There is no clear harmonic or formant structure and no visible gliding pitch, which wooden creaks need.
The tail=false variant cuts off abruptly at about 1.2 s and leaves 40% silence. It reads as a hard truncation, not a natural decay.
Seeds differ in shape more than expected. Seed 3 has a gradual swell and a clear tonal line, while the defaults and seed 2 are spiky and front-loaded, so they do not read as takes of one sound.

The minimum-range render is short and dominated by a single spike with a smeared noisy spectrum, so it loses the groan identity entirely. The size switch changes length and centroid but not the creak character.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a distinctive physical sound (a groan, creak or squeal), build its defining feature, such as a gliding tonal resonance with stick-slip modulation, and verify it is visible in the spectrogram. Do not rely on filtered noise with an envelope, and make sure tail or toggle options end naturally rather than truncating.

flaws: The waveform opens with a sharp, loud transient and then a long, rambling noisy body. A groaning tread should show a slow-building, creaky stick-slip texture with a pitch that wanders. Here the body reads as a rough noise burst with little tonal structure.

The spectrogram shows only faint, scattered pitch lines. There is no clear sliding fundamental or stick-slip pulse train. The energy is mostly a low smear at the bottom, so it reads as a generic wooden thump or rustle more than a groan.
The 'squeal' and 'nail rattle' components are not clearly separable in the renders. They show up as faint blips, so it is unclear that the knobs give distinct, usable layers.
Turning the tail off cuts the sound abruptly at about 1.3 s, leaving 40% silence of dead air. The ending looks chopped instead of faded.
The seeds vary a lot in spectral layout. Seed 3 has a sustained tonal line and seed 1 does not, so the seeds drift toward being different sounds rather than two takes of one.
Minimum ranges give a short, mostly noisy burst with a fairly broad spectrum, which loses the groan character.
grades.lesson: Build the defining characteristic of the sound (here, a gliding, stick-slip tonal creak) as a clearly visible, dominant element in the spectrogram, rather than relying on filtered noise and a loud transient. Make sure every toggle ends with a natural fade, not an abrupt cut.

brief: Two-square-oscillator cowbell; knobs: circuit (808|tr606|cr78), detune 0..1, decay 0..1, bandpass 0..1, pitch 500-900 Hz, tail toggle

flaws: The default envelope has a slow-ish smeared decay with a soft onset, so it reads a little less like a snappy 808 cowbell. The spectrogram shows many horizontal lines, which fits the square-pair partials but sounds slightly metallic-buzzy.

The max-range render is very long and washy, with a broad sustained spectrum and only about 6% silence. It sounds more like a bell or gong than a cowbell, so the decay and bandpass extremes drift in character.
The tr606 circuit is much shorter and dryer than the others (56% silence), while cr78 is much longer (8% silence). The circuit choices are clearly different, but the loudness and length gap is large.
The tail toggle only shortens the sound to 0.36 s. It works, but the sound is not tightly gated and it looks nearly the same apart from length.
grades.lesson: Check that the extreme knob settings still match the target sound's real-world envelope. Cap decay and resonance so that the maximum setting does not turn a short percussive hit into a long wash or gong.

error: build failed: interrupted

brief: Gull flapping off a post; knobs: size (small|large), flap strength 0..1, feather rustle 0..1, rate, tail toggle

errors: knob tail: build failed: interrupted
knobs with no audible effect: tail

flaws: Defaults read as a regular series of broadband noise bursts with a long, even tail. A gull takeoff should be a few hard flaps that start slowly and speed up, then fade as the bird leaves. These bursts are evenly spaced and nearly identical in level, so it sounds more like a machine or helicopter than a bird.

The spectrogram is broadband noise with a low thump at each flap and no real feather detail such as high-frequency swish, flutter or fine texture. The centroid of about 1700 Hz and the flat wash suggest filtered noise, not wings.

Size=large and the minimum-range render are mostly low-frequency thumps with a clear gap between each flap. The minimum render has 32% silence and sounds like isolated, disconnected hits. The maximum render is a dense, continuous noise wash where individual flaps are lost. The extremes do not read as the same event.
The tail=false render cuts off abruptly at about 1.4 s, then the file runs silent to 2.0 s. That is a hard stop, and the silence is padded out to the fixed length.

The flap envelope does not accelerate or build, and there is no wing-clap transient. The 2 s length is fixed, so the rate knob does not change the number of flaps in a natural way, which weakens the takeoff gesture.
The seeds differ only slightly in flap amplitude. They share the same rigid periodic spacing, so they feel like the same loop rather than separate takes with natural timing jitter.
grades.lesson: Model the physical gesture, not just its texture. Give repeated events natural timing and level evolution (acceleration, decay, jitter) instead of a fixed periodic pulse. Make sure each knob extreme still produces recognisable discrete events, and that optional tails fade out smoothly instead of cutting off.

flaws: Each wing flap is a broadband noise burst with energy from the bottom to the top of the spectrogram, so it sounds like a series of thuds or a burst-noise gate. It lacks the airy, feathery texture and the whoosh-and-snap character of a real wing beat.

Large size is simply darker and slower (centroid 1600 Hz). It reads as a heavy thumping or a low-frequency drum pattern, not a bigger bird. The flaps are evenly spaced and decay smoothly like a bouncing ball, and the rustle is barely visible.
The takeoff has no arc. A gull leaving a post should start with a few hard, slow flaps and then accelerate and fade as it flies away. Here the flap rate stays steady and the amplitude simply decays.
At minimum range the flaps are sparse, with 44% silence and long gaps between them. The result reads as isolated thumps, not a bird flapping.
The rustle layer is not audible as a separate continuous texture between flaps, so the 'feather rustle' knob adds little character. At maximum range the flaps merge into a dense noise wash.
Seeds share the same shape, but the flap spacing varies in a way that sounds mechanical.
grades.lesson: For organic, repeating events like flaps, steps or wingbeats, shape each event's spectrum and envelope (attack, noise colour, a distinct body) and add an overall gesture over time (acceleration, fade, a dominant first hit). Do not stamp identical broadband noise bursts at a regular interval with a decay.

flaws: Each wing flap is a broadband noise burst with energy from the bottom to the top of the spectrogram, so it reads as a series of noise puffs or breaths, not wings and feathers. There is no tonal or whoosh character and no airy high-frequency rustle layer.

The default takeoff has no convincing arc. Flaps decay steadily like a bouncing ball, and a real takeoff starts slow and heavy, speeds up, then fades as the bird leaves. The flap spacing does not speed up in a natural way.
At maximum settings the flaps merge into one dense noise wash about 2 s long, with no flap definition left. It sounds like wind or static, not a gull.
At minimum settings the result is sparse, with 50% silence and a few weak, isolated pops, so it no longer reads as a takeoff.
Size = large mostly lowers the pitch and spaces the flaps further apart. The time-domain shape is the same, so it feels like a pitch shift instead of a bigger bird.
The seeds differ noticeably in flap count and spacing, and seed 2 is much denser than the default. They read as slightly different events, not as takes of one sound.
The tail toggle only shortens the sound by about 0.7 s. It is a crude cut, not a distinct natural decay.
grades.lesson: Layer a sound by its physical components (impact or body, airy texture, motion arc) and check that each knob extreme keeps the event's identifiable structure, instead of collapsing into generic broadband noise bursts.

brief: Mouse sliding across a desk surface; knobs: surface (mouse pad/laminate/glass), speed rate, friction grit 0..1, cable drag 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Default envelope is a symmetric swell-and-fade lasting about 0.7 s, then a gap with a small isolated click-like blip at the end. A mouse drag should be a steady, friction-driven noise bed that follows the hand's speed. This reads as a generic noise burst, not a sliding object.

The end-of-sound blip with silence before it (about 29% silence) looks like an unrelated artifact, not a natural lift-off or cable tick. It makes the sound feel stitched together, and the tail-off option shows the sound is better without it.

Surface variants differ mostly through a few narrow horizontal tonal lines (glass, laminate), which read as whistling or resonant ringing, not a surface texture. Glass and laminate look like pitched hum over noise, not smooth scraping.

Maximum range collapses to 0.71 s with 40% silence and looks like a short crunchy burst, a different kind of event from the 1.6 s steady noise at minimum. Speed changes the length radically, so it is a duration control more than a speed control.

The spectrum is dominated by low-frequency noise (centroid about 590 Hz). A plastic mouse on a desk should have more mid and high scrape content. The default sounds muffled and more like wind or a rumble than friction.
Seeds share the same overall shape but have different loudness (rms 0.137 to 0.192), so the takes feel uneven in level.
grades.lesson: For continuous-contact sounds (sliding, scraping, rolling), build a steady friction texture that follows a gesture, and do not use a one-shot swell envelope. Make speed change pitch and brightness, not just duration, and avoid end artifacts that sit apart from the body of the sound.

flaws: Every render, including defaults, both surface extremes, min and max ranges, and tail off, shows the same broadband noise burst with a centroid of roughly 3.5-4.2 kHz. The spectrogram is a flat, uniform wash with no visible texture, so a mouse pad does not read differently from glass.

The surface choice moves the centroid by only about 700 Hz. A soft mouse pad should be dull and low, and glass should be bright and squeaky. These need to be clearly different sounds, but here they are close to one noise with a slight tilt.

The speed and grit extremes change the envelope slightly (one hump, two humps, three humps) but not the character. A fast swipe should be brighter and louder, and a slow drag should be quieter and grainier. The min and max renders are all still 1.30 s, so speed does not change duration or pacing.

A real mouse slide is a stroke-based, quasi-periodic scrape with micro-stick-slip grit, but here the spectrum is static noise. The cable-drag component has no distinct visible signature, such as low thumps or rubbing, so it cannot be heard as a separate layer.
The waveform is a dense, fat envelope with a roughly 9% silent tail. Spectrally the sound reads as generic filtered noise or a wind or air whoosh rather than a hard plastic object on a desk.
The tail toggle only removes the fade-out, 1.30 s to 1.15 s. It is a minor knob that adds little, and the sound with the tail off ends abruptly.
grades.lesson: Make each categorical choice (such as surface or material) change the spectral shape and texture, not just a filter cutoff, and check that your render extremes look visibly different in the spectrogram, not merely numerically different.

flaws: The tail is a single sharp click/thump at the end. It reads as a mouse being set down rather than a drag tail, and it is the loudest event in the render, which is odd for a slide.
The default is two slide strokes with large silent gaps (14% silence). That is plausible for a mouse being repositioned, but it is not a continuous drag.
At the minimum range setting the drag almost vanishes into a faint low-level hiss followed by the end thump. It reads as a different sound and is mostly the thump.
The surface choice is clear (mouse pad is low and warm, glass is bright at 2840 Hz), but laminate is not shown, so I can't tell whether it sits distinctly between the two.
The slide texture is plain broadband noise with little stick-slip detail, so it sounds more like a generic swish than a mouse on a desk.
grades.lesson: Make the signature event of a sound proportionate to the main body of the sound. A tail or end event that is the loudest thing in the render makes the result read as something else, so check that the extremes of the range still sound like the same thing.

brief: Loose shutter knocking repeatedly in gusts; knobs: material (wood|tin), gust strength 0..1, irregularity 0..1, knock rate, tail toggle

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.85); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: The tin material reads more like a sustained, swelling tone burst than a metallic knock. The envelopes are slow with long sustained ringing, so it sounds like a bell or hum and not a loose shutter rattling.
The minimum-range render is mostly one big knock followed by near-silence (19% silence), so it works poorly as a repeated knocking loop. The 'repeatedly in gusts' brief isn't met at that extreme.
At the default setting the knocks are sparse and decay fast, so the gust structure is not very obvious. Gusts show up as spacing and amplitude changes rather than a clear swell.
With the tail off, the knocks are isolated clicks with dead air between them, which sounds mechanical and sparse.
grades.lesson: Make sure each material or mode choice keeps the same event type (an impact stays an impact, with a fast attack and decay), and check that range minimums still deliver the repeated or continuous behaviour the brief describes, not a single event followed by silence.

brief: Window shutter blown shut against the wall; knobs: material (wood|tin), force 0..1, bounce 0..1, glass shiver 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The 'silence 45%' figure is mostly the fixed 1.8 s render tail, which is empty after about 0.8 s. The default sound is a short slam followed by dead space, so it is not a real tail.
The default wood render shows a quick decay with a low-heavy centroid. It reads as a single thud with weak evidence of distinct bounces, so the bounce rhythm is hard to see.
The tail=false variant cuts the length to 1.1 s and the spectrogram shows blocky, sparse content. It works but sounds thin.
The tin variant is a clear step brighter and more ringing, which is good. The glass shiver is faint in the spectrogram at the minimum setting.
grades.lesson: Make the render length follow the sound's actual decay, so the file does not end in a long stretch of digital silence. Make rhythmic events such as bounces clearly visible as separate transients at default settings.

brief: Bright clave ping from resonant filter; knobs: material (rosewood|plastic|metal), pitch 0..1, decay 0..1, brightness 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: meta.duration 0.5s but the default render is 0.24s
knobs with a subtle effect: brightness

flaws: The metal setting shows a visible beating or amplitude modulation, which sounds more like a bell or a detuned pair than a clave. It is not a real clave, but it is a usable metallic ping.

At minimum range the sound is only 0.13 s, with a centroid of 993 Hz and a smeared low-frequency transient. It reads more like a dull thud than a bright ping, so it loses the brief's 'bright' quality.
The tail toggle adds a diffuse noisy wash across the whole spectrogram. It sounds more like generic room noise than a natural resonance of the block.
The default 0.24 s decay is slightly long for a dry rosewood clave, which is usually under 0.15 s. The plastic setting is closer to the right length.
The spectrogram shows only a few narrow horizontal lines, so the sound is quite pure and tonal, with little of the woody click transient at the onset.
grades.lesson: Check that the extremes of every range knob still meet the brief's defining quality (for example 'bright'), not just that they stay audible. Add a short noise or click transient at the onset so percussive sounds read as an impact rather than a bare resonant tone.

brief: Tuned percussion one-shot (zap/marimba-ish); knobs: wave (sine|triangle|fm), pitch 0..1, decay 0..1, pitch-env 0..1, resonance 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Every render is exactly 0.70 s with a long exponential decay, so it reads as a pitch-dropping zap or kick-like thump rather than a marimba-ish tuned strike. A marimba has a sharp, woody attack with a clear stable pitch, and the spectrogram instead shows a prominent falling pitch line.
The decay does not change the length. Min and max renders are both 0.70 s, so the sound cannot be a short blip or a long ring. The title says 'Blip' but the default tail is long and washy.
Minimum range settings give a very low, dull, buzzy thud with a centroid of 501 Hz. It does not read as tuned percussion and would be of little use to a designer.
Maximum range settings give a noisy, broadband wash with a long, near-constant-amplitude envelope. The pitch sweep dominates and the tonal identity is lost, so it sounds like a different sound.

The tail toggle works, but with tail off the sound dies by about 60% of the render and leaves 22% silence, a trailing dead zone. With tail on, the tail looks like noise or sustain rather than natural resonance.
The wave choice changes timbre, but fm is much noisier and brighter, with a broad smear across the spectrum. It is not a clean marimba-like option.
The seeds are very similar. This is acceptable, but it suggests the random variation is mostly noise detail rather than musically useful pitch or timbre variation.
grades.lesson: Make sure the length and envelope respond to the decay knob and that the sound's defining features (a stable pitch and a sharp attack for tuned percussion) survive at both range extremes; a sound whose extremes become an unrelated thud or noise wash is not a usable instrument.

flaws: Default render is a plain decaying sine at about 100-200 Hz: one fundamental line with almost no attack transient and no mallet click, so it reads as a generic sine blip rather than a marimba or zap.

Spectral centroid of 462 Hz is low for a tuned percussion hit, which would normally have a bright strike and inharmonic partials. Triangle and fm add only faint overtones, so the three waves sound very similar.
Seeds 1, 2 and 3 are nearly identical in waveform, spectrogram and centroid (454-470 Hz). Seed barely changes anything, so takes would not feel like separate hits.
The pitch-env drop is not visible as a falling line in the defaults, so the 'zap' character is weak at default settings.
Range minimum gives a 0.21 s thud with centroid 211 Hz, which is more of a low tick than tuned percussion. Maximum gives a 1.49 s pure sine ring, which is long and sterile for a one-shot.
The tail toggle makes a noisy, smeared low-frequency decay unlike the clean tonal body, so it sounds like a different sound rather than a reverb tail.
grades.lesson: A one-shot needs a distinct attack and a spectrum that identifies the instrument. A single decaying sine is not enough, so add a transient click and inharmonic partials. Make the seed vary details such as partial ratios, strike noise and detune so takes differ audibly while keeping the same overall shape.

flaws: Default envelope is a plain exponential decay on a steady tone with a very low fundamental (roughly 100-200 Hz in the spectrogram). It reads as a generic sine blip, not marimba or zap. There is no bright, fast-decaying strike transient and no inharmonic partials.
The partials are sparse, faint horizontal lines that stop abruptly at about 1/3 of the duration. They sound like static overtones that cut off rather than a natural higher-mode decay.

The pitch-env knob at default is barely visible. A zap needs an obvious falling pitch line, but it only appears at the maximum extreme, where the fundamental sweeps down and the sound reads as a different kind of sound (a kick-like thump).

The min extreme (0.23 s, centroid 285 Hz) is a dull low thud and the max (0.83 s, centroid 2922 Hz) is a long ringing tone. They span too much of the sound's character, so these extremes are not the same instrument.

The tail toggle adds a noisy low-frequency smear and drops the signal to about 27% silence. It sounds like a separate noise burst glued on, not a resonant body tail, and it changes the envelope shape noticeably.
The wave choices differ only slightly in the picture. Sine, triangle and fm have nearly identical envelopes and a similar low-frequency-dominated spectrum, so the choice is weak as a timbre control.
The seeds differ mainly in a few faint upper partials and the centroid. The variation is real but very subtle, with no change in pitch or attack character between takes.
grades.lesson: Make the signature trait of the brief clearly visible at default settings (e.g. a strike transient, inharmonic partials, a pitch sweep). Keep the knob extremes within the same instrument, so a sweep does not turn the sound into a different one.

brief: Desk telephone ringing pattern; knobs: phone type (digital VoIP/analog bell/conference speaker), ring pitch, ring count rate, volume 0..1, distance 0..1, room tail toggle

errors: knob rate: build failed: interrupted

flaws: Default analog-bell ring reads as three dense, buzzy noise-like blocks with a hard cut-off at the start and end. It lacks the bell-strike transients and resonant decay of a real desk phone, so it sounds more like a tone burst or buzzer.

Three rings fill the 3 s render and the last one is cut off at the end of the file. With no clean tail, the loop or placement point is awkward. The room-off render has no decay at all, so the rings are hard-gated rectangular blocks.

Digital VoIP and conference speaker types use nearly the same block-gated envelope and differ mainly in spectral tilt. They read as the same tone burst with different EQ, not three distinct phone types. The conference type is dull and sparse, with a low centroid of 799 Hz.

The minimum-range render drops to two short rings with 25% silence and a hard, abrupt cutoff. The maximum-range render changes the envelope to rounded swells that sound like a different sound. The extremes are inconsistent.
Seeds are only slightly different. The ring blocks are identical in timing and only the fine texture changes, so they sound like the same take.
Knobs are generic: 'ring count rate' is ambiguous, and there is no control for ring cadence (on/off timing) or bell brightness or strike character.
grades.lesson: Model the physical source of a sound, such as the strike and resonant decay of a bell, instead of gating a tone or noise with a rectangular envelope. Make each variant type differ in its excitation and envelope, not only its EQ, and let tails ring out rather than cutting off at the file end.

flaws: The default render is two soft swells with a rounded attack and decay. A desk phone ring is a sharply gated, repeating pattern, usually a double-burst with a clear gap. The smooth swells sound more like a pad or a siren than a bell or electronic ringer.

The default and seed renders show only two rings in 3 s, with a long dead tail of roughly 15-18% silence. That does not read as a repeating ring cadence, and a loopable ring would need at least 3 cycles.

The analog bell type is not clearly an analog bell. The spectrogram shows a few narrow horizontal lines and no strike transient or metallic inharmonic partials. The conference speaker type reads as two decaying clangs with 39% silence, which is a different kind of sound from the other two types and not a phone ring cadence.

The three phone types do not share one ring pattern. VoIP is a gated tone, the speaker is a decaying clang, and the default is a smooth swell. This makes the type switch feel like three unrelated sounds.

Seed variation is mostly pitch and centroid drift (1344 vs 1696 Hz) with the same two-swell layout. Seeds shift the timbre without changing the performance, so they read as slight retunes rather than different takes.
Range extremes change the ring count from 2 to 3 swells with near-continuous overlap at max (4% silence). The maximum rate loses the gaps that define a ring pattern, so it reads as a warble.
The room tail toggle has little visible effect (29% silence vs 15% at default). It is unclear that it adds a reverb tail, and the render looks truncated rather than ringing out.
grades.lesson: Make the temporal pattern the first thing you check against the brief. Cadence, gating and attack shape define sounds like rings, alarms and footsteps, so give every variant of the sound the same crisp, recognisable pattern and vary only timbre, and keep gaps audible at the extremes of the rate knob.

flaws: The default render does not read as a desk phone ring. It is two soft, rounded, swelling bursts in about 3 s, with a long fade on the second. A real ring is a hard-gated burst of a double-ring cadence, and the swelling envelope sounds more like a pad or a breath.

The analog-bell type (the default) has no visible bell character. There is no sharp strike transient, no inharmonic metallic partials, and no clapper-rattle amplitude modulation. It is just a smooth, roughly tonal burst, so the type doesn't deliver the classic brrring-brrring.

The default and the VoIP type are very different in envelope, yet both are meant to be phones. The VoIP type has hard-gated blocks, which is plausible for a digital ring, but it still looks like a plain gated tone with no warble or melodic structure.

The conference speaker type is a single-pulse, heavily decaying ping with 39% silence. It reads more like a notification chime than a ringing conference phone, and it shows little resemblance to the other types.

At maximum range the ring count rate gives three overlapping swells with almost no gaps (4% silence). The pattern blurs into a continuous drone rather than distinct rings, so the extreme loses the ringing identity.
The room tail toggle only slightly changes the look of the render. The 'false' version cuts off cleanly, but the benefit is small relative to the knob's presence.

Seed variation is mostly in the amplitude envelope shape and the centroid (1344 vs 1696 Hz). The takes are close to the same pattern but the spectral character shifts noticeably, which is a little more than just detail.
grades.lesson: Make the signature of the real object the primary design target, not a generic tone with an envelope. Build in the characteristic transient, cadence gating and timbre (for a phone: hard-gated rings, metallic or warbled tones). Then check that every type and range extreme keeps that signature, so the sound still reads as the named thing.

brief: Handset lifted off or set back on cradle with hook-switch clack; knobs: action (pickup/hangup/slam), plastic weight (light/heavy), force 0..1, cord rattle 0..1, dial tone amount 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: meta.duration 1.2s but the default render is 2.05s

flaws: The default (pickup) has a 2.05 s tail with a sustained dial-tone line at about 400 Hz. This is a long, loud-ish drone for a handset clack, and it leaves the transient feeling like a small part of the file.
With the tail off, the dial tone becomes a hard-edged flat bar that starts late and stops abruptly. It looks like a gated tone rather than a natural decay, so it would sound unnatural in a scene.
The maximum-range render is dominated by the sustained tone and a swelling rattle. It reads more like a tone with a clack than a handset clack, and it is far from the minimum render.
Hangup and slam are quite similar: both are short decaying clacks with 56-60% silence. Slam does not look much heavier or more violent than hangup.
Seeds keep the same shape, but peak level varies noticeably (0.84, 0.74, 0.72). The secondary transient position also shifts. This is acceptable variation.
grades.lesson: Make sustained elements such as tones and ambient layers optional or low by default, and give them a natural fade-in and fade-out at every setting, so the signature transient stays the main event and no setting produces a gated bar.

brief: Single drip from a rusty tap into a basin; knobs: basin (porcelain|metal|puddle), drop size 0..1, resonance 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: A single drip should be a short, sharp plink with a rising bubble-like pitch glide, then silence. The default is a 1.30 s decaying wash with a long noisy tail and 25% silence, which sounds more like a struck object or a noise burst than one water drop.

The spectrogram shows broadband noise smeared across the low-mid band for the whole length, plus static horizontal lines (fixed resonances). There is no visible rising chirp from the bubble, which is the defining feature of a drip.
The puddle basin has a sharp transient followed by a thin noise bed. It reads as a click and a hiss, not a water-in-water plop.

The tail toggle only cuts the length to 0.75 s and leaves the sound essentially the same shape. At 0.75 s the waveform is still a long decay and 62% silence. The tail=false version is the one closer to a drip, which suggests the default is over-long.

The metal basin has a hard, stable ring that is plausible, but it sounds like a generic struck-metal tone rather than a drip into a basin. The porcelain default and the metal option are not clearly distinct in the spectrogram.

The knobs are fine in concept (drop size, resonance, pitch), but the 'rusty' character from the title has no control. The default length is wrong for a single event, so the drip body and the tail are not independently adjustable.
grades.lesson: Before tuning knobs, check that the default render shows the signature feature of the named event (for a drip, a short rising-pitch plink then silence, not a long decaying noise wash). Make the default's length and envelope match the real event, and make toggles such as tail change the character rather than just trimming length.

flaws: The default is a sharp transient with a short ring and a faint secondary blip. That reads as a drip, but the 0.9 s file is about 40% silence with a very faint tail, so it is slightly sparse.

The basin=metal render is a sustained ring of near-static horizontal partials. It sounds more like a struck bowl or bell than a drip into a metal basin, and the characteristic pitch-up 'bloop' of a drip is weak.
The 'puddle' basin looks nearly the same as the default (similar decay, a downward-sweeping line, similar noise tail), so the three basin choices are not equally distinct.
With tail=false the file is cut to 0.5 s, and the rendered envelope has an odd secondary bump near the end. Switching the toggle changes the length and also the character.
The secondary blip at minimum range is an isolated spike after the main hit and looks like a stray click rather than a natural secondary drip.
The noise wash in the tail is broadband and mushy, which does not suggest rust or a resonant basin.
grades.lesson: When a categorical choice (material, surface) is meant to change the sound's character, make each option clearly different in the spectrogram. Check that none reads as the wrong object, such as a bell instead of a drip, or as a near-duplicate of another option.

brief: Merchant unrolling a bolt of fabric across a stall. Knobs: fabric (linen/wool/silk), length 0..1, snap force 0..1, rustle density 0..1, tail toggle.

flaws: The unroll is a series of 6-7 evenly spaced bursts, each a vertical stripe in the spectrogram. It reads as a rhythmic ratchet or machine-gun pattern, not continuous cloth friction sliding across a table. Real unrolling would have a continuous rustle bed with irregular small events.

The final snap is a loud broadband thud with a low pink-red blob at the bottom, so it sounds like a door slam or a drum hit, not a cloth flap. It is far louder than the preceding rustle, and the 'snap' dominates the sound.

Silk is a different sound from linen and wool. Its rustle is very sparse and quiet, and its snap has a long ringing tonal decay (~0.6 s) with a different envelope. It could be mistaken for a different event.
The 'tail = false' option leaves 35% silence and just clips the decay, with a faint trailing tick. This is a minor effect that does not justify a toggle.
At minimum length the pattern changes: the snap comes mid-sound and is followed by a long decay of noise, so the structure (rustle then snap) is inconsistent across the range.
Seed variation is mostly the same burst timing with different amplitudes. The regular spacing stays identical across seeds, so the takes feel like one rigid template.
grades.lesson: For continuous, organic friction sounds, build a continuous noise bed and modulate it with irregular, randomised event timing. Evenly spaced bursts read as a mechanical rhythm, and a single loud accent should be kept in proportion to the body of the sound.

flaws: The spectrogram is a flat, broadband noise wash with almost no spectral movement. It reads as generic noise bursts rather than cloth, with no fibre texture, friction detail or distinct unrolling pulses.
The 'snap' at the end is a thin vertical line with a weak transient. It reads as a click artifact rather than a fabric flick.

Silk has a centroid of about 4.4 kHz and the default about 3.9 kHz, so it sounds hissy and white-noise-like. Linen and silk are close to each other, so the fabric choice is only a modest tonal change.
The 'tail = false' render ends with a hard-ish fade and a very different envelope, with no snap and no decay. This is a bigger change than a tail toggle should make.
At minimum settings the sound turns into a single swell with a sparse, ragged tail, and the tail gaps have isolated blips. That reads as less like unrolling and more like random noise events.
