The seeds are similar in length and spectrum, but the amplitude envelope varies a lot, so some takes feel unrelated, such as a mid-swell versus a front-loaded burst. There are also stray small blips in the tails.
grades.lesson: Make a sound's identity come from structured texture and distinct events, such as friction grain, pulse timing and a real transient. Broadband noise shaped by an amplitude envelope alone reads as a generic whoosh, so check that the spectrogram shows more than a flat wash.

flaws: Default render is a dense, flat, full-band noise block (centroid ~3.6 kHz) that is nearly constant for ~1.5 s. It reads as a noise burst or white-noise wash, not fabric being drawn off a bolt. Real unrolling has discrete friction pulses, fibre crackle and speed-driven variation in rustle.

The 'snap' is a single vertical line followed by a quiet tail. It looks like a click or gate cut, not a cloth flick. The tail after it is a short decaying noise wash that sounds like reverb, not cloth settling.

Fabric choices differ mainly in spectral tilt (wool 1.1 kHz, silk 4.5 kHz). Silk is a very flat bright hiss and wool looks like muffled noise. Neither has a distinct texture (grain, crispness, scrunch), so they read as filtered noise rather than different fabrics.

The spectrogram is a uniform noise carpet with almost no transient or grain structure at default or at max length. The rustle looks like slow amplitude modulation on noise rather than individual fibre or fold events.

At minimum length the unroll and snap are fine, but the body is still a continuous, abruptly cut noise block. The cut just before the snap is very hard, so the end of the unroll looks truncated rather than naturally finishing.
grades.lesson: For textured, friction-type sounds, build the texture from discrete micro-events with their own spectra and timing (grains, scrapes, crackles) rather than amplitude-modulated, filtered noise. A smooth noise bed with a bandwidth change will read as a hiss no matter how many material presets sit on top of it.

brief: Leather bellows pumping air into a forge, with an ember flare. Knobs: bellows size (small/large), pump rate, airflow 0..1, leather creak 0..1, fire roar 0..1, tail toggle.

flaws: Defaults read as a generic band-limited noise swell repeated about 4 times, not leather bellows. There is no distinct inhale/exhale asymmetry, no valve flap, and no air-puff transient.
The ember flare from the brief is not visible. There are no crackle or spark transients above the noise and no distinct flare event.
Leather creak is not visible in the spectrogram. I see no tonal or stick-slip creak components, only broadband noise, so the knob's character is unclear.
The pump modulation is shallow at defaults. The troughs never drop far, so it reads as wobbling wind or a surf-like roar more than discrete pumps.

At minimum range the sound turns into sparse isolated blobs with 14% silence and a different, brighter centroid (1862 Hz), one hard-onset first pump and then soft ones. It no longer reads as a continuous forge. The maximum is a fast, dense, uniform ripple with no clear pump articulation.
The tail toggle makes almost no visible difference (the render looks near-identical to the default), so it is a weak knob.
The large size has weaker pump contrast than the default, and its envelope is less distinct, so the size choice does not clearly change the character.
grades.lesson: Make the signature events of the brief (e.g., valve flaps, puffs, crackles, creaks) visible as distinct features in the render, not just a modulated noise bed. Check each knob has a clear visible effect, and that range extremes keep the same event structure rather than turning into a different texture.

flaws: Defaults read as a handful of noise bursts, not as bellows. Each pump has a sharp percussive attack at the start, like a thump or clap. Real bellows have a soft push of air (a swell) and a separate intake phase, and neither is visible here.

The spectrogram is broadband noise with a centroid near 1.2 kHz, and there is no clear fire or ember character. The fire roar and ember flare are not recognisable as low rumble plus crackle, so the brief's ember flare is essentially missing.
The pump rhythm is irregular and weak at defaults, with 3-4 uneven bursts across the 3.8 s and a long decaying tail. It reads as scattered impacts, not a pumping cycle.

The 'every range at maximum' render collapses into one smooth swell with no distinct pumps, so the pump rhythm is lost and it no longer reads as bellows. The minimum render has only two sparse bursts. The extremes read as different sounds.

The 'tail = false' render has distinct sharp spikes with gaps of near-silence between them and a very different feel from the default. A toggle should only remove the tail, not change the character of the pumps.
The leather creak has no visible tonal or resonant content in the spectrogram. It is not distinguishable from the noise, so that knob likely does little a designer could hear as creak.
The 'size' choice changes the pump count and rhythm more than it changes the sound's weight or pitch. The centroid barely moves (1250 vs 1227 Hz), so large does not sound bigger.
grades.lesson: Model the physical cycle of the source (for bellows: soft push swell, then intake, then sustained fire bed) with clear envelopes, and check that each knob and toggle changes only its own attribute, so extremes and toggles keep the sound's identity.

flaws: Bellows pumps do not read as distinct air gestures. Each pump is a sharp broadband transient with a decay, closer to a thump or impact than a whoosh with a inhale/exhale shape. There is no visible airy push/pull envelope.

The spectrogram is a uniform broadband noise wash with energy concentrated in a thin low band. The centroid sits around 1.2 kHz with no clear tonal or filtered movement. This sounds like generic noise bursts, not leather and air, and the ember flare or fire roar is not distinguishable.
Max-range extreme loses the pump structure entirely. It becomes one swelling noise blob with no discrete pumps, so it no longer reads as bellows, and it differs in kind from the default.

Pump spacing is irregular at default and in the large size. The large size shows only 2 big events versus 4 at default, so it changes the rhythm rather than just the scale. The no-tail version has abrupt gaps between pumps that make it sound choppy.
The sharp transient spikes make the sound feel like a series of impacts or clicks rather than sustained airflow, and the 3.8 s tail fades to nothing rather than into a forge fire bed.
Seeds are similar in overall shape, but the loudness and pump placement vary enough that one take is not clearly the same rhythm as another. Seed 3 has 10% silence.
grades.lesson: Check that the dominant envelope of each event matches the physical gesture of the source (for example, a soft air push rather than a sharp transient), and that range extremes keep the sound's defining structure, not just change its loudness or density.

brief: Loopable 3s engine idle heard from inside sealed cabin; knobs: engine size (4cyl/V6/V8), rpm wobble 0..1, firewall muffling 0..1, seat vibration rumble 0..1, pitch

flaws: Spectrogram is nearly all energy in a thin low band with almost nothing above it. It reads as a pulse train or low buzz rather than a layered cabin idle with firing-order harmonics and muffled mid content.
The waveform is a dense, uniform comb of spikes. The amplitude is too regular for a real idle, so it sounds synthetic and mechanical.
Engine size choice barely changes the picture: 4cyl, V8 and default all look like the same comb at 100-126 Hz centroid. The V8 does not read as a lumpier, lower, more irregular idle.

Minimum range extreme looks like a perfectly regular, almost sinusoidal pulse train with a higher 145 Hz centroid. It sounds like a machine buzz, not an engine. The maximum is a different texture with a flatter, noisier envelope. The extremes do not read as one sound family.
Seeds differ mostly in RMS and envelope wobble, with the same underlying comb. They are acceptable as takes but have little character variation.
No visible loop-point or crossfade evidence; the brief requires loopability. The knob list is also truncated and the pitch knob's range is unclear.
grades.lesson: Make every discrete choice and range extreme change the spectral and temporal structure that defines it, not just a few Hz of centroid. Check that the picture shows a layered texture (harmonics, body, noise) rather than one repeated pulse pattern, and that the minimum setting is still a believable instance of the sound rather than a mechanical, over-regular buzz.

flaws: Every render is a nearly identical dense low-frequency pulse train. The spectrogram is only a bottom band with no visible harmonic structure, so it does not read clearly as an engine idle and sounds like a generic buzz.
Engine-size choice is weak. 4cyl, V8 and default differ mostly in pulse spacing and a small centroid shift (100 vs 126 Hz). They are not clearly different sounds, and the V6 option was never shown.

The all-minimum render is a rigid, perfectly regular pulse train with no wobble or variation, so it reads as a mechanical tone or buzzer rather than an engine. The all-maximum render turns to noisy mush with the centroid dropping to 86 Hz. Neither extreme is a usable sound.

The firewall muffling and rumble knobs show almost no change in the spectrogram, which stays low and narrow. The sound lacks mid-frequency combustion detail that muffling would have something to remove.
Loopability is not evidenced. No crossfade or seam is shown, and a 3 s loop with a periodic pulse train needs a whole number of cycles to avoid a click.
Seed variation is mostly a change in RMS (0.221 to 0.247) with the same envelope shape. That is acceptable but subtle.
grades.lesson: Make the sound's defining character visible in the spectrogram (harmonic stack, formants, or transient structure). Check that the categorical choices and the extremes of the knobs still sound like different, usable variants and not the same texture with a small shift in centroid.

flaws: Range is weak. At both extremes the render is a dense, flat rumble band under about 300 Hz with centroid between 116 and 191 Hz. Minimum and maximum look nearly the same, and the three engine types differ only slightly in centroid (207, 171, 148 Hz). A designer would struggle to tell 4cyl from V8 by ear.

The waveform is a constant-amplitude block with almost no slow amplitude movement, so it reads as steady filtered noise. A real idle has a visible firing-order pulse and uneven combustion, which here is only faintly suggested by vertical striations in the spectrogram.

The V8 and maximum-range spectrograms show a thin band of energy at the very bottom and little else. Harmonic structure is not visible, so the firing-rate fundamental and its overtones do not come through, and the sound has little character.

The knob list is cut off in the brief (the pitch knob is incomplete). 'Engine size' is a discrete choice that shifts the centroid only a little, so it does not behave like a clear identity switch. The rumble, muffling and wobble knobs have effects that look subtle at their extremes.
Loopability is not demonstrated. The waveform ends at the same level it starts, but the seeds show slight envelope drift, and nothing confirms a seamless loop point.
grades.lesson: Make each choice and range knob produce a clearly visible, audibly distinct change in the spectrogram (shifted harmonics, different pulse rate, different bandwidth). Check that the extremes do not collapse into the same texture, and that the sound's defining structure, such as the periodic pulse of an engine, is visible and not smeared into noise.

brief: Mechanical step-button press on drum machine panel; knobs: switch (rubber|tact|clicky), force 0..1, release-click 0..1, room 0..1

errors: knob room: 81% of the buffer is silent

flaws: The default is 0.30 s, and the tail is long for a button press. A drum-machine step button is usually 0.05-0.15 s, so this reads like a thunk with a room tail rather than a tight tactile click.

The press and release transients are two separate events with a visible gap. The release comes about 0.1-0.15 s after the press, which is longer than a real button's travel, so it sounds like two separate hits.
The 'maximum' range extreme smears the two clicks into a noisy wash. The release transient is lost and the result reads as a short noise burst rather than a button press.
The rubber and clicky switches differ mostly in brightness (362 Hz vs 1985 Hz). The spectrograms look broadly similar, so the character difference is less distinct than it could be.
The brief's 'room' knob is blended in the same way as the others, so reverb tail length pushes the sound toward 0.5 s, which is too long for a UI-style sound.
grades.lesson: Anchor a sound's duration and event timing to the real physical object (for example, a button's travel time) and keep range extremes from stretching it into a different kind of sound. Separate ambience or tail controls from the core transient so the main event stays tight.

brief: Coiled rope dropped onto a dock; knobs: surface (wood-plank|stone|steel-deck), weight 0..1, slither 0..1, wetness 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Defaults read as a generic noise burst with a slow decay, not a rope coil landing. There is no distinct initial thump followed by softer secondary slithering and settling, so the 'coiled rope' character is missing.

Steel-deck is a wash: a long, dense, almost constant-level body with 3% silence and a sustained low band. It reads as a rumble or sustained noise bed rather than rope on metal, with no ringing or metallic resonance to separate it from wood.

The tail=false render is an unconvincing take. It is 0.8 s with a flat, choppy, noisy body and no clear impact, and it ends on residual energy rather than a clean cutoff. It does not read as the same event minus its tail.

The minimum extreme has a strong low-frequency band and a centroid of 517 Hz, which sounds like a muddy thud. The maximum extreme is a long, dense wash. Neither shows the rope-coil structure, so the range is more a change in noise density than a change in the event.
A persistent horizontal low-frequency line sits in every spectrogram. It suggests a fixed tonal or rumble component that sounds artificial for a rope.
Seeds look like the same noise burst with a different envelope shape. The variation is acceptable but is not clearly different rope-landing detail such as individual coil slaps.
grades.lesson: Build the structure of the physical event, such as a distinct impact followed by discrete secondary contacts and a decay, rather than shaping a single noise burst with an envelope. Make sure each categorical option changes the resonance and spectral character, not just the level or brightness.

flaws: Rope coil drop should be a soft, dull, low-energy thud followed by a short rustle/slither. The renders show a loud, dense, noisy burst with peak 0.88 and a long 1.2 s decaying wash, so it reads more like gravel or a generic noise impact than a floppy rope.

The waveform at defaults has no clear initial transient followed by quieter settling. It is a sustained noisy blob with a few random spikes, so the rope landing and the slither afterwards are not distinguishable.

The steel-deck render has strong horizontal tonal lines, which read as a ringing resonance. A rope on metal would give a clank or ring from the deck, but here the ring is sustained and gives a synthetic, pitched sound that does not match a soft rope.

Stone and steel-deck differ mostly in level and brightness. The stone render is quieter and sparser, and the steel one is a ringing tone, so the surfaces do not feel like the same rope on three materials.

Seeds differ in structure, not just detail. Seed 3 has a distinct second hit near 0.6 s and seed 2 has none, and the tail=false render has several scattered spikes. These read as different events, not two takes of one drop.
The tail toggle is confusing: with tail off the render still has several late discrete impacts, and its silence drops to 9%, so it does not behave as 'no tail'.
Every peak sits at 0.88 regardless of weight, wetness or surface. Level is normalised, so a light coil and a heavy coil do not differ in loudness, and the knobs cannot convey weight.
grades.lesson: Before normalising, check that the sound's defining character (a soft, dull landing with a sparse secondary rustle, say) is visible in the picture. Make sure each knob changes one perceptual thing, and that toggles like 'tail' remove what they claim to remove.

flaws: Defaults read as a generic low-mid thump with a few separated bursts, not a rope coil. There is no clear slither or rustle texture, and the cluster of low-frequency impacts looks more like a footstep or box drop than coiled rope landing.
The default centroid of 365 Hz is very dark for rope on planks. Rope slap and slither should have noticeable mid and high content, and the spectrogram is dominated by energy below about 500 Hz.

The surface choices do not differ enough. Wood, stone and steel-deck all share the same envelope and burst layout, and only the centroid and decay shift slightly. Steel-deck has no metallic ring and stone has no hard, bright crack.

At maximum the sound turns into a long, scattered sequence of separate hits with a hiss section at the end. It reads as several unrelated events, not one coil settling, and it is 1.4 s with obvious gaps. At minimum it is a short thud with little rope character.
With tail=false the sound ends with an isolated late burst. The tail toggle seems to change the event structure and not simply remove a decay, which is confusing.

The seeds are the same shape but the amplitude envelope differs noticeably from the default. Seed 2 and seed 3 have different RMS (0.106 and 0.125) from the default (0.079), so the loudness consistency between takes is weak.
The 38% silence at defaults is mostly the tail decaying to nothing, so the effective sound is shorter than the 1.25 s stated length.
grades.lesson: Check that the spectrum and texture carry the identity of the source (for example the rustle or ring), not only the timing of impacts. Make each categorical option (such as surface) change the spectral character and resonance, not merely the centroid and decay, so the choices are clearly distinguishable by ear.

brief: Smartphone buzzing against a desk; knobs: surface (wood/laminate/metal), buzz pattern rate, rattle amount 0..1, drift slide 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The buzz bursts are broad noisy blocks with a flat-topped envelope and nearly identical spacing. A real phone vibration has a steady motor fundamental at about 150-250 Hz with amplitude modulation, and this reads closer to gated noise.

Energy is concentrated in the bottom band and the upper spectrum is washy noise. There is little of the hard percussive contact of a phone hitting a desk, so the surface differences are subtle except for metal.
The minimum-range render collapses to 3 wide, dull bursts with a centroid of 662 Hz. It is much less buzz-like and borders on a muffled hum.
The tail toggle only trims the decay, and the tail-off version ends fairly abruptly.
Wood and laminate look almost the same, so the surface choice has uneven impact.
grades.lesson: Build the defining physical mechanism of the sound (here a motor tone with its modulation, plus distinct contact impacts) rather than shaped noise bursts, and make each categorical choice change the spectrum or transient noticeably so the options aren't near-duplicates.

brief: Old plumbing groaning and knocking in walls; knobs: pipe (copper|iron), pressure 0..1, knock amount 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: Spectrogram energy is a flat band of low-frequency noise (roughly 100-800 Hz) with horizontal streaks, which reads as a rumble or wind wash rather than a groaning pipe. There is no clear gliding resonant pitch or the stressed-metal creak a groan needs.

The brief promises knocking, but the waveform shows no distinct knock transients. There are only faint vertical ticks in the spectrogram, and the envelope is a smooth swell with a lump in the middle. Knocks should be sharp, identifiable hits with ringing decay.
The envelope is a fixed spindle-shaped swell over 3 s in every render, including the extremes and the tail=false render. Only the spectral weight changes, so the knobs do not change the gesture.

Pipe copper/iron and the min/max ranges mostly shift the centroid (275 to 979 Hz) and brightness. They do not change the character, so the variants read as the same filtered noise rather than different materials.
Tail=false only reduces the decay slightly, and silence rises to 21%. It gives a truncated, lopsided shape rather than a clean dry version.
Seeds share the same swell shape but differ in detail only slightly. They are acceptable as takes, but none has a distinct event structure.
grades.lesson: When a brief names discrete events (knocks, hits, drips), build them as explicit sharp transients with their own resonant decay on top of the sustained layer, and check that they are visible in the waveform at defaults. Do not let a smooth noise bed with a fixed envelope stand in for them.

flaws: The groan is a flat, steady band of noise-like harmonics with stripe-like spectral lines. It reads as a synthetic drone rather than a pipe that creaks and wavers, and it has little pitch movement.
The knock is a single hit with a smooth exponential decay, so it sounds like a generic thump. It has no metallic ring and no resonance of the pipe, so it is not convincingly a pipe knock.
The 3 s length is fixed and the knock sits in a similar place in each render. The wide silence fraction (17–30%) suggests the groan fades in and out rather than sustaining.
The tail=false render still has a long decay, so the toggle's effect is subtle. The pipe=iron render has the knock buried in the groan, so the transient barely reads.
Seed 3 has two knocks while the other seeds have one. This is plausible, but it makes the takes differ more in structure than in detail.
grades.lesson: For impact or resonant sounds, give the transient its own material character (ring, inharmonic partials, a distinct attack envelope) instead of a generic noise burst with an exponential decay. Check that each choice option changes the transient as well as the sustained body, so it stays audible and readable.

brief: Synthesized analogue crash cymbal; knobs: metal (bronze|brass|thin), decay 0..1, spread 0..1, tone 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The crash has no distinct attack transient. The waveform opens at near-full level and decays smoothly, so it reads as a noise swell or a gong wash rather than a stick strike.
The spectrogram looks like flat, uniformly distributed noise. It shows no inharmonic partials, no ring structure, and no shimmer, so it sounds like filtered white noise rather than cymbal metal.
The centroid is about 6 kHz at default and the energy is spread evenly, with little low-mid body. The result is likely hissy and thin, with no bell or body component.
The three metal choices look nearly identical (centroids 6276, 6091, and 6131 Hz) and differ mainly in length. Brass and thin are hardly distinguishable timbrally.
The tail toggle barely changes the picture (2.50 s either way, centroid 6327 vs 6276 Hz), so it adds little value as a control.
The decay curve is a smooth, almost linear exponential taper with no initial fast drop followed by a long shimmer tail, which is the characteristic crash envelope.
grades.lesson: Do not build a metallic percussion sound from shaped noise and an envelope alone. Add the structure that defines the material (inharmonic partials, a sharp attack transient, a two-stage decay) and make each material choice change the timbre, not only the length.

flaws: The envelope is wrong for a crash. A real crash has a sharp attack, an instant broadband splash, and a long shimmering decay. Here the waveform swells and holds, with a slow, rounded decay and no sharp initial hit, so it reads more like a gong or a swelling noise burst.

The spectrogram shows discrete horizontal bands, with strong low-frequency lines at the bottom (a few hundred Hz). That means ringing tonal partials, not dense inharmonic cymbal wash. A cymbal's energy should be mostly 3-10 kHz and noise-like. The low bands make it sound like a bell or a pitched metal pot.

The default decay ends abruptly at about 2.0 s. The waveform drops to a flat line and the spectrogram cuts off in a hard vertical edge, with about 20% silence at the end. A cymbal tail should fade out naturally, and a truncated one will be audible in a scene.
With tail=false the sound is quieter, darker (centroid 2111 Hz), and still has a long thin trailing stub. It doesn't read as a clean choked crash, and it doesn't change the character in a useful way.

The metal choices are not clearly different. Bronze and brass are similar, and thin is just brighter with sparser partials. The extremes of the ranges (min and max) change length and brightness but still sound like the same tonal, non-cymbal source.
The seeds share the same overall shape, which is good. The partial structure is similar across seeds, so the variation is subtle, though acceptable.
grades.lesson: Check the reference sound's defining envelope and spectrum, not just its length and loudness. For noise-like percussion like cymbals, use dense inharmonic content with a sharp attack and a smooth natural fade, avoid strong low-frequency tonal lines, and never end on a hard cutoff.

flaws: The envelope does not read as a crash cymbal. A real crash has a near-instant, sharp attack followed by a fast initial drop and a long shimmering tail. Here the waveform swells over roughly 0.3-0.5 s into a fat spindle shape, which sounds like a reverse-ish or bowed cymbal or a noise swell.

The spectrogram is a uniform wash of noise across the whole band with no visible metallic partials, no inharmonic ring, and no brightness decay over time. High frequencies do not die faster than lows, so it reads as filtered white noise rather than a cymbal.

The default centroid of about 5.5 kHz with energy spread evenly is hissy. It is not the bright, complex shimmer of a bronze crash, and the metal variants (bronze, brass, thin) differ only slightly in the pictures.
The tail toggle and the ranges at minimum give a bumpy, uneven envelope with a secondary lump around 0.8 s. That sounds like a glitch rather than a deliberate decay.
The default has about 26% silence, which is trailing near-silence. The long thin tail then stops abruptly at about 2.5 s, and the sound ends in a hard cut rather than a natural fade.
grades.lesson: Before polishing knobs, check that the default's amplitude envelope and spectral evolution match the real source's signature: for percussive sounds, a near-instant attack and a decay that is faster at high frequencies. Broadband noise with a generic envelope reads as the wrong object, however many knobs it has.

brief: Breathy wind gust through a crack that almost sounds like a voice; knobs: gap size (keyhole|window|chimney), breathiness 0..1, vowel shape 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The envelope is a symmetric swell and fade with the same shape on every render. It reads as a processed noise burst more than a wind gust, which should have a ragged, uneven onset and a slow decay.
The spectrogram shows broad low-mid noise with no clear formant bands or vowel-like structure. The 'almost a voice' character is weak at default and at the extremes.
About 30% of the 3 s default is near-silent at the head and tail, so the usable body is closer to 1.5-2 s. That makes it awkward as a loop.
The gap presets (keyhole, window, chimney) mostly change the centroid and low-end weight. They don't clearly change the character, so the three read as EQ variants of one sound.
With tail=false the sound is shorter, but the envelope is still a symmetric blob and the tail removal barely changes the shape.
grades.lesson: When the brief names a distinctive quality (such as 'almost a voice'), make it visibly present in the spectrogram at default, for example with resonant formant bands. Also give the amplitude envelope irregular, natural motion instead of a smooth symmetric swell.

brief: Starter motor crank catching into engine fire and settling; knobs: engine size (4cyl/V6/V8), crank length 0..1, catch roughness 0..1, rev flare 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

warnings: slow: 1636 ms worst render

flaws: Waveform at defaults is a swelling mass with no clear starter-crank phase (a slow, pulsing, ratcheting whine) and no distinct catch moment; the 'crank, catch, settle' story reads as a generic rising drone.

The envelope barely settles: the sound is loudest near the end and cuts off abruptly. The spectrogram shows no obvious fade into a steady idle, so the 'settling' part of the brief is missing, and the tail toggle doesn't fix it.

Centroid is about 220 Hz across engine types and settings, and the 4cyl and V8 renders look almost the same. Engine size is a weak differentiator, with no clear change in firing rate or low-end weight.

Range extremes are inconsistent. The minimum setting produces a flat, dense block with no visible crank or catch, while the maximum shows a clear sawtooth pitch wobble. They don't read as the same event with different intensity.
Seeds differ too much in timing. Seed 2 has a long quiet build with a late catch, while the default and seed 3 catch early. They read as different events rather than two takes of one.
Fixed 3.8 s length, with crank length controlling the timing of the catch only loosely. A designer cannot reliably get a short crank-then-idle or a long grinding crank.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes a multi-stage event (crank, catch, settle), make each stage a visibly distinct section in the render with a clear transition between them. Keep the overall timeline and end-state consistent across seeds and knob extremes, and verify the final stage actually settles and decays instead of ending at peak level.

flaws: The waveform shows a slow ramp-up and a mostly sustained, roughly constant-level body, with no obvious sharp catch event. A real starter crank, catch and settle needs a distinct crank phase (slow chugging), a sudden ignition and then a rev flare falling to idle. This reads as a swell of low rumble.

The spectrogram energy is almost entirely below about 500 Hz, with a centroid around 220 Hz. Starter whine, ignition pops and engine harmonics are barely visible, so the cranking is not recognizable as a starter motor.

The engine size variants (4cyl and V8) look almost identical in envelope and spectrum, with centroids of 241 vs 238 Hz. Cylinder count changes mostly the level, not the firing cadence or pitch character, so the choice does not give clearly different sounds.
The minimum-range render turns into a uniform, dense, flat-topped slab (rms 0.31) with no visible catch moment, so the 'catch' disappears at the extremes. The sound loses its defining structure.
Seeds differ mostly in the overall envelope shape (seed 2 swells late while seed 3 peaks early), which makes them read as different events, not as takes of the same one.
The tail toggle makes the ending an abrupt stop on a loud body in the waveform instead of a natural settle, and the default end is a cut-off at high level as well.
grades.lesson: When a sound is defined by an event sequence (crank, then catch, then settle), make each phase visibly distinct in the envelope and spectrum, and check that every knob extreme and variant choice preserves that structure instead of flattening it into a sustained texture.

flaws: Envelope reads as a slow swell rather than a starter crank catching into a fire. The default waveform ramps up over about 2 s with no distinct crank phase, no sharp catch transient and no clear settle to idle.

The spectrum is concentrated in the low band (centroid about 220 Hz). The crank/starter whirr and the combustion pulses are not clearly separated, so it reads as a low rumble with a faint wobbling line.
Engine size choices (4cyl vs V8) look almost identical in waveform and spectrogram, with centroids of 241 and 238 Hz. The choice knob does not give clearly different characters.

The crank length minimum produces a dense, flat, near-constant-level 3.8 s block, and the maximum shows a visible oscillating crank line with a long quiet lead-in. These don't read as the same event, and the minimum has no catch moment.
The total duration is fixed at 3.80 s, so crank length changes the content but not the length. A longer crank just fills the same window, which cramps the catch and settle.
Seeds differ mainly in overall envelope shape: seed 2 swells late and seed 3 is blocky. They read as different performances rather than takes of one sound.
The tail=false render still has no clean ending and stays loud to the cut. The tail toggle doesn't produce a convincing settle to idle.
grades.lesson: Make the defining event of the sound (here the catch transition from crank to fire) a clearly visible, separate stage in the envelope and spectrogram, and check that each choice knob changes the picture visibly rather than only the numbers.

brief: Rope wrapped and cinched on a cleat; knobs: cleat (iron|wood|nylon), friction 0..1, speed 0..1, snap 0..1, rate

flaws: The rope-wrap section is a series of noisy bursts, and the cinch at the end is a single pluck with tonal ringing. The ringing lines in the spectrogram read as a pitched, metallic or tuned resonance, which is odd for a rope on a cleat, especially on wood and nylon.
The final cinch has a long smooth exponential decay at defaults, more like a struck or plucked object than rope tightening. Rope on a cleat would end with a creak or grip, not a ringing tail.
The cleat choices differ mostly in brightness, with a different tone on the final hit. Iron does not clearly sound like a metal cleat, so the materials are less distinct than they could be.
Silence is about 20%, mostly from the decay tail and gaps between bursts. This is acceptable, but the wraps sound a bit mechanical and evenly spaced.
grades.lesson: Check that the tonal parts of a sound match what the real object would do. Resonant ringing lines on a soft or fibrous source read as a pitched strike, so damp or remove them unless the material really rings.

brief: Rotary pot or detented knob twist; knobs: knob (smooth|detented|stiff), speed 0..1, steps 1-20, scrape 0..1

flaws: Default (detented) shows a ~1 s broadband noise wash with faint periodic clicks. A detented knob should read as discrete, sharp transients (clicks) with short gaps between them. Here the clicks are buried in a continuous noise bed, so it sounds like a scrape or hiss, not a click-click-click.
The 'smooth' variant is a plain noise burst with a rising and falling envelope and no features. It reads as a generic whoosh or noise pad, not a pot being turned.

Minimum extremes stretch to 1.28 s and become a thin, low-level noise strip (rms 0.053) with only a click at the start and one near the end. This reads as a different sound, and it is too long and too weak for a knob twist.
Maximum extremes turn into a dense, loud noise burst (rms 0.151) with no discernible step structure. The detents disappear, so range does not hold the same character.
Every render ends with a separate loud click and tonal blip after a gap. It looks like a stray tail artefact, makes the sound feel unfinished, and sits oddly after the noise.
The speed, steps and scrape controls do not give clear, distinct step counts. At the extremes the detents are not countable, so the knob is not usable as a detent control.
grades.lesson: When a sound is defined by discrete events (clicks, steps, ticks), keep the events as sharp, separated transients over a quiet bed at every knob setting, and check that the extremes still show countable events instead of dissolving into continuous noise.

flaws: The default detented render is a row of 8 near-identical clicks at an even spacing. This sounds mechanical and machine-gun-like, with no accelerating or decelerating twist feel.
The click-then-tail shape is plausible for a detent, but each click is a sharp broadband tick with little body or resonance. It reads a little thin and generic.
Minimum range collapses to 0.30 s with just two clicks and 64% silence. It is valid but very sparse, and the second click is oddly offset from the first.
Smooth mode is a dense, continuous buzz that ends in a stray click and tail. It reads as a scrape or friction noise rather than a smooth pot turn, and the final tick looks tacked on.
The 'speed' and 'steps' knobs interact with total length (0.30 s at minimum, 0.60 s at maximum), so the duration is not clearly controlled by any one knob.
Max range at 20 steps is a dense blur of clicks. It is no longer distinguishable as individual detents.
grades.lesson: Add timing and amplitude jitter to repeated events, and make sure the end-state of a gesture (the final click or release) is tied to the same mechanism as the rest, not a separate tacked-on sound.

brief: Engine cutting off with shudder and cooling ticks; knobs: engine size (4cyl/V6/V8), shudder 0..1, tick density 0..1, fan run-on 0..1, ticking tail toggle

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.69); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: Ticks read as isolated full-height spikes spread across the spectrogram, more like clicks than metal cooling ticks. They lack the short resonant ping and the tonal, pitched character a real exhaust or manifold tick has.

The shudder section is a short, flat burst of low-frequency pulses at the start, about 0.5 s. It has no clear deceleration, so no falling pitch or slowing pulse rate is visible. It reads as a generic thump train and not an engine winding down.
Engine size barely changes the sound. The 4cyl and V8 renders have near-identical centroids (284 vs 291 Hz) and the same overall shape, so the choice knob is nearly cosmetic.
The fan run-on has no visible signature in any render. The spectrogram shows no sustained broadband or tonal band, which makes this knob questionable.
At max ranges the tick density turns into a dense, constant spray that fills the whole 4 s. It stops sounding like cooling and sounds like rain on metal.
At min ranges the render is mostly empty (66% silence) with only a few isolated ticks, so the sound feels sparse and unfinished.

The first 0.5 s has the spectral energy concentrated below about 500 Hz, with almost nothing above. The shutdown lacks the mechanical and combustion detail a designer would need, such as a final cough or valve clatter.
grades.lesson: Make every knob and choice produce a distinct, visible signature in the render (e.g. a falling pitch line, a sustained band, a different spectral shape). A knob that doesn't change the picture reads as broken. Give each event type its own character, such as a resonant ping versus a bare click, and don't let one generic impulse stand in for several different sounds.

flaws: The shut-off reads as a continuous low-frequency buzz fading over about 1 s, with little sense of the engine spinning down. The waveform shows a dense pulse train, but the spectrogram shows no clear pitch fall as RPM drops, which a convincing shut-off needs.
The cooling ticks are very sparse, isolated broadband clicks with long gaps. They read as a few random clicks, not as the denser, pitched metallic ticking of cooling metal.
About 35% of the 4 s is silence at defaults, and the minimum-range render hits 43%. The tail has long dead stretches, so it feels thin and empty.
Turning the ticking tail off leaves a 2.4 s clip. This is a sensible toggle, but the remaining body is mostly a low rumble with little character.
Engine size changes the pulse rate and centroid only modestly (309 to 484 Hz), so 4cyl, V6 and V8 are not strongly distinct.
grades.lesson: When a sound is defined by a change over time, such as an engine spinning down, make that change (a falling pitch or rate) clearly visible in the spectrogram. Check that sparse event layers, like ticks, have a sensible density and do not leave long dead gaps.

brief: Three knocks from somewhere inside the walls; knobs: surface (wood|plaster|metal), force 0..1, distance 0..1, knock rate, tail toggle

flaws: The default centroid of 185 Hz sits very low. The knocks read as dull thuds more than wood hitting a hollow wall cavity, and some top-end or resonant body would help.
Plaster and metal differ mainly in centroid. Metal shows some ringing partials, but plaster is just a darker version of wood and the spread between surfaces is modest.
The tail toggle at false leaves 32% silence and a hard cut after the last knock. That is acceptable for a toggle but a bit abrupt.
Extreme settings change the length from 2.0 s to 3.0 s, and the spacing between knocks shifts a lot. Rate extremes are less distinct than a designer might expect.
The knock envelopes are quite uniform, with almost no variation in force from knock to knock. This sounds mechanical and not like a person or a presence.
grades.lesson: Give each categorical choice, such as a material, its own spectral and resonant character, not just a filter shift. Add per-event randomness in level and timing so repeated hits do not sound like copies.

brief: Mooring line creaking under strain; knobs: rope (hemp|nylon|wire), tension 0..1, stretch 0..1, grit 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The waveform is a single swell-and-fade envelope over 3 s that looks like filtered noise, not a creak. A rope creak should have discrete stick-slip pulses or groans with pitch glides, and nothing like that is visible.

The spectrogram shows broadband vertical striping from a dense noise-like texture, with little clear resonant pitch movement. Only faint low arcs appear, so it reads as a wash rather than strained rope.
The rope types differ mainly in brightness. Nylon, wire and hemp all keep the same blob envelope and texture, so they sound like EQ variants and not different materials.

At the minimum range settings the sound becomes more clicky and darker (centroid 441 Hz), which is a different character. At the maximum it becomes a diffuse hiss-like wash, so the extremes are not clearly the same kind of sound.
The 17% silence is mostly the faded-out tail, and the envelope is a symmetric fade in and out. A creak under strain should have uneven, event-based dynamics, not a smooth bell shape.
The tail toggle only shortens the sound and trims the ending, which is a minor change for a dedicated knob.
grades.lesson: Make sure the sound's defining event structure (for a creak, discrete stick-slip pulses with gliding pitch) is visible in the render. A shaped noise bed with a smooth envelope reads as a generic wash, and material or preset choices need to change that structure, not just the brightness.

flaws: Waveform is a single symmetric swell: it fades in, peaks mid-way and fades out, which reads as a noise burst rather than a rope under strain. There are no discrete stick-slip creak events, which are the defining feature of a mooring creak.

The spectrogram is mostly broadband, vertically striped noise with only faint curved low-frequency lines. A creak should show resonant, pitch-gliding tonal content with sharp onsets, and that is barely visible.
The rope choices differ mainly in centroid (928 vs 1154 Hz) and in texture. Nylon and wire look very similar in the waveform, so they would not read as clearly different materials.
The range minimum is a sparse, clicky, low-centroid texture (441 Hz) and the maximum is a dense wash (1319 Hz). Those read as different sounds, not as the same creak with different settings.
The 3 s default has about 17% silence, mostly in the tail. Turning the tail off ends the sound at 2.5 s with a slightly abrupt cut, so the toggle adds little.
The sound is one fixed-length swell with no creak rate or density control, so it is hard to loop or fit to a scene. A designer would find it a generic rough noise swell and would not pay for it.
grades.lesson: Build the signature event of the sound (here, discrete stick-slip creaks with pitched resonances and sharp onsets) rather than shaping filtered noise with a smooth envelope, and check that the spectrogram shows that structure at the default settings.

flaws: Default render does not read as a creak. It is a series of 4-5 separate noisy bursts with long silent gaps (43% silence), more like footsteps or scrapes than a continuous rope groaning under strain.

Every render ends with a loud, sharp transient followed by a low sustained horizontal band. This sounds like a thump or snap and is unrelated to the creaking. It appears at the same point in every take, which is artificial.
The spectrograms show broadband noise bursts with little of the tonal, stick-slip pitch-wobbling resonance that defines a creak. Hemp is mostly low-frequency mush.
Nylon and wire do show some tonal lines, but they are thin, static and horizontal, like whistles, with no pitch glide from stretch. Wire turns into rhythmic beeping pulses.

The range minimum is almost all silence (53%) with tiny blips, which is too sparse to use. The maximum turns into dense noise washes that lose the creak character. The extremes sound like different sounds.
With tail=false the final thump goes away, but the result is still four noise bursts with gaps, so the sound still does not read as a creak.
The seeds share the same structure, with a bang at the end and gaps in between. They are fine as takes, but the repeated final hit is a tell.
grades.lesson: Model the physical mechanism that defines the sound (here, stick-slip friction giving a gliding, resonant pitch) instead of triggering noise bursts with gaps. Avoid fixed signature events, such as a loud final hit, that are not part of the real sound.

brief: Electric car ready-to-drive swell tone with inverter whine; knobs: tone style (warm/futuristic), whine amount 0..1, swell length 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The swell is a symmetric diamond, with a rise and fall of similar length. A real EV ready-to-drive chime usually rises and then holds or decays more softly, so this sounds more like a generic pad swell.

The inverter whine is shown as rising harmonic lines that glide and level off. It reads as a pitch sweep and not as the steady, slightly gritty high-frequency switching whine of an inverter, so the character is only loosely matched.
At minimum ranges the output is dark (centroid 384 Hz) and the whine almost disappears. The sound loses its EV identity and becomes a low hum.
Setting tail=false shortens the sound but does not clearly change its shape. Without a tail the envelope still fades out slowly instead of ending cleanly.
The warm and futuristic styles differ mainly in brightness. Futuristic has dense, flat harmonics that look somewhat noisy. Both are usable.
grades.lesson: Check that the signature element of a sound (here the inverter whine) stays recognisable at both extremes of every knob, and give the envelope an asymmetric, purpose-specific shape instead of a generic symmetric swell.

brief: Chair tilting back and creaking under weight; knobs: chair build (mesh/leather/cheap plastic), recline depth 0..1, creak density 0..1, spring twang 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: Defaults read as a chain of broadband clicks and thumps rather than a creak. A real chair creak is a sustained, pitch-wobbling friction tone with visible harmonic bands. The spectrogram shows vertical bursts and smeared low-frequency blocks, and no clear stick-slip harmonic structure.
The centroid is around 411 Hz and the energy sits mostly low, which is too dull for a creaking sound. The leather and mesh builds look like muffled rattles or knocks, not chair creaks.

The 2.44 s clip has a few large isolated spikes (about 0.5 s and 1.3 s) and then a long decaying tail. This reads as a series of impacts, not a gradual recline under weight, and the pattern looks unmotivated.
The cheap plastic build is the best of the three. Even so, its horizontal bands look like steady low hums rather than squeaks, and it still has a thumpy low end.
At the minimum range the clip is 46% silent and has only two sparse transients. It barely reads as a creak, just two knocks.
At the maximum range the clip is dense, noisy and smeared, with no clear creak character. It sounds like a rumble.
The tail toggle only trims the clip. When the tail is off, a hard transient lands at the very end of the clip, which looks like an abrupt cutoff artifact.
grades.lesson: Check that the spectrogram shows the defining structure of the sound (for a creak, sustained pitched harmonics with wobble) and not just generic bursts of noise with a matching envelope. If the signature feature is missing, the sound reads as the wrong thing even when length and loudness are plausible.

flaws: The spectrogram shows a harmonic stack with glides, which reads as creak or squeak, but the broadband noise fill is somewhat even and sounds more like vocal-ish groans than a creaking chair.
The 'tail' of 2-3 decaying bursts at the end looks like a repeated pattern (big, medium, small). It is too regular and mechanical, like a bouncing ball, rather than the settling of a chair.
At minimum every range collapses to a few blobs of similar shape and the creaks lose their rhythm, so the low-density case reads as sparse rather than a slow, tense creak.
The chair build presets differ mostly in centroid and burst count, not in character (no obvious plastic crackle or leather squeak). The differences are real but subtle.
The 'spring twang' knob is hard to see in the pictures, so its effect is unclear.
Seeds share the same overall shape (big burst, then two small ones) but with varied internal detail, which is acceptable though the layout is fairly fixed.
grades.lesson: Make event timing (spacing and size of repeated bursts) vary organically and depend on the physical story, such as load shifting and settling, rather than a fixed decaying pattern. Make the categorical presets differ in character, not just in brightness.

brief: 1/4-inch jack plugged/unplugged with hum pop; knobs: action (insert|pull), force 0..1, hum-pop 0..1, buzz 0..1

flaws: The sound is a short transient burst with a quick decay. It reads as a plausible jack click, but the spectrogram shows little structure, so the hum pop is hard to identify. A low-frequency thump is present but smeared, and there is no distinct mains hum with harmonics.
The insert and pull defaults look nearly the same in the spectrogram. The main difference is that pull is front-loaded, so the two actions are not clearly distinct.
The minimum extreme has a much higher centroid (1806 Hz vs about 1000 Hz) and 55% silence. It reads as a thin, tick-like click with much of the body missing, a noticeable change in character.
The 0.5 s duration is short for a plug event with a hum pop and a buzz tail. The tail fades out quickly, and the buzz is barely visible in the picture.
Seeds are consistent in shape but similar in detail. Seed 3 is almost identical to the default.
grades.lesson: Make each knob produce a distinct, visible feature in the spectrogram, such as a hum line at fixed frequencies or a buzz band. Check that its extremes keep the sound's core character instead of thinning it to a bare click.

brief: A single coin dropped and spinning on a surface. Knobs: coin metal (copper/silver/gold), surface (wood/stone), drop height 0..1, spin length 0..1, pitch, tail toggle.

flaws: The default waveform does not match a coin drop and spin. A real coin gives a sharp impact, a few bounces, then a spin whose rattle gets faster and louder before it ends in a quick buzz and a final clink. Here the spin is a long, smooth swell that keeps rising for about 2 s, then a late second hit and a short decay. That reads as a swelling drone, not a coin.

The default is 3 s with 33% silence. The spin has no visible acceleration of the ring-down pulses, and the spectrogram shows mostly flat horizontal bands. Those sustained tonal lines sound like a synth or bowl, not metal on a surface.

At maximum spin length the sound is almost continuous, with 4% silence, and it rises toward the end like a riser. It no longer reads as a coin that settles. At minimum it collapses into a single short blip with 65% silence, so the extremes are not the same kind of event.
The metal choices change mostly brightness and level (centroid 2191 to 2420 Hz). Copper and gold look almost identical in envelope, so they are not clearly different materials.

The tail toggle makes only a small difference, with a slightly shorter decay after the final hit. It is a weak control. The long, loud final clink after the swell also sounds like a separate event stuck on.
Seeds share a general shape, but the peak ranges widely (0.61 to 0.82) and the level changes noticeably between takes.
grades.lesson: For a physical event with a known time structure (such as a coin settling), model its dynamics (such as the accelerating rattle that ends in a clink) rather than a smooth envelope with sustained tones, and check that the length knob scales that structure instead of turning the event into a drone.

flaws: The default envelope does not look like a coin drop. A drop should give a sharp initial impact followed by bouncing ticks that get faster, then a spinning whir that ends in a rattle. The default waveform instead shows a slow swell: a loud onset, a dip, then a second, larger build near 1.2 s and a long decay. That reads as a swelling tone, not a coin.

The spin is a smooth amplitude swell with no accelerating pulse train. A real spinning coin has a rising-frequency wobble that ends in a rapid chatter. The spectrogram shows steady horizontal partial lines with no visible acceleration.
Silence is 24% at default and 30% for copper. The waveform shows a flat low-level run in the tail. Parts of the sound are either quiet or cut off, so the ending is not a natural decay.

The stone surface looks wrong. It is a dense, continuous 2.2 s sustained wash with only 3% silence, and its centroid (4444 Hz) is higher than the default. A stone surface should give a harder, shorter, more distinct impact, not a long sustained buzz. Stone and wood do not sound like a change of surface.
The tail=false render is 1.56 s of continuous sustained energy with a slow swell and an abrupt end. It has no clear impact transient and still does not resolve into a rattle.

The metal choices change the centroid (1500 to 3379 Hz) mostly through level and brightness, and copper looks very different in shape from the default. The partial structure is not clearly identifiable as different metals.
Across seeds the peak level varies (0.764 vs 0.85) and the internal structure changes. The overall shape is similar, but the timing of the swell moves around, so the takes feel loosely related.
grades.lesson: Check that the time envelope matches the physical event's signature (for example impacts that accelerate into a rattle, with a sharp transient at the start), not just its spectrum, and render each categorical choice so it differs in transient and decay as well as brightness.

flaws: The default looks like a single decaying burst of about 2 s with a smooth envelope. It has no initial drop impact followed by a rattle. A real spinning coin shows accelerating, increasingly dense bounces that end in a sudden buzz and settle, and that structure is missing.
The spin is a slow amplitude swell and fade rather than an accelerating series of discrete hits. The sound reads as a bell or metallic ring, not a coin on a surface.

Stone surface shows a long, dense, ringing wash with only 4% silence and a 4.7 kHz centroid. It is broad and noisy, and the tail never ends in a rattle. It does not read as a coin on stone and is quite different from the other renders.

The tail=false render is the only one with discrete rapid hits that look like a coin rattle, yet it is the 'no tail' option. The most characteristic part of the sound only appears when the toggle is off, and the default does not show it.

The metal choices differ mostly in centroid. Copper at 1.2 kHz and gold at 1.5 kHz are both dull and close together. Gold has a double-hump envelope that suggests a second impact rather than a different metal.
Seeds differ a lot in silence fraction (22% vs 15%) and in peak and envelope shape. They are different enough that they do not clearly read as two takes of the same sound.
Silence of 25% in the default means gaps inside the sound, which suggests the ring is gated or broken up rather than a continuous decay.
grades.lesson: Model the physical event structure the brief names (for a spinning coin, an impact followed by accelerating bounces and a final rattle) rather than a generic decaying resonance, and make sure that defining structure shows in the default render, not only behind a toggle.

brief: Classic dashboard warning chime ding pattern; knobs: chime type (gong/beep/bell), repeat count 0..1, brightness 0..1, rate, decay tail toggle

flaws: The default has three dings, but the last one looks the loudest with a long tail. Real dashboard chimes keep a steady level, so the crescendo reads as odd.
The gong type has uneven spacing and a rising amplitude, and its centroid is low at 549 Hz. It sounds more like a gong roll than a warning chime.
The minimum setting collapses to a single ding. A repeat count of 0 should probably still give the minimum pattern, and the control reads more like an on/off switch than a range.
The 'bell' type was not shown, so it could not be judged.
The decay tail is long, about 1 s of wash after the last ding. This is a bit long for a car chime, though the toggle does help.
The seeds differ only slightly, mainly in the high-frequency detail. The timing is the same, so they sound like near-identical takes.
grades.lesson: Make each repeated event in a pattern match the others in level, and use a seed to vary timing and detail slightly. Make sure each range extreme still gives a usable pattern, not a collapsed single hit.

brief: Office chair rolling across the floor on casters; knobs: floor (carpet/hard floor/chair mat), roll speed rate, caster rattle 0..1, creak amount 0..1, distance 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Default render (hard floor) is a 3 s swell-and-decay wash. A chair rolling on casters should be a steady, continuous rumble with a rhythmic caster/seam bump texture, not a single envelope that fades out like a one-shot hit.
The spectrogram is vertical broadband streaks with a slightly bright centroid (~1.4 kHz) and little low rumble. It reads as noisy impulses or surface scraping, not a plastic wheel on hard floor.
No visible creak: no tonal or pitched stick-slip components in the picture at default, so the creak knob does not seem to contribute a recognizable chair sound.

Floor choices differ mainly by low-pass brightness. Carpet is a muffled low blob with a centroid of 382 Hz, while chair mat and hard floor look similar. The surfaces are not distinct enough in character.

Minimum-range render turns into sparse isolated bursts with gaps, which reads as a series of separate clicks rather than rolling. Maximum is a smooth noise swell. The two extremes feel like different sounds.
The tail=false render has no decay but also no clear start or stop, and it is shorter (2.3 s). It sounds like cut-off noise, not a chair that rolls in and out.
grades.lesson: Model the physical mechanism of a continuous, sustained sound (steady rolling or friction texture with periodic detail) rather than shaping noise with a one-shot attack-decay envelope, and make each surface or material option differ in its excitation pattern, not just its filter cutoff.

flaws: The default render reads as a 3 s noise burst with a swell and a fade, not a chair rolling. The waveform is a spindle shape with no mechanical periodicity. A real caster roll has a steady rumble with rhythmic rattle ticks and an even body.

The spectrogram is a broadband wash with a few discrete clicks near the bottom. It doesn't show the hard-floor thump-thump of casters crossing seams, or the low rumble plus mid-high whirr you'd expect.

The envelope is the same on every floor. It rises, peaks around 1 s, then decays, so a roll that should be sustained and constant ends up as one gesture. Rolling across a floor is a steady-state sound, and the swell reads as a pass-by instead.

Carpet gives a centroid of 288 Hz, which is too dark and muddy, almost a low-frequency rumble, while the chair mat gives 690 Hz and the default hard floor 1301 Hz. The floors differ mostly by low-pass filtering of the same noise, not by distinct surface character. Hard floor should have the clear rolling-plastic whirr, and carpet should be a soft, muffled hiss.
The 'tail = false' render ends abruptly at full level, with no fade. That is acceptable for a toggle, but it also exposes that the body is just continuous noise with no real mechanical structure.

The min/max range renders look nearly identical to default in shape and differ mainly in level and brightness, so the knobs give little audible character change. The rattle and creak details are barely visible in the spectrograms.
The seeds share the same swell shape, which is fine, but the fine detail is generic noise, so they sound like takes of the same noise burst and not of a chair.
grades.lesson: For continuous mechanical motion sounds (rolling, scraping, sliding), build the sound from the mechanism, such as periodic impacts at a rate tied to speed, resonances and a steady-state body, instead of shaped noise with a one-shot swell envelope, and make surface or material choices change the excitation, not just the filter.

flaws: Defaults read as a generic noise swell: a broadband wash with a slow fade-in and fade-out, not a recognisable chair-caster roll. No visible rolling rhythm (periodic thumps from caster seams or floor joints) and no distinct rattle or creak events in the spectrogram.

The floor choices are too similar. Carpet (1211 Hz) and chair mat (1109 Hz) look almost identical, and carpet is not clearly duller or softer than the hard-floor default. Hard floor lacks the bright, hollow rumble expected, so the surface knob does not change the character much.

The 'tail = false' render shows a different overall shape: constant-level noise right up to the cut with no fade. It ends abruptly, which is a hard chop, and a 3 s fixed length with a tail on a rolling sound is odd. The result is not a usable loop or a clean one-shot.

The extremes smear into broad noise. Min and max differ mainly in level and centroid (1488 vs 888 Hz), and the max setting loses the transient structure. The extremes do not read as clearly different chair behaviours (slow gentle roll vs fast rattly roll).

The seeds share an envelope, but the detail is mostly random noise texture rather than distinct rattle or creak events, so a designer cannot hear 'two takes of a chair'. Creak, which should be tonal and pitched, shows no visible harmonic or resonant lines.

Knobs are reasonable (floor, speed, rattle, creak, distance, tail), but the sound lacks a duration control and a roll-start/stop shape control, and rattle and creak do not produce visible, separable features.
grades.lesson: Build each knob's signature feature as a distinct, visible event (periodic caster thumps, tonal creak with harmonics, discrete rattle ticks) rather than shaping one noise bed with filters. If the spectrogram shows only noise with an envelope, the sound will not read as the named object.

brief: Pneumatic chair height lever hiss and drop; knobs: direction (drop/rise), cylinder size (small/large), hiss amount 0..1, clunk at end 0..1, duration rate, tail toggle

flaws: The hiss is a flat broadband noise block with a hard onset and no spectral movement, so it sounds more like generic white noise than gas escaping. Gas flow usually softens and shifts in pitch as pressure falls.
The clunk at the end is a thin click followed by a ringing, narrow-band tail. It reads as a tone ping rather than a mechanical thud, and it is somewhat disconnected from the hiss.
At minimum ranges the clunk is almost absent and the sound is a plain 2 s noise decay. This is the weakest extreme, though it is not broken.
Rise and drop are nearly identical in spectrum. Only the envelope shape differs, so the direction switch is subtle.
The seeds are very similar, with only small differences in the noise texture. This is acceptable, but there is little variation in the clunk.
grades.lesson: Give noise-based sounds some spectral or pitch movement over time, such as a filter sweep that follows the physical process, so they don't read as static white-noise blocks. Make sure impact elements have body (low-frequency thud plus a short decay), not just a click or a ringing tone.

brief: Small level fader slid on panel; knobs: fader (plastic|metal), distance 0..1, speed 0..1, friction 0..1

flaws: At defaults the render reads as a series of discrete bursts ending in a loud thump or click, not a continuous sliding friction sound. The waveform has gaps and a late spike, which sounds like several taps and not a fader slide.

The spectrogram shows narrow, tonal horizontal lines at the end (a ringing hit). That is an end-stop clack, and it is not requested or controllable. It is the loudest part of the sound, so it dominates the take.
At minimum ranges the sound is almost nothing: a few ticks plus one isolated click, with 41% silence and no sense of a slide. That is a single click, not the same kind of sound as the defaults.

At maximum ranges the sound is a dense noisy burst that ends abruptly at 0.56 s. It is shorter than the default even though distance and speed are at their maximum, so the length does not scale as a designer would expect.
The plastic and metal choice is audible, but the difference is mostly a brighter centroid and a different final ring. It does not change the character of the friction texture.
The loudness of the seeds varies noticeably (peak 0.69 to 0.85), and the placement of the end spike also varies. The seeds are recognisably related but inconsistent in level.
grades.lesson: Check that a continuous-contact sound (slide, scrape, drag) is rendered as a sustained, evenly textured friction layer, and that incidental events such as end-stop hits are not louder than the main texture. Make sure the range extremes still behave like that same continuous sound, and that duration follows the intuitive knobs (distance, speed).

flaws: The default render is a flat, diffuse noise burst with a symmetric swell and fade. It is a generic noise envelope, not a fader slide. A real slide has a quick stick-slip onset, a steady scrape, and visible grain or texture from friction.

The spectrogram is a uniform broadband wash with no tonal or resonant structure. Plastic and metal differ only by a centroid shift (2445 to 3506 Hz), so metal reads as a brighter version of the same noise. Neither has a distinct body or a resonant ring.

There is a stray transient spike at the very end of every render, visible as a vertical line in the spectrogram. It reads as an artifact or a click, not a natural end to a slide, and it would be noticed in a scene.

At minimum the sound is only 0.44 s, with a hard cut at the end and 29% silence. This reads as a truncated burst, not a short slide. At maximum the envelope is a smooth symmetric lump with no stick-slip detail, so the extremes look like the same blob at different sizes.
Speed and distance do not clearly change the texture. Duration and level change, but the amount of friction grain does not, which makes the sound feel synthetic.
The seeds are near-identical in envelope and spectrum, with only minor peak jitter. That is acceptable consistency but offers little real variation in the slide gesture.
grades.lesson: Do not build a mechanical-interaction sound from a shaped noise burst with a smooth envelope. Model the physical process, such as stick-slip pulses, resonant modes per material and speed-dependent grain, so the texture and spectrum identify the object and the motion. Also check that no stray transient is left at the end of the render.

flaws: Defaults read as a generic noise burst: a flat, dense amplitude envelope with a hard start and stop, and no visible slide structure such as stick-slip, a speed ramp or a track texture. A fader on a panel should have a gentle onset, a slight movement contour and a short end-stop or release, and this has none of those.

The spectrogram energy is almost all at the very bottom, with a faint broadband wash above it. There is no characteristic plastic or metal rubbing or scraping texture or resonance. The metal setting only raises the centroid and drops the RMS, so it reads as an EQ change rather than a different material.

The minimum-range render is 0.67 s with 41% silence, and its short bursts look like discrete clicks rather than a slide. The maximum render is 1.2 s with a low centroid of 472 Hz and thumpy, rumbling energy, so it reads like a different sound (handling rumble). The extremes do not hold together as one fader sound.

Around 25% silence in a continuous slide is mostly the tail, but the sound ends abruptly. Even the longest setting is only about 1.2 s, so 'distance' barely gives a long slide, and the fader never really reads as travelling along a track.

The knobs overlap in effect: speed, distance and friction all change the length, level and brightness together. They do not give independent control of pitch/scrape texture, stick-slip grain or end-stop, which a designer would expect.
grades.lesson: Build the signature structure of the physical action (onset, contour, texture, release) into the sound itself, rather than shaping filtered noise with an envelope, and make each knob control one distinct perceptual quality so extremes don't drift into a different sound.

brief: Insistent unbuckled-belt reminder beeps escalating; knobs: tone (soft/harsh), urgency 0..1, volume ramp 0..1, rate, pitch, tail toggle

errors: random combination 2: 72% of the buffer is silent
random combination 3: 77% of the buffer is silent

flaws: The beeps have a fast attack and a decaying tail, so they sound more like bell or chime strikes than a flat-topped car-cluster beep. The default reads a little soft for something meant to be insistent.
Escalation at defaults is mild: five beeps with a modest level rise and a slight spacing change. A real belt reminder should clearly speed up or intensify.
At minimum range only four beeps with 20% silence appear, and the escalation is almost gone, so urgency and ramp collapse. The result is still usable but dull.
The maximum setting produces a long, overlapping beep train with no gaps and a washy mass. It loses the discrete beep character and reads as a swell rather than a reminder.
The harsh tone is mostly noisy and smeared across beeps, with a less clear pitch. It sounds closer to a buzzer, which is acceptable but less clean than the soft tone.
grades.lesson: When a sound is defined by a recognisable device or signal, such as a beep, make the default envelope match how that device really behaves (for example a flat-topped gate rather than a decaying strike). Also check that the extreme settings keep the sound's discrete structure instead of smearing into a continuous wash.

brief: Single wiper pass with motor whir and rubber squeak; knobs: blade condition (new/worn), glass wetness 0..1, squeak amount 0..1, motor whine 0..1, sweep speed

flaws: The default shows two swells with a thump at the midpoint, so it reads as a back-and-forth double stroke rather than the single wiper pass the brief asks for.
The spectrogram is dominated by low harmonic motor lines. The rubber squeak, which should show as bright, pitch-wandering streaks, is barely visible at defaults, so the squeak feels buried.
At minimum ranges the sound stretches to 3.00 s with 16% silence and a sparse, thin look, and it loses the sweep envelope. That reads as a different sound and is too long for a single pass.
At maximum ranges the sound shrinks to 1.00 s and loses its two-lobe shape. Sweep speed therefore changes the structure and length a lot, with no way to hold the length fixed.
The blade condition change from new to worn is subtle in the image: the centroid moves from 1263 to 1517 Hz and the transient detail is only slightly different.
grades.lesson: Make each source feature (such as squeak or whir) clearly visible in the render at default settings, and keep the sound's structure and length stable across knob extremes, so that a knob changes character rather than turning the sound into a different event.

brief: Leather purse of coins jingled or shaken. Knobs: purse size (small/fat), coin count 0..1, shake intensity 0..1, leather muffle 0..1, rate, tail toggle.

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 2.16); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: Each shake event is a broad, fairly smooth 100 ms bump with a few static tonal lines, so it reads more like a bell or metallic ping than a dense scatter of coin-on-coin clicks. The individual coin transients are not clearly resolved.
At default the rhythm is a regular, evenly spaced series of 5 bursts, which sounds mechanical rather than like a hand shaking a purse.

The minimum setting leaves only 3 sparse hits and 71% silence, so it reads as a few isolated drops rather than a quiet jingle. The maximum setting is a dense, noisy blob in which the shake events merge together.
The 'small' size has a brighter centroid and is reasonably distinct, but its tonal lines look similar to the default's, so the size change is subtle.
grades.lesson: For granular or impact-cluster sounds like coins, gravel, or keys, make each event a very short, sharp transient with randomised pitch and timing. Avoid evenly spaced bursts with smooth envelopes, which read as tonal pings or machinery rather than a natural scatter.

brief: Bell buoy clanging as it rocks; knobs: bell size (small|medium|large), swell 0..1, clapper hits 0..1, rust 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.63); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: The spectrogram energy sits mostly in a low band with broadband noise-like hash and only a few thin horizontal partial lines. A real bell has strong, clearly inharmonic partials that ring and decay, with a bright strike. This reads more like a dull, thudding metallic rumble than a bell. The centroid of about 800 Hz and the low-heavy energy support that.

The two clangs at defaults are well spaced, but they sit in a 3.5 s window with little sense of rocking. A bell buoy should have irregular clusters of strikes driven by wave swell. Two isolated hits do not convey that, and the second hit at the very end is cut off by the file edge.
The 'tail = false' render still shows long sustained decays and a ringing second hit, so the toggle barely changes the character. It is unclear what it removes.

At minimum, the whole render is one hit with a long, flat, noisy sustain and almost no second strike, so it no longer reads as a buoy clanging. The sound looks like a gong or drone rather than a bell.
The size knob mostly shifts the centroid and loudness, and the pitch differences are subtle. Large and small do not clearly convey different bell sizes through distinct partial spacing.
The knobs 'swell' and 'clapper hits' overlap in effect. Their roles are not obvious from the renders, and the maximum setting produces a cluster that looks cramped on top of a loud noise bed.
grades.lesson: Check that the spectrogram shows the defining spectral signature of the object (for a bell, distinct inharmonic partials with a bright strike) rather than a noise bed with a few lines. Make sure each toggle visibly changes the render, and that events do not get clipped at the end of the file.

flaws: Defaults read as a continuous swelling drone rather than discrete clangs. The waveform is a sustained amplitude blob with no sharp bell strike transients and no clear decaying ring between hits, so it does not sound like a bell buoy.

Spectrogram shows mostly broadband noise-like texture with only a few faint horizontal partials. A bell should show distinct inharmonic partials that ring and decay after each strike, and that is largely missing.
Energy sits at the low end with little structure, so the sound is more a wash or rumble than metal. The tail toggle and rust knob do not add convincing metallic character.
The large size has a swell-shaped envelope with no attack, centroid 490 Hz and a muddy low band. It reads as a fog horn or rumble, not a large bell.
The 3.5 s render gives the rocking motion an irregular, ill-defined rhythm. Strike timing is not legible, so seeds differ mainly in envelope shape rather than clapper pattern.
grades.lesson: Make sure the defining event of the sound (here, each discrete bell strike with a sharp attack and a ringing, decaying pitched tail) is clearly visible in the waveform and spectrogram at defaults; don't let a swell or noise layer smear it into a continuous wash.

flaws: The extremes break the sound. At every range minimum the render is a symmetric swell of noisy, broadband energy that fades in and out, with no strike transient and no ringing partials. It reads as a wash of noise, not a bell.

Seed 3 starts with about 1.5 s of near-silence before the first strike. Seed 2 starts after a gap, and its energy sits further right than the default. Onset timing therefore varies too much between takes, and the first hit may be late or missing in a game cue.

Seeds differ more than takes of one sound should. The hit placement, the number of strikes and the amount of leading silence all change, so seed 2 and seed 3 do not look like two takes of the same event.

Size 'small' loses the low partials and goes bright (centroid 2.5 kHz), with a weaker, thinner spectrogram. Size 'large' puts most of its energy in a low rumble (383 Hz). Both sit well away from the medium default. The large render has a late second strike and an uneven shape, with no obvious bell inharmonics.
The tail toggle only trims the decay and leaves 41% silence. The tail-less version is still the same length, 3.5 s, which wastes space in an asset meant to be short.

Every render is a fixed 3.5 s, so there is no way to control the length of a rocking cycle. Sounds meant to be a buoy clang cycle need a tempo or rocking-rate knob, which is missing. Because the strike timing is random, a designer cannot place the hits.
grades.lesson: Test every knob combination at its extreme, not just one knob at a time. If the extremes turn the sound into a generic noise swell or remove its defining transient, those ranges need to be narrowed or rebuilt. Also keep the seed from randomizing structural things like the first-hit time, so that takes differ only in detail.

brief: Short sequencer step tick for menu navigation; knobs: tone (hat|rim|blip), pitch 0..1, brightness 0..1, length 0..1

errors: knob length: too quiet (peak 0.187)
knob length: 79% of the buffer is silent

flaws: The default hat tone is a noise burst with a centroid near 6.7 kHz. It reads as a closed hi-hat, which is acceptable for a sequencer tick but is somewhat harsh and not especially 'LED' or menu-like.

The tone choices differ a lot. Rim and blip sit around 1.2-1.3 kHz and are pure ringing tones, while hat is broadband noise. Brightness and pitch will behave very differently across the three, so they are not equally useful on each.
The blip decays slowly, at 0.21 s with a visible tail. That is on the long side for a menu tick that gets rapid repeats.
