At minimum length the hat is 0.07 s with 52% silence, a very short click that may be too thin. At maximum it is 0.25 s, which is only a modest change in decay.
grades.lesson: When one selector switches between very different sound sources (noise vs. tonal), check that the continuous knobs still do something comparable in each mode, and keep the modes' loudness, length and spectral weight in a similar range so the choice reads as a variant of one sound.

brief: Canvas stall awning flapping in a breeze. Knobs: canvas weight (light/heavy), wind strength 0..1, flap rate, rope strain 0..1, tail toggle.

errors: knobs with no audible effect: strain
warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.86); takes should stay the same sound
seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.98); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: At defaults the sound reads as bursts of broadband noise with a regular low-frequency thump pattern, closer to a rhythmic wind gust or a distant engine pulse than canvas flapping. There are no sharp snap transients, which a flap needs.

The spectrogram shows a repeating low-frequency 'E E E' pulse at the bottom, a mechanical-looking comb of equal-spaced thumps. This is what makes it sound artificial, and it is present in nearly every render.

The range extremes are not the same kind of sound. The minimum setting gives sparse, decaying, isolated impacts that look like a bouncing object or footsteps. The maximum gives a dense, continuous noise wash that loses the flap articulation. The two do not read as one awning at different wind strengths.

Seed variation is inconsistent. Seed 2 collapses into two or three long swells with no discrete flaps, while the default has about 6 separate bursts. The seeds differ in event structure, not just detail, so they don't look like takes of one sound.
The tail toggle changes the sound little. Its effect is hard to distinguish from the seed differences, so it is a weak control.
The rope strain knob has no clearly visible or audible identity in the renders. It is unclear whether it adds creak or tonal content, and the spectrograms show no distinct creak band.
grades.lesson: Make sure the defining transient of the sound (here the sharp canvas snap) is clearly present in every seed and at every knob extreme, and avoid regular low-frequency pulse patterns that sound mechanical; vary event timing and level so the seeds look like takes of one process.

flaws: At defaults the sound reads as bursts of broadband noise with a low-frequency thump at the start of each, closer to a distant rhythmic rumble or breathy gusts than canvas flapping. There is no crisp snap or slap transient and no cloth-like texture, only soft wash with a low pulse.

Flap events are not clearly separated. Defaults and the max setting merge into a continuous noise bed with only a pulse at the bottom, so the sound loses the discrete 'flap-flap' character and tends toward wind or surf.

The minimum setting is a different sound: sparse isolated thuds with long decays and 22% silence, closer to distant knocks or a dripping, damped impact than an awning in a breeze. The range spans from percussive hits to a continuous wash, not just a variation in intensity.

Seeds differ in structure, not just detail. Seed 2 collapses into two broad swells with little rhythmic definition, while seed 3 keeps a more distinct pulse. They read as different gust patterns more than takes of one sound, and the pulse regularity varies a lot.

The low-end pulse is a regular tonal 'thud' at the same low frequency each time, which sounds mechanical and artificial for canvas. The knobs do not appear to give control over the snap brightness or the cloth texture.
Tail toggle gives a modest change, and the 'rope strain' knob has no obvious visual signature, so it is unclear what it contributes.
grades.lesson: Make the defining transient of the sound (here a crisp cloth snap) clearly visible and distinct at defaults and at every extreme, and confirm that range extremes change intensity or character within the same sound, not turn it into a different one such as a wash or sparse thumps.

flaws: Default render reads as 4 discrete, widely spaced clap or thump events with a long dead tail. Canvas flapping in a breeze should be a continuous, irregular snapping and billowing texture, not a sparse sequence of hits.

Silence is 19% at defaults, 28% at heavy and 33% at minimum. The ends of the renders are empty, so it does not loop or sit as a bed under a scene. The final events decay into nothing, which feels abrupt for an ambience.

Heavy canvas has no clear low-end weight. Its centroid actually rises to 3067 Hz, and the spectrogram looks like the same broadband clicks with fewer harmonic bands. Heavy canvas should be darker and thumpier, not brighter.

Strong narrow horizontal bands (red harmonic lines at low frequency) recur in some flaps. They read as tonal or musical rope or resonance, not fabric. They appear in some hits and not others, which sounds inconsistent.

Each flap is a broadband vertical line with a pronounced tonal ladder underneath and little cloth-like noise body between the hits. The sound is more like a door slamming or a wooden knock than flapping canvas.

Minimum range is just sparse, thin clicks (rms 0.034, centroid 3595 Hz) and does not read as a flapping awning. Seed variation is large: seed 2 has a dense cluster of hits and a different rhythm, so the takes feel less like the same sound.
The tail toggle gives a final hit rather than a tail, which is confusing as a control. A flap-irregularity or gust-variation knob would be more useful than a toggle.
grades.lesson: For a continuous or semi-continuous environmental texture, build a fabric-like noise body between discrete events and fill the whole duration, so the result does not turn into a few sparse hits with silent gaps. Make sure each knob moves the spectrum in the physically expected direction (heavy means darker).

brief: Unintelligible whispered phrase drifting past; knobs: voice (child|adult|choir), intensity 0..1, reverse amount 0..1, pan motion 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Spectrogram is broadband noise with vertical syllable-like bursts and no formant structure. It reads as amplitude-gated hiss, not a whisper. The voice choices (child/adult/choir) barely differ in spectral shape.
Centroid is around 2.5 kHz at default and in most variants. The voice switch only moves it between 1.9 and 2.5 kHz, so child, adult and choir are not clearly different characters.

The brief says 'drifting past', but the waveform and spectrogram give no visible sign of pan motion or distance movement. The images are mono-collapsed, so it is unclear the movement is audible or convincing.

Seeds differ a lot in structure. Seed 1 has two gaps and a big pause, seed 2 is a near-continuous block, and seed 3 has a different rhythm. RMS ranges from 0.074 to 0.104. These read as different phrases, not takes of one sound.

The tail=false render is not much shorter, still 3.2 s with a hard cutoff. Intensity and reverse extremes change the phrase rhythm rather than the character, and the all-max render has isolated blips that no longer read as a phrase.
Fixed 3.2 s length with no duration control, and silence of 23-39% in the middle of the sound makes it awkward to loop as an ambience layer.
grades.lesson: When imitating speech or voice-like sound, put in real spectral structure (formant bands, vowel and consonant contrast) and make each character option audibly distinct in the spectrogram. Gated broadband noise only reads as hiss. Keep seeds as variations of one gesture, not different rhythms.

flaws: Spectrogram is broadband noise with vertical syllable-like bursts and no formant structure, so it reads as chopped, amplitude-modulated noise rather than a whispered phrase.
The brief's 'drifting past' is barely visible in the renders, and the pan motion cannot be judged from them.

The voice presets look nearly alike, with only a centroid shift (1885 vs 2269 vs 2538 Hz) and no clearly different formant character for child, adult and choir. Adult reads as a continuous noise bed rather than a phrase.
The tail=false render shows a hard cutoff, so the ending is abrupt rather than a natural fade.

At the maximum extreme the render breaks into 4 isolated blips with long gaps, reading as separate clicks or thumps rather than one whispered phrase. Silence is 33-39% in several renders, so the phrase fragments.
Seeds differ a lot in density and gap structure (silence 20% vs 31%, rms 0.104 vs 0.088, and seed 3 looks like a continuous wash). They read as different sounds rather than takes of one phrase.
Peak is identical at 0.664 in every render, so the loudness ranges are normalised flat, and intensity does not change perceived dynamics.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a human or organic source, check that the spectrogram shows that source's defining structure (formants, harmonics, phrase rhythm). Shaped noise with amplitude gating only imitates its envelope. Make presets differ in structure, not only in brightness, and keep seed variation to detail within one phrase shape.

flaws: Spectrogram is broadband noise blobs with no visible formant structure or breathy vowel/consonant detail, so it reads as gated noise bursts rather than a whispered phrase.
Syllable bursts have hard rectangular edges, especially with tail=false, where it sounds like stuttering gated noise instead of speech-like articulation.
Tail toggle barely changes the overall shape and the tail is not a convincing ghostly reverb. The ending at default fades abruptly and the tail=false render is chopped.
Voice choices (child/adult/choir) differ mainly in rhythm and centroid, not in clear formant or timbre character. Choir does not read as multiple voices.
Seeds vary a lot in density and rhythm: seed 2 and 3 are near-continuous, while the default is sparse with gaps. They feel like different sounds rather than takes of one phrase.
Extremes of the ranges (min and max) have quite different structures, with the max splitting into isolated blobs. The sound loses the continuous phrase feel.
Pan motion and reverse cannot be seen as meaningful controls. Reverse amount shows no obvious reversed (swelling) envelopes.
grades.lesson: When synthesizing speech-like or vocal sounds from noise, give each voice type distinct formant/spectral shaping and smooth, articulated envelopes. Gated noise bursts alone read as stuttering static, not voice.

brief: Stack of paper squared up and shuffled on a desk; knobs: stack size (few sheets/ream), handling energy 0..1, tap-to-square amount 0..1, crispness 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The shuffle is a dense, uniform noise block of about 0.8 s, which reads as a noise burst or white-noise swish. It has no individual sheet flutter, slide texture or grain.

The squaring taps are nearly identical, evenly spaced low-thump clicks. They have a strong low-frequency blob at the bottom, so they sound like knocks on a desk, not paper edges being tapped. They look like a mechanical repeat.
Minimum range collapses to a single tap, and the shuffle becomes a sparse series of ticks that reads as a different sound (a clock or Geiger counter) rather than a quiet paper shuffle.
The maximum setting yields a loud, solid noise block with five taps, which is dense and artificial.

The tail is off by default, so the taps stop dead on silence (52% silent). The tail is only audible in the toggle-on state, and it looks like a faint sparse wash. Without it the sound feels cut off, with no room or desk resonance.
The stack-size knob changes mostly the density and centroid of the noise, not the character of the paper (stiffness and weight), so few sheets and ream sound alike.
grades.lesson: When a sound is made of distinct event types (such as a rustle and a tap), give each its own believable spectral and temporal texture, and check that the extremes of every knob keep the sound's identity. Noise blocks and identical repeated thumps read as synthetic, not as the real material.

flaws: The shuffle section is a noisy wash of broadband bursts with little paper-like texture. It reads as generic filtered noise more than riffling sheets.

The tap-to-square thumps are very narrow vertical lines with a strong low resonant band near the bottom. This sounds like a tonal desk knock, and the same fixed resonance recurs on every tap. It reads slightly synthetic.
The tail=false setting leaves 40% silence, with hard gaps between taps. This is acceptable as a toggle but sounds choppy.
At minimum ranges the shuffle is sparse and weak and the taps drop to two. It still reads as paper, but it is thin.
The stack-size choices change the centroid sensibly (few sheets 3225 Hz, ream 1639 Hz). The difference in the spectrogram is modest, mostly pitch of the noise rather than mass or sheet count.
grades.lesson: Give percussive or contact events natural variation in resonance and timbre per hit, and check the spectrogram for fixed horizontal lines that mark a repeated tone, since those make a sound read as synthetic.

brief: Confirm chime from two-tone cowbell blip; knobs: interval (fifth|octave|third), pitch 0..1, decay 0..1, sparkle 0..1

flaws: The spectrogram shows mostly steady horizontal partials, with little of the inharmonic metallic clank a cowbell has. It reads more like a damped two-note mallet or marimba blip than a cowbell.
The first tone is quieter and shorter, and the second tone has a long tail of roughly 0.4 s. A confirm blip would be tighter, so the default feels a little long and washy.
Minimum settings give a dull tone (centroid about 966 Hz) with the gap between the two notes widening to around 29% silence. The two hits no longer read as a single gesture.
The interval choices differ mainly in spectral weight and are not easy to tell apart in the pictures. The third and fifth look nearly identical.
Sparkle has no clearly visible effect in the renders. The knob set is minimal and has no control for gap time between the tones or for note order (ascending or descending).
grades.lesson: Check that the defining timbre of the named object (such as the inharmonic metallic partials of a cowbell) is visible in the spectrogram, not just the right envelope and pitch. Give each knob an effect large enough to see in the picture.

brief: Coins counted and slid across a wooden counter. Knobs: coin metal (copper/silver/gold), count rate, stack clink 0..1, slide amount 0..1, tail toggle.

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.74); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: The slide/scrape segment at the end looks like a broadband noise burst with a hard-edged rectangular spectrogram block. It reads more like a noise swish than wood-on-wood friction, and it is the least convincing part.

At the default setting the individual coin hits have sharp transients with long ringing decays. These sustained tonal lines read as bell or metal-plate ringing rather than short coin clinks. Copper is shorter and drier, which is better.

The minimum range gives only 3 hits with 31% silence, and the hits have long ringing tails. It still reads as coins, but it is sparse. The maximum range packs the hits densely and is close to a washy mess.
The counted hits are nearly evenly spaced. Real counting has more human timing jitter, and a 'humanize' knob is missing.
There is no wooden counter body or thunk under the clinks, so the wood surface is not conveyed. A surface or material knob is missing.
grades.lesson: When the brief names a surface or contact (wood counter, slide), model that surface's response (body thump, damping, friction texture) as its own layer rather than only the main object's ring. Add timing jitter to repeated events so they don't sound mechanically spaced.

brief: Fingernail scratching behind plaster; knobs: surface (plaster|wood|wallpaper), pressure 0..1, length 0..1, speed, tail toggle

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.69); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: Defaults show three discrete, evenly spaced bursts with a ~1 s dead tail. That reads as three taps or knocks, not a fingernail dragging across plaster. A scratch should be a continuous or stuttering friction texture with a rising and falling envelope, not separate blocky bursts.
The spectrogram shows broadband vertical striations and hard-edged bursts, so the sound is impulsive and clicky. Real scratching has a noisy, gritty, mid-to-high band with fine granular texture.

Default centroid is 822 Hz, which is too low for fingernail friction. Only wallpaper (2599 Hz) moves into a plausible range, and wood at 483 Hz sounds like knocking. Plaster, the brief's headline surface, is dull and does not sound like a nail.

Range minimum collapses to two sparse clicks with 33% silence. That reads as isolated ticks rather than a gentle scratch. The maximum is the same three-burst pattern, only louder, so the extremes are not clearly different sounds.
The tail=false render is 54% silence and ends abruptly after the third burst. The 3 s file is mostly empty, so the toggle does not behave like a real reverb or room tail.
Across seeds the burst count and spacing are almost identical. Variation is mostly in detail, which is acceptable, but the rigid three-stroke structure makes takes feel templated.
The knobs are reasonable, but 'length' and 'speed' appear to control the same burst spacing. There is no knob for grit or texture density, and no stroke-count control.
grades.lesson: Check that the temporal structure matches the physical action. Continuous-friction sounds such as scratching, scraping and rubbing need a continuous granular texture with modulated energy, not a few discrete impulses, and the spectral centroid should match the real material and contact.

flaws: At defaults the render reads as a dense, continuous noise wash with a fade, not fingernail scratching. There are no clear individual scratch strokes, no stroke-start transients and no rhythmic gaps.
The spectrogram is broadband, evenly smeared noise from bottom to top. It lacks the gritty, friction-like texture and the formant or resonant character of a nail dragging on plaster behind a wall.
The surface variants differ mostly in brightness. Wood is a low-centroid noise bed and wallpaper is a bright one, so they read as filtered noise rather than different materials.
The minimum-range render turns into a few isolated clicks and thumps with a low rumble. It no longer sounds like scratching, and 19% silence makes it feel broken in comparison with the other renders.
The tail=false render has 44% silence. It becomes four loud, uniform bursts, which reads as footsteps or knocks rather than scratches, and the sound ends abruptly at about 1.3 s of a 3 s file.
The seeds share a similar fade-out shape but differ a lot in loudness (rms 0.077 vs 0.12). The default seed is quieter than the others, and none of the takes has a distinct stroke structure.

Rendered length is fixed at 3.00 s whatever the settings, so the 'length' knob doesn't visibly shorten or lengthen the sound. A designer would expect it to change the duration or the number of strokes.
grades.lesson: Make the event structure of a sound legible, such as discrete strokes, hits or gestures with a clear onset, gap and decay. Filtered noise with a fade-out gives the right loudness but not the right sound, and the extremes of each knob should still keep that structure.

flaws: At defaults the render reads as a diffuse broadband noise wash with a decaying envelope, not a fingernail scraping behind plaster. The spectrogram is a uniform hazy fill with no visible stroke structure, so the 'scratch' character is weak.
Individual scratch strokes are hard to separate. The envelope is a continuous bumpy blob across 3 s, which sounds like rustling or static rather than discrete nail drags.

The 'tail = false' render shows four clean, evenly spaced bursts, which is much closer to a real scratch. It also has 44% silence. The default, with its smeared texture, is therefore the weaker take, and the tail adds a wash rather than a natural decay.

The range minimum collapses into a few sparse clicks and one low thump with an odd low-frequency band. It no longer reads as scratching, and the maximum is a dense, continuous noise bed. The extremes sound like different sounds.

Surface choices differ mostly in EQ (wood 536 Hz, wallpaper 3672 Hz centroid). Wood and wallpaper are the same noise with a filter on it, not different materials with different stroke behaviour. The brief's 'behind plaster' muffling is not apparent.
Seeds share a similar blobby envelope, but their detail differs only modestly. Seed 3 is almost a flat plateau, so the takes are not clearly distinct strokes.
Output is fixed at 3 s regardless of the length knob, so 'length' appears to change density rather than duration. That is confusing for a designer who wants a short single scratch.
grades.lesson: Build the sound from discrete, individually audible events (strokes, hits, steps) with clear gaps and per-event shape, and make material knobs change the event's character, not just apply a filter to continuous noise. Check that the default render shows the events as separate marks in the picture.

brief: Power toggle with relay thunk and speaker pop; knobs: switch (rocker|toggle), pop 0..1, hum-rise 0..1, relay 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Roughly 1.6 s long for a power switch with relay thunk and speaker pop. The transient occupies the first ~0.1 s, then a thin low-level hum sustains, so it reads as a click followed by a long buzz rather than a punchy switch event.

Centroid is about 250 Hz at defaults, so the sound is very bottom-heavy. A relay click and speaker pop should have audible mid and high content, and the spectrogram shows almost nothing above the low band. It sounds muffled rather than crisp.
The two switch types (rocker vs toggle) look nearly identical in waveform and spectrum, so the choice knob gives little real difference.

The minimum-range render has 24% silence and a centroid of 529 Hz, with a very short transient and a long empty tail. That is a different character from the default, and the long dead tail makes it feel unfinished.
The tail=true render has a visibly different, smeared reverb-like texture and a lower peak (0.69), which makes it inconsistent in level with the other renders.
Hum-rise is meant to be a gradual rise, but the waveform shows a flat low-level hum from the start with no clear rising envelope, so the knob's intent isn't visible.
The spectrogram's low band is a constant horizontal smear, so the sound does not read as a sequence of distinct events (relay thunk, then pop, then hum).
grades.lesson: Make each described component (e.g. thunk, pop, hum) a distinct, audible event with its own spectral region and timing, and check that the spectrum has energy where the real object would, rather than letting a low-frequency body dominate everything.

flaws: Length is wrong for the brief: every render is a fixed 1.10 s. A power switch with a relay thunk and a speaker pop should be a short event, not a long ringing tail. The waveform shows a sustained, slowly decaying ~100 Hz-ish buzz well past the transients, so it reads as a hum or resonance rather than a crisp switch.

The spectrogram is dominated by a hot band at the very bottom and persistent horizontal lines (a constant hum or resonance) across the whole duration. The mechanical click/thunk transients are small by comparison, so the relay character is weak and the sound is bass-heavy (centroid ~380 Hz) for a switch.

The 'every range at minimum' render still has the same 1.10 s length and a similar shape, and the maximum render is nearly identical to the defaults (centroid 378 vs 384 Hz, same envelope). Range extremes are not clearly different, so the knobs have little audible leverage.

The switch choice (rocker vs toggle) changes the render noticeably: a tall single transient and a more sustained hum body. This works as a variant, but the fixed duration and low-frequency body make both read as a boomy thud rather than distinct hardware.
Seeds are similar in overall shape, with only small differences in transient spacing. This is acceptable for variation but does not offset the other issues.

The 'tail' toggle adds broadband noise and raises the centroid to 477 Hz, but it does not read as a meaningful decay or room tail. The silence figure (7–11%) at the end suggests an abrupt cutoff, which looks unnatural.
grades.lesson: Make the sound's length and envelope match the real event (a short mechanical action should end quickly), and make sure knob extremes change the picture clearly. A constant low-frequency hum that dominates the whole render hides the transients that give the sound its identity.

flaws: The waveform has a long swelling envelope: after the initial transients, a pulsed low-frequency hum builds to a second peak at about 0.4 s and then decays. A power switch with a relay thunk and speaker pop should be a sharp click or thunk followed by a short decay, so this reads as a slow swell rather than a switch.

The spectrogram shows isolated vertical bands separated by gaps, with a sparse comb-like structure above them. These read as a few discrete clicks with nothing between them, not a single mechanical event, so the relay thunk and speaker pop do not fuse into one gesture.

The hum-rise component is the dominant energy and sits as a pulsed low-frequency pattern, so it sounds like a separate tremolo effect and not mains hum. The waveform spikes are widely spaced, which suggests a low-rate buzz or flutter.

The minimum-range render is clearly different from the default. It loses the hum swell, drops to 0.41 s with 21% silence, and has a sparse, thin tail, so the sound does not stay one kind of thing across the knob range. The maximum render grows to 0.96 s, which is long for a switch.

The 'tail' toggle changes the sound character: the render goes to 1.38 s with a noisy broadband wash, and the hum structure disappears. A toggle named 'tail' should only append decay, not change the body of the sound.

The 'switch' choice (rocker vs toggle) barely changes the picture: the two renders have nearly the same envelope and the same swell, with only a small centroid shift (553 to 614 Hz). It is not a meaningfully different mechanism.
The knob set is reasonable (pop, hum-rise, relay), but the defaults give a swell-dominated sound, so the most important element (the thunk) is not the lead.
grades.lesson: Keep the defining transient of a short mechanical sound dominant in the envelope, and make sure secondary layers like hum or tails support it instead of forming a second, louder peak; check that each toggle or choice changes only what its name says.

brief: Loopable 4s wipers swishing over rain drumming on roof; knobs: rain intensity 0..1, wiper rate, squeak 0..1, roof patter density 0..1, blade type (new/worn)

flaws: The wiper swish is a broadband noise swell with a flat spectrogram. It has no visible rain texture or roof patter underneath, so it reads as pulsing noise rather than wipers over rain.

The minimum-range render breaks into two isolated swells with near-empty gaps between them (4% silence). That is not the continuous rain bed the brief asks for. Rain should stay dense and even when its knobs are low, and only the wipers should change.

The wiper sweeps in the defaults start and end at different points, with the last swell cut off at the 4 s boundary. This makes the loop uncertain, and the minimum render has a hard transient at the end that would click on repeat.
The squeak is barely visible. It shows up as a few low-frequency blips at the bottom of the spectrogram, not as a high-frequency tonal chirp, so it would not read as rubber on glass.
The blade 'worn' option mostly lowers the centroid, which makes it sound duller. Worn blades should chatter or squeak more, so the difference is not the one a designer would expect.
At the maximum setting the wipers merge into a near-constant modulated wash, and individual swipes are hard to pick out. The wiper rate range is too wide for the 4 s loop.
grades.lesson: Build the constant background bed (e.g. rain) as its own layer that stays continuous at every knob setting, and let the knobs act on the foreground events (wipers) only. Check that event timing divides the loop length so the loop is seamless, and that each knob changes the property its name promises.

flaws: The wiper swishes show up as broad amplitude swells over a continuous noise bed. At defaults they are fairly soft and the sweep is not very distinct from the rain.
The spectrogram is mostly a flat, uniform wash. There is little visible roof patter transient structure or low-frequency thump to separate drumming from rain hiss.
The squeak is hard to see in the pictures. It appears only as small bright specks in the lower band, so it may be subtle.
At minimum ranges the wipers are clearer and the rain thins, but the swipes are still similar in shape. Differences between blade types are mainly a centroid shift, meaning a duller tone.
grades.lesson: Make each layer of a composite sound clearly identifiable in the render, with its own distinct spectral region and envelope, so that a layer such as a wiper swish or squeak is not buried in the broadband bed.

brief: Error/deny buzz from detuned low tom; knobs: wave (square|saw), detune 0..1, length 0..1, grit 0..1

flaws: The brief says detuned low tom, but the spectrogram shows no pitch drop and no tom-like thump. It reads as a generic buzzy pulse pair, not a drum.
The centroid is around 500 Hz and the energy is a flat smear of buzz. The low-end body of a tom is weak and mostly a thin line at the bottom.
Both buzzes have an abrupt, almost rectangular onset with a flat sustain and a fast fade. There is no distinct attack transient or resonant tail.
Range is narrow. Length only moves 0.34 s to 0.58 s, and the minimum and maximum renders look almost the same as the default, just shorter or longer.
The wave knob (square vs saw) changes the spectral detail only slightly, so the choice is weakly differentiated.
The knobs are few and partly vague. Grit and detune are abstract, and there is no pitch or tom-body control.
grades.lesson: Check that the signature trait in the brief (here, a tom's pitch drop and low body) is visible in the spectrogram at defaults. Don't settle for a generic buzz of the right length, and make sure each knob moves the sound enough to be heard as a different variant.

brief: Washer pump whine and fluid spritz on windscreen; knobs: pump strength 0..1, spray hiss 0..1, glass splatter 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The spritz is a roughly 1.4 s block of broadband noise with a slow fade-in and fade-out. A real washer spritz is a short burst (about 0.3-0.8 s) with a quick onset when the pump kicks in, so this reads as a generic noise wash rather than a spray.

The spectrogram shows full-band noise at nearly constant level from 0 to 8 kHz with only a thin pump-whine line at the bottom. The hiss dominates and the pump whine is weak and sits too low, which makes it sound like a rumbling motor, not a pump whine.

The glass splatter is not convincing. It shows up as sparse, thin vertical ticks in the tail, and at default they are barely visible and read as clicks. They should be dense droplet impacts on the glass during and after the spray.
The tail toggle makes only a small difference. With it on, a few stray ticks appear after a silent gap near the end, which looks like an abrupt or odd ending rather than a natural drip-off.

At minimum settings the noise body is still full length and the sound just goes darker, with an awkward isolated tick train at the end. At maximum settings the whine wobbles, which looks like a different sound. The extremes don't read cleanly as one sound.
Seed variation is mostly in amplitude wobble and where the end ticks fall. The body is the same noise, so the two takes feel only slightly different.
grades.lesson: Shape the temporal envelope to the real event (onset speed, duration, decay) before adding detail. A sound made of a long, slowly faded noise block reads as generic noise, and its distinguishing features (tonal whine, discrete droplets) must be clearly audible at defaults.

flaws: Envelope reads as a bloated blob with a slow ramp-up, not a spritz. A real washer squirt has a quick pump spin-up, a sharp spray onset and a distinct cutoff. Here the body is a near-constant slab of noise for about 0.8 s, then a ragged decay.

The pump whine is a few flat horizontal lines at low frequency, around 200-600 Hz, with a slight drop at the end. It sounds like a steady hum rather than a motor spinning up and down. There is no visible pitch ramp at the start.
The spray hiss is uniform broadband noise with no spritz character. There are no distinct droplet impacts on glass at defaults, and the 'glass splatter' only appears as a fuzzier tail.

The tail toggle barely changes anything. Tail=false looks almost identical to the default, with only a slightly shorter decay. The sound is also a fixed 1.40 s in every render, so there is no duration control.

At the minimum setting the sound is mostly pump hum with a thin noise bed, and the whine dominates, so it reads as an electric motor rather than a washer spray. The maximum setting becomes a diffuse noise wash and the pump is mostly buried.
grades.lesson: Give a sound a recognisable envelope and event structure (attack, onset, cutoff, discrete micro-events) instead of a steady noise bed with tonal lines. Check that toggles and layer knobs produce an obvious change in the picture, not a marginal one.

flaws: The defaults show a roughly 0.8 s pump and spray burst, then droplet ticks on the glass. That reads as a washer spritz, but the burst is dense and noisy, and the pump whine is only faint harmonic lines under the hiss.
At the minimum range the spray thins and the droplet tail turns sparse and tonal, with ringing lines in the spectrogram. This sounds less like fluid on glass.
At the maximum range the pump whine is partly buried in the broadband noise.
With the tail toggled off, the sound ends abruptly at about 0.85 s, followed by 42% silence. The result is a hard cut instead of a natural fade, though the toggle does what it says.
The droplet tail is a handful of discrete, evenly spaced ticks and may sound artificial.
grades.lesson: When a sound has a tonal layer and a noise layer, check that the tonal layer stays audible at the top of every knob range, and that sparse event tails (drips, ticks) keep a natural, irregular spacing and a tapered ending.

brief: Bronze church or market bell tolling once. Knobs: bell size (handbell/tower/great), strike force 0..1, inharmonic shimmer 0..1, distance 0..1, pitch, decay-tail toggle.

flaws: The default waveform has a long, near-constant low-level plateau after the initial decay. A real bronze bell fades continuously, so this reads as a sustained drone rather than a natural ring-out.
Size choices are not clearly separated by decay. Handbell and default both run the full 4 s and have similar envelopes, so the difference is mostly pitch.
The spectrogram shows a few strong horizontal partials and little of the bright strike-transient energy. The strike is less metallic and hammered than a real bell.
With tail=false the sound stops at about 2 s and 47% of the file is silence, so it feels abruptly truncated rather than naturally shortened.
At max range the envelope has pronounced amplitude beating and swelling, closer to a gong or synth pad than a single toll.
grades.lesson: Check that the decay envelope falls continuously to zero rather than settling on a flat plateau. Make each categorical choice (such as size) differ in envelope and decay time as well as pitch, so the options read as distinct objects.

brief: Small boat diesel idling at the quay; knobs: engine (outboard|inboard-diesel|old-two-stroke), rpm 0..1, roughness 0..1, exhaust burble 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.70); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: Brief is a small boat diesel idling, but the engine choices are outboard, old-two-stroke and a default that is not clearly a diesel. The spectrogram shows a plain train of pulses with energy mostly below ~500 Hz and little harmonic structure. This reads as a generic pulse or tick generator rather than a diesel with combustion thump and low-frequency body.
Pulses are very regular and sharp, like a metronome or tractor. There is no visible cylinder-to-cylinder firing pattern, rpm wobble or slow load variation, so it does not sound like a lived-in idle.
The engine choice barely changes the picture. Outboard, two-stroke and the default all look like the same pulse train with slightly different density, so it adds little real variety.
At minimum range the pulses are sparse, with long gaps between thin spikes. This reads as a ticking clock rather than a slow diesel idle with overlapping thumps.

The tail toggle just ends the sound and fades to a thin, near-silent wash after about 1.7 s. This leaves most of the 3 s file as dead space and does not suggest an engine spooling down. Having 7% silence in the tail render with a hard cutoff in the waveform looks abrupt.

The default has no 'quay' character such as water lap, hull resonance or surrounding ambience, so it is not a usable scene bed. There is also no obvious high-frequency exhaust burble content in the spectrogram, so the burble knob's effect is unclear.
grades.lesson: Build the sound's defining character (for example the low-frequency body, firing pattern and slow drift of an engine) rather than just a periodic pulse train. Make categorical options differ in spectrum and rhythm, not only in pulse rate, and make tail or end-state options decay naturally instead of cutting out.

flaws: The default inboard-diesel idle shows a broadband, noisy texture with a centroid of about 377 Hz and a dense comb of vertical pulses. It reads as rough filtered noise with a buzzy click train, not a heavy diesel thump with a clear low firing-rate fundamental and harmonics.

The spectrogram shows almost no tonal or harmonic structure and no low-frequency band that stands out. The energy is smeared. A diesel idle should have a steady, countable pulse rate with strong low harmonics.

The engine choices (outboard, old-two-stroke) are not diesels, and the brief asks for a boat diesel idling at the quay. The outboard and two-stroke variants look similar to the default apart from a slightly higher centroid, so they are weakly differentiated.
The tail toggle adds an abrupt amplitude drop and a restart-like section near the end, and the waveform dips and rebounds in a way that does not read as a natural engine shutdown. It looks glitchy.
There is no quay context (water lap, hull resonance, reflections). The sound is a dry engine texture, so the sense of place is weak.
At the minimum range the pulses are very regular and mechanical, like a metronome. This is not the loose, uneven idle that the roughness knob should give.
grades.lesson: Check that the signature of the sound is clearly visible in the spectrogram (here, a countable low-frequency pulse train with harmonics). Do not let broadband noise with a pulse overlay stand in for the source. Make each variant of a category choice differ in structure, not only in brightness.

flaws: The brief is a small boat diesel idling at the quay, but the default centroid of 176 Hz and the spectrogram show almost all energy in a low band at the bottom. There is no visible harmonic firing structure and no water or hull character. It reads as a low rumble, not a diesel idle.
The waveform is a dense, uniform buzz at constant amplitude. A diesel idle should have a clear, slightly irregular firing pulse, and this shows no audible cylinder rhythm or lope in the picture.

The 'tail = true' option turns the sound into a 3 s file that decays after about 1.2 s and then goes nearly silent with a faint bump. That is an engine shut-off with a stray late event, not an idle tail. The ending is ambiguous and the bump looks like an artifact.

The engine choices differ mainly in brightness (708 Hz and 408 Hz against 176 Hz). Outboard and two-stroke look like noisier versions of the same buzz, and the default is not even labelled inboard-diesel in the sweep. The 'inboard-diesel' character is not clearly distinct from the others.
The max-range render loses the periodic pulse and becomes a flat noisy band with a lower RMS, so the extreme reads less like an engine than the defaults do.

Knobs are partly misdirected for the brief. There is no control for the quay setting (water lap, hull resonance, distance) and no cylinder count or firing irregularity. 'Tail' as a toggle is an odd choice for a looping idle, where a loop-point or seamless-loop option would be more useful.
grades.lesson: Check the spectrogram for the signature structure the brief names (for an engine, a visible firing-rate pulse with harmonics), not just the right loudness and length. Make sure each categorical choice changes the character, not only the brightness, and that every toggle produces something a designer would actually use.

brief: Sheet crumpled into a ball and optionally tossed; knobs: paper type (printer/glossy/tissue), crumple speed rate, crackle density 0..1, toss-and-land amount 0..1, tail toggle

errors: defaults: 70% of the buffer is silent
knob speed: 76% of the buffer is silent
knob toss: 77% of the buffer is silent
seed 2: 71% of the buffer is silent
random combination 2: 71% of the buffer is silent
random combination 3: 73% of the buffer is silent

flaws: The crumple is built from six near-identical, evenly spaced rectangular noise blocks. Real paper crumpling is a dense stream of irregular crackles with varying amplitude. This reads as a machine-gun or helicopter chop, not paper.
Each block has a hard, flat-topped envelope and uniform spectral colour from bottom to top. There are no individual crackle transients inside the block, so the crackle texture is missing at defaults.

The toss-and-land tail is only a few sparse clicks after a long gap, which looks like scattered ticks, not a ball bouncing and settling. The silent gap between crumple and toss is about 0.5 s, which feels disconnected.
At the minimum range setting the sound turns into a continuous, evenly pulsing noise bed with no toss. It no longer reads as crumpling and differs in character from the default.
The paper types differ mostly by centroid and burst loudness. Printer, glossy and tissue all share the same six-block rhythm, so they sound like the same sound with a filter change.
The tail=true render shows a smeared wash with no gaps, which makes the toggle behave more like a different sound than an optional tail.
Seeds share an almost identical block pattern, with differences mainly in the tail clicks, so the takes are too similar for variation.
grades.lesson: Do not build organic, irregular textures from a few regular, evenly spaced envelope blocks. Make the micro-events (crackles, impacts) the actual substance, with randomised timing and amplitude, and use a slow envelope only to shape their density.

flaws: The crumple is six near-identical, evenly spaced, dense noise blocks, each with a flat rectangular envelope and a hard edge. Real paper crumpling is a stream of irregular crackles with uneven spacing and amplitude. This reads as a machine-gun or helicopter pulse, not paper.

The spectrogram is the same broadband noise in every block, with no individual crackle structure inside the blocks. Paper crinkle should be many tiny, sharp transients, so the sound is closer to gated white noise.

Paper types are only weakly differentiated. Glossy and tissue look like the same pulse pattern with a slight brightness and level change, and the centroid shifts only about 1 kHz, so the three types do not read as clearly different materials.

The minimum-range render turns into continuous, even noise bursts with no real gaps and a regular pulse across the whole 2.4 s. That no longer reads as a crumple, and it is a different sound from the default.

The toss/land section is a few faint, thin ticks after a long silence. The landing is weak, with no body or thump, and the gap after the crumple is too long to feel like one gesture. Silence is 35% at defaults.
The tail=true render fuses the pulses into a smeared wash with a slow decay. It reads as noise rather than a paper tail, and it differs strongly from the default shape.
Between the crumple and the toss there is an empty gap of about 0.5 s, which makes the sound feel like two disconnected events.
grades.lesson: Organic crackle and impact sounds need irregular timing, amplitude and spectrum inside each event. Evenly spaced, identically shaped noise blocks sound mechanical, however they are filtered, so randomise event intervals and build each burst from many micro-transients.

flaws: The crumple is built from six near-identical, evenly spaced noise blocks of about 0.3 s each. Each block has a flat plateau envelope and a hard start and stop, so it sounds like a gated noise machine. Real paper crumpling is a dense, irregular cluster of tiny crackles and pops with uneven amplitude, not a regular pulse train.
Every burst has the same duration, spacing and level, so the rhythm is mechanical. Real hand motion would speed up, slow down and vary in intensity.

The spectrogram shows broadband noise with no spectral movement within a burst. Paper crackle should have sharp micro-transients with a bright, sparse texture. This reads as band-limited noise swells.

The toss and land section (the sparse ticks after about 1.3 s) is a few weak, scattered clicks. It does not read as a ball bouncing and landing, and it is much quieter than the crumple. About 35% of the default render is near silence.

At the minimum range the crumple stretches across the whole 2.4 s as continuous, evenly spaced noise bursts with no toss and no ending. At the maximum the toss tail becomes a long, distinct second event. The sound changes structure across the range rather than reading as one object.

The paper type presets differ mostly in brightness, with only slight shifts in centroid and RMS. Printer, glossy and tissue are not clearly distinct in crackle character. Tissue should be softer and quieter, but it is the loudest preset.
The tail toggle has a large effect, but it fills the silence with a continuous noise decay rather than adding a tail. That makes it a different sound, not an optional tail.
grades.lesson: For textured, impulsive sounds such as crumpling, rustling or crackling, build the sound from many randomized micro-events with varied timing, amplitude and spectrum. Do not use a few uniform noise blocks, which sound like a machine rhythm. Check that each knob changes one thing and leaves the sound's identity intact.

brief: Huge sub kick drop for trailer hits; knobs: size (room|arena|cinematic), sub 0..1, distortion 0..1, sweep 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The 'huge' trailer hit has a centroid of about 103 Hz and almost no visible pitch sweep. The spectrogram shows a flat low band rather than a falling line. A sub kick drop should fall audibly from roughly 120 Hz to 30 Hz, and this reads as a short buzzy low-frequency burst.

The waveform looks like a dense, flat-topped burst for the first 0.5 s, then a thin decaying hum. That suggests heavy distortion or hard saturation on the body and little of the long boom-and-decay a trailer hit needs. The 3 s render is mostly a near-silent tail.

The size choices do not read as room, arena and cinematic. Room and arena have the same shape, differing only in level and a little tail. Cinematic is a longer sustained block, not a larger space. All three have centroid about 103-106 Hz, so there is no audible change in space or weight.

The sweep range does little. Min and max renders both show a nearly flat low band with no clear falling pitch line, and the centroid shifts only from 78 to 134 Hz. The signature knob of a kick drop barely changes the sound.
The tail toggle just trims the tail, and the 'false' render still has the same length and a long quiet stretch. The body is not shortened, so it is not a usable dry hit.
Missing knobs a designer would want: pitch start and end frequency, decay length, a click or transient layer, and a low-pass or tone control. Size is a categorical choice that does too little.
grades.lesson: Make the knob that defines the sound (here, the pitch sweep) produce a clearly visible, audible change across its range. Check in the spectrogram that categorical choices differ in more than level, and that the signature feature, such as a falling pitch line, is actually present.

flaws: The brief asks for a huge trailer-hit sub drop, but the renders show a short low-frequency burst of about 0.5 s followed by a flat, near-silent tail. The 3 s file is mostly dead air (30% silence at defaults, up to 50% for 'room'). A trailer hit needs a long, audible sub decay or boom tail.

The spectrogram shows no clear falling pitch line. The energy sits in a flat band at the bottom, so the signature kick pitch drop is not visible. The 'sweep' knob moves the centroid only 78→134 Hz, which is too subtle to read as a sweep.

The size presets are not clearly different. 'Room' and 'arena' have nearly identical centroids (106 vs 103 Hz) and almost the same duration and shape. 'Cinematic' mostly adds a longer sustained body. None gives the sense of scale a 'huge' hit needs, and all stay 3.00 s.
The 'tail = false' render is almost the same length and shape as the default, so the toggle barely changes anything. Both renders still show a long, nearly silent stretch.

The waveform looks like a dense, buzzy low-frequency burst, which suggests a rough or distorted sine and no distinct click or beater transient. The sound lacks the layering (click, thump, sub, boom) that makes a trailer hit useful.

The knob set is thin for the job. It has no pitch start/end or drop time, no decay length, and no impact transient control. The 'size' preset mixes several parameters into one switch, which hides the controls a designer would want.
grades.lesson: Make each knob produce an obvious, measurable change in the picture, such as a visible pitch line, clearly different lengths or tail energy. Make sure the sound fills its rendered duration, since long silent tails and presets that look the same make the sound read as a generic, weak version of what the brief asked for.

flaws: Waveform looks like a flat-topped, near-constant-amplitude oscillation that decays only slowly and then sits at a steady low-level line for about 2 s. A trailer sub hit should show a punchy transient, a clear falling pitch line and a smooth decay to silence. The spectrogram shows no visible pitch drop, just a static low band.
Centroid of about 73 Hz with almost all energy in one thin low strip means there is no click or body layer. It reads as a sustained sine buzz rather than a huge cinematic hit.
The tail is mostly a constant-level hum that is cut abruptly at 3.00 s. The fixed 3 s length ends with a visible step rather than a fade.

size=room has 47% silence, so the sound ends at about 1.6 s and the rest is dead air. Room, arena and cinematic differ mainly in length and level, not in character. Cinematic is only marginally different from the default.
The sweep knob at its minimum and maximum shows almost no visible change in the pitch contour. The range extremes look very similar to each other.
tail=false still runs the full 3 s with a sustained low-level line, so the toggle does not clearly remove a tail.
Seeds are near-identical in shape, with only slight detail differences. That is acceptable but unremarkable.
grades.lesson: Check that the signature feature of the sound, such as a pitch drop, transient or decay, is visible in the spectrogram at defaults and responds visibly to its knob. Make sure a tail or length control really changes the ending, and fade every render to silence instead of cutting it at a fixed length.

brief: Town crier swinging a handbell to gather attention. Knobs: bell size (small/medium), swing rate, intensity 0..1, clapper rattle 0..1, distance 0..1, tail toggle.

flaws: Handbell reads as a sustained drone with swelling envelope rather than discrete bell strikes: the spectrogram shows long horizontal partial lines persisting through the whole 3 s with no decay between rings, so strikes smear together.
Strike transients are weak and soft; each swing is only a small bump on a continuous bed, with no clear clapper impact, so it doesn't sound like a bell being swung.

Swing rate at max collapses into one long continuous wash with a slow envelope. Individual rings are no longer distinguishable, which is a broken extreme for a swing-rate knob, and the spectrum turns noisy and smeared.
Swing rate at min gives only 3 hits with a pulsing amplitude envelope, which sounds like tremolo rather than a swung bell; the range between min and max is not the same kind of sound.
Size knob (small vs medium) changes little visually: the centroid shifts only slightly and the partial structure looks similar, so the choice is weakly differentiated.
tail=false only slightly changes the end: the 3 s duration is unchanged and the decay is still long, so the toggle does little.
Seed variation is mostly timing and level jitter on the same drone; the strike spacing is irregular in a way that looks random rather than a human swing rhythm.
grades.lesson: Make each event (strike, step, hit) a discrete transient with its own decay, and check at the extreme parameter settings that individual events stay distinct rather than smearing into a continuous drone or wash.

flaws: Range extremes break the sound: with every range at its maximum the render becomes a single smeared swell with no discrete bell strikes, so it no longer reads as a swung handbell.
At minimum ranges there are only 3 widely spaced strikes with silent gaps, which sounds like a slow tolling rather than a handbell being swung.
Strike transients are weak and the decay is long, so strikes overlap into a continuous wash by the final hit. A handbell should ring and fade between swings with a clear clapper attack.
The default has a very long final-strike ring, and the last hit is louder than the earlier ones, so the pattern looks like a crescendo rather than a steady swing.
Clapper rattle and distance are hard to see in the spectrograms. The size knob changes the centroid but the sound stays tonally generic with little inharmonic bell partial structure.
The tail toggle leaves 38% silence when off, so the ring does not carry over between strikes, which sounds unnatural for a bell.
grades.lesson: Test the knob extremes combined, not just individually: if all ranges at maximum merge discrete events into a smear, clamp the combined ranges so the sound keeps its defining structure, such as separate strikes.

flaws: The maximum-range render collapses the individual bell strikes into a continuous dense wash with a swelling envelope, so it reads as a sustained drone or noise bed instead of a swung handbell. This is the weakest point of the sound.
Strikes at default are fairly uniform in decay and spacing, so the swing feels mechanical. A real handbell has uneven clapper hits and alternating strong and weak strokes.
The bell size 'small' option raises the centroid but looks thin: partials are sparse and the tone is noticeably less bell-like and more pingy.

The default ring lasts about 3 s with an overlapping tail, which smears the final strikes. This may be fine for a crier, but the tail toggle gives a different last strike (a long sustained ring) rather than simply omitting the tail.
Knob ranges are not clearly labelled, and the extreme of swing rate seems to merge strikes into a continuous sound.
grades.lesson: Test knob extremes against the sound's defining identity: if a rate or density knob at max merges discrete events into a continuous wash, cap it where the individual events remain distinguishable.

brief: Paper torn in a single rip or slow peel; knobs: paper type (printer/cardstock/notepad perforation), tear speed rate, fiber grit 0..1, sheet count 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The waveform is a dense, near-constant noise block with a rounded envelope. It reads as a generic noise burst, not a rip. A real tear is a series of irregular crackly micro-transients with gaps and a speed-dependent pitch and rate.
The spectrogram is a flat, diffuse wash across the whole band with no visible fiber-snap structure, and the energy is concentrated in the lowest band. It looks like filtered noise, not paper.

The 38% silence figure is odd for a single continuous rip. The waveform's flat line is a trailing tail of nothing, so the sound sits in the first ~65% of the file and the rest is dead air, which is poor for a registry asset.

The paper types differ mainly in centroid (1271 / 1928 / 2470 Hz). The envelope and texture are almost the same, so printer, cardstock and notepad perforation do not read as different materials. Notepad perforation should be a ratchet of discrete ticks, but it shows none.

At minimum the sound stretches to 2.1 s and becomes a smooth, sustained swell, much less like a tear. At maximum it shrinks to 1.05 s with a hard cutoff. The extremes change the character instead of just the speed.

The tail toggle has little audible effect: the waveform shape is nearly the same and only the silence fraction changes slightly. The 'single rip or slow peel' brief is not clearly served, because there is no real slow-peel behaviour.
Seeds share the same blocky noise body and differ only in peak positions, so variation is shallow.
grades.lesson: Build the defining micro-structure of the sound (for a tear, discrete irregular fiber snaps with rate tied to speed) instead of shaped continuous noise, and make each categorical choice differ in texture and envelope, not just in filter centroid.

flaws: At defaults the render is a smooth spindle-shaped noise swell over the full 1.30 s, with no sharp onset and no fibre-snap transients. It reads as a filtered noise burst or a fade-in/out wash, not a rip. A real tear starts abruptly and is a rapid train of crackly micro-impulses.
The spectrogram is a uniform noise wash across the whole band, with no visible transient structure. The 'single rip or slow peel' character is missing.
The minimum-range render is flat, steady noise for 1.3 s with no envelope shape. It sounds like a hiss bed rather than a tear, so the extremes do not hold as the same kind of sound.
The maximum-range render has 21% silence, with the sound ending abruptly at about 1.0 s followed by a flat line. This is a hard cut.

The tail=false render is the only one that shows discrete rip pulses, so the correct rip texture exists but is hidden at defaults. It also has 49% silence and a hard cutoff. The tail toggle effectively switches between a noise wash and a short stub, not between natural and dry versions.
Tear speed does not change the duration: every render is exactly 1.30 s. A rate knob that leaves the length fixed misses the point of a slow peel versus a fast rip.
Seeds 2 and 3 share the same smooth swell shape with only small differences in detail. That is acceptable variation, but they all share the wrong shape.
Paper types differ little in the spectrogram. Cardstock and notepad are distinguishable mainly by centroid, and notepad perforation shows no clear periodic ticking.
grades.lesson: Build the defining micro-structure of the sound (for example, the impulse train of a tear) into the default render, and make sure the envelope has the right attack. Do not use a smooth noise bed with an amplitude curve, which reads as generic noise. Check that time-related knobs such as speed actually change duration, and that toggles end naturally rather than by hard cut.

flaws: The default render has a ~1.4 s noisy body followed by a short tail. This reads as a plausible rip but is a bit uniform, with no clear start transient or speed ramp, so it sounds closer to a generic crackle burst than a single tear.
The minimum-range render is 2.6 s with 46% silence and sparse isolated clicks. It reads as a slow peel of scattered ticks, not a tear, and is far from the default in character.
The maximum-range render is dense and loud (rms 0.164) and only 0.92 s long. It sounds more like a fast scrub or noise burst than paper.
The notepad perforation variant has a very regular comb of evenly spaced pulses. This suits perforation but looks mechanical, like a zipper.
The tail toggle changes the length a lot (1.06 s vs 1.40 s), and tail=false ends abruptly at full level. Acceptable, but a designer would want a short fade.
Seed variation is fine: the same envelope shape with different detail.
grades.lesson: Make the extremes of every knob still read as the same sound: check that the slowest and fastest settings keep the defining features of the source (here a continuous fibre-tearing texture, not isolated clicks or a dense scrub), and give hard-cut options like a tail toggle a short fade so they don't end abruptly.

brief: Stacked gated toms and snare slam; knobs: size (studio|hall|stadium), punch 0..1, gate 0..1, layering 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Defaults read as a short noisy burst, not stacked toms plus snare. The spectrogram shows broadband noise with a low smear and no falling pitch lines, so there is no tom body or pitch drop.
Waveform is a dense block of roughly constant amplitude that cuts off abruptly. This may be intended for a gate, but there are no distinct hits in the stack, so it sounds like a gated noise burst.
The 'size' choices barely differ: studio, hall and stadium all have the same length and similar envelope. Only the burst width and centroid change slightly, so they do not read as three room sizes.

The gated reverb character is not convincing. With the tail off, about 64% of the 1.6 s file is dead silence. Tail on gives a long natural decay that contradicts the 'gated' brief, so the tail toggle changes the sound's identity rather than acting as an option.
The extremes of the ranges are inconsistent. The minimum setting is the widest and densest, and the maximum is similar to the default, so the knob direction is unclear.
Seeds share the same envelope but the detail looks like noise variation. Without distinct tonal elements, the seeds are hard to tell apart as separate takes of tom hits.
grades.lesson: Check that the spectrogram shows the defining features named in the brief (e.g. pitch-dropping tonal bodies for drums) instead of only a matching envelope, and make enum choices change the sound's structure, not just a few percent of its width.}

flaws: Waveform has a roughly flat, noise-like envelope that builds up slowly, and the main hit arrives late (about 0.25 s into the clip) instead of a sharp transient at the start. A gated tom slam should hit hard and cut off, but this reads as a swell.

The spectrogram shows no falling pitch line. The tom body is not visible as a tonal drop, so the low end is just a smeared band of energy. Centroid of about 540 Hz with mostly broadband noise reads as a noise burst rather than stacked toms plus a snare.

The gate is not audible as a gate. Defaults decay gradually instead of cutting off hard, and the 'tail = true' option adds a mostly silent 24% stretch with a small trickle, which is weak as a reverb tail and does not behave like gated reverb.
The faint vertical ticks before the main hit are odd pre-hit artifacts and look like stray clicks, not intentional layers.

Size changes the length and onset time in a non-obvious way (studio 0.62 s, stadium 0.87 s), and the hit position shifts, so it is not a clean difference in room size. The 'every range at its minimum' render has a front-loaded decaying shape, while the maximum looks like a different sound, so the extremes do not read as the same kind of sound.
Seeds change the envelope shape noticeably (seed 2 is more of a swell, seed 3 is flatter), so the takes are only loosely the same sound.
grades.lesson: Check that the render has the defining shape of the sound in the picture, such as a sharp transient at t=0 and a visible pitch drop for a drum, rather than only meeting length and loudness numbers. A noise-heavy build-up with a late onset will read as the wrong sound however well the knobs are named.

flaws: Default render reads as a noise burst rather than stacked toms plus snare. The waveform is a dense, flat, noise-like block with no visible pitched tom body and no pitch-drop line in the spectrogram. Energy is a broad wash with a hot band only at the very bottom.
Gated-reverb character is weak: the sound is a steady plateau that then cuts off, but there is no distinct transient hit or snare crack at the start, and no discrete layered hits are visible.

The size choices barely differ in character. Studio and hall are both about 0.9 s with a similar shape, and the stadium one is just a longer gate plateau. The size names suggest room size, but the changes are mostly gate length and level.

The tail toggle is the only way to get a natural decay. With it off, the sound ends abruptly in a hard cut with 40% silence in a 0.9 s file, which sounds like a clipped sample. Gated is the intended style, but the default has a dead second half and no tail.

The range extremes shift the centroid from 442 to 817 Hz without changing the structure much. At minimum, the sound is a long noise block with little punch; at maximum, it is a shorter, cut-off burst.
Spectral content is mostly low and mid noise with almost nothing above a few kHz, so there is no snare crack or sizzle. The low-end energy is a thin band instead of a tom fundamental.
grades.lesson: When the brief names pitched or tonal elements (toms, kicks, snares), make sure the render shows them: a visible fundamental with a pitch sweep and distinct onsets. Noise shaped by an envelope reads as a generic burst, not the named instrument.

brief: Engine cranking and catching; knobs: engine (outboard|diesel), crank attempts 0..1, choke sputter 0..1, smoke cough 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The brief is an engine cranking and then catching, but the defaults show a flat noise-like envelope for the full 3.5 s. There is no clear crank rhythm of starter pulses, and no distinct moment where the engine catches and settles into a steady idle.

The spectrogram energy sits almost entirely in a low band below roughly 400 Hz, with only faint vertical ticks above it. There are no visible harmonic lines or a rising firing rate, so it reads as rumbling noise rather than an engine with combustion pulses.

The diesel option is almost indistinguishable from the default outboard in both waveform and spectrogram. The centroid shifts from 341 to 267 Hz, but no diesel-specific character such as knock or a slower firing rate shows up.

At the range extremes the structure changes a lot. The minimum is a flat, steady wash with no catch event, and the maximum has a swelling burst near the end with fades at both ends. The catch moment moves around, so the sound does not stay the same kind of event.

The seeds differ in where the loud section lands: seed 1 peaks mid-way, seed 2 has a central burst, and seed 3 is fairly flat. The take-to-take overall shape is therefore inconsistent, and the narrative is not clearly the same.
The tail toggle makes little visible difference. The sound already ends abruptly at 3.5 s with no decaying idle or shutoff.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes a sequence of events (e.g. crank, then catch, then idle), render a clear, visible structure for each stage at default settings, with distinct spectral and rhythmic changes between stages. Do not rely on a continuous noise bed with a modulated amplitude.

flaws: The brief is crank, then catch, then settle into idle, but the default waveform is one swelling and decaying blob. There are no distinct crank cycles (rhythmic starter-motor pulses that slow and speed up), and no clear moment where the engine catches.

The spectrogram energy is almost entirely below about 500 Hz and there is little structure. It reads as a low rumble or noise burst, not a combustion engine with firing pulses and harmonics. A sound designer would hear a generic whoosh.

With the tail off, the render has about 25% silence and shows isolated bursts at the start with gaps, then a short cluster. It does not read as a start that catches and runs. It sounds like a few disjointed hits, not an engine.

Min and max range renders look nearly identical in envelope, and the min lacks any visible crank or sputter structure. The crank attempts, choke sputter and smoke cough knobs are not distinguishable in the pictures, so they likely add subtle noise variation rather than clear events.
The diesel and outboard choices differ only slightly (centroid 309 Hz against 345 Hz) and have the same envelope. They do not give a distinct diesel clatter or outboard buzz.
The 4 s length with a swell-and-fade envelope means the engine never settles into a steady idle. The ending is a fade, not a running engine that a designer can loop or cut.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes a sequence of events (crank, catch, run), make each stage visibly distinct in the render with its own rhythm and spectrum, and check that the knobs change those events, not only the overall level or noise.

flaws: The waveform is a steady, regular pulse train with a loud spike near 1.4 s, then a long flat plateau. It does not read as cranking and catching: there is no slow, uneven starter cadence, no clear failed attempt, and no firing that accelerates into a stable idle.

The catch moment looks like a single sharp transient on top of an otherwise uniform texture. Pre-catch and post-catch sections have similar level and spectrum, so the engine start has little narrative arc.

Spectrograms are dominated by low-frequency energy with faint vertical striping. Nothing visible suggests choke sputter, a smoke cough, or the diesel/outboard difference, which is mostly a centroid shift (468 vs 324 Hz).
The 'tail = false' render changes the structure of the sound, with the loudest burst moving and the crank section looking different, rather than just removing a tail. Its silence rises to 8%.
The 'crank attempts' minimum and maximum renders look nearly the same in structure (a similar steady pulse train). That makes the knob feel weak compared with the choke and smoke controls.
The sound runs a fixed 4 s with no length control, and it ends abruptly at full level with no wind-down or settling. The tail toggle alone does not fix this.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes a sequence of events (fail, fail, catch, settle), render and check that the waveform shows distinct phases with different density, level and spectrum. A uniform texture with one transient does not tell the story.

brief: Picture frame or mirror falling and cracking; knobs: glass size (small|mirror|window), force 0..1, shard scatter 0..1, tail toggle

errors: random combination 4: 70% of the buffer is silent

flaws: Reads as one broadband noise burst with a smooth exponential decay, not a glass crack. There is no distinct initial crack transient followed by separate tinkling shards. The spectrogram is a diffuse wash, and the impact and debris layers are not separable.

The brief says the object falls and cracks, but nothing in the envelope shows a fall, impact and then shard scatter. Shard scatter only shows up as faint isolated ticks in the tail at the max setting, and at default they are barely visible.

The three glass sizes look nearly identical in envelope and length, all 1.76 s. The size choice mostly shifts the centroid slightly (3285 to 4248 Hz) and does not change decay, resonance or ring. A window should sound very different from a small frame.

Defaults have about 42% silence, with a long, almost inaudible low-level tail past roughly 1.1 s. The tail toggle off gives a more usable sound, which suggests the default tail is padding rather than content.
Spectral energy is concentrated in a low band at the bottom, and tonal glass ring or high sparkle is missing. The sound reads as a generic noise crash, or even a thud, rather than glass.
grades.lesson: Build a sound from its distinct physical events (for example a sharp impact transient followed by separate resonant or scattered secondary events), and make each categorical choice change the decay, resonance and spectrum rather than just shifting a filter, so the picture shows layers rather than one noise burst with a decay.

flaws: The brief is a falling mirror or frame cracking, but every render shows one big impact followed by a smooth exponential decay. There is no distinct crack, no separate fall or impact event, and no scattered shard tinkles. Glass breaking should have a sharp broadband crack followed by many discrete, randomly timed high-frequency ticks. The picture shows a dense continuous wash with a few faint tick marks, so it reads as a generic crash or thud.

The sound lasts about 2 s, and roughly 50% of that is silence, so the decay tail is long and empty. The spectrogram energy is concentrated in the low end, with a hot red band at the bottom. That suggests a boomy thud, not bright glass, even though the centroid is around 3 kHz.

The 'mirror' size option is not among the renders shown, and the small and window options differ mainly in tonal ringing. Window shows long sustained horizontal lines, which sound like resonant ringing or a bell, not glass shattering.
With tail=false the sound is still 1.57 s and the envelope barely changes. The tail toggle does not give a clear, usable difference, such as a dry crack versus a crack with shard tinkles trailing.

Shard scatter should visibly control the density and timing of the discrete shard events, but the renders show little distinct separation of events. The high-frequency ticks are sparse and faint, so the most characteristic part of glass breaking is underdeveloped.
grades.lesson: When a sound is defined by discrete events (shards, drips, clicks), build them as separate, clearly timed transients over a distinct initial impact, and check that the spectrogram shows individual events, not a smooth decaying wash that could be any impact.

flaws: The brief is a mirror or frame falling and cracking, but the render is a single broadband burst with a smooth exponential decay. There is no separate impact thud, no crack transient, and no discrete shard tinkles. It reads as a generic noise crash, not glass.

The shard scatter should produce visible, irregular, sparse high-frequency ticks in the tail. In the spectrogram the tail is a smeared wash that fades smoothly, with only a few faint speckles. Scatter at max looks denser rather than more scattered.

The centroid is around 5.4 kHz and the energy is spread evenly from low to high frequencies. Glass breakage should be bright and ringing, with resonant tonal partials. Here the low-end energy and noise-like texture dominate, so it sounds more like a crashing debris pile than a mirror.

The size options (small, mirror, window) differ mostly in duration (1.39 s, 1.57 s, 1.81 s), and the centroid barely moves (5792, 5407, 5330 Hz). The sizes do not read as clearly different pitch or character.
Turning the tail off just truncates the sound to 1.07 s, and the decay ends abruptly at about 0.8 s on the waveform. The result is a clipped-looking ending, not a clean no-tail variant.
The 'every range at minimum' render is still a full crash at 1.29 s. Force at minimum does not give a gentle crack, so the force knob has limited range in character.
grades.lesson: Make the defining event structure of the sound audible and separately controllable, for example a distinct impact, a crack transient, and sparse discrete debris events. A single noise burst with a decay envelope is not enough, even if its length and loudness are plausible. Check the spectrogram for the discrete features the brief implies, such as tonal ringing and isolated ticks.

brief: Child's music box tune slowing and detuning to a stop; knobs: comb (tin|brass), slowdown 0..1, detune 0..1, start pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The waveform is a dense, continuous wash with a slow decay and no visible separate note onsets. A music box is a sequence of plucked tines, each a sharp transient with a short ring. Here it reads as a sustained drone with faint ticks.

The spectrogram shows long horizontal bars that persist and overlap, so notes ring far too long and blur together. A tune that slows to a stop should show note spacing clearly widening, and that is hard to see. The default only shows a loose stretching of the ticks.
The brass comb setting has an almost flat, swelling envelope with no clear attacks. That is a pad or organ, not a metal tine, so the comb choice changes the sound into a different instrument.

The minimum-range render is a dense continuous texture with no visible slowdown or distinct notes, so the wind-down idea is lost at that extreme. The maximum render has sparse, widely spaced notes that read much better but behave very differently from the minimum.

The tail toggle makes almost no visible difference (centroid 1504 vs 1491 Hz, same envelope), so it is a near-redundant knob. The knob set lacks a tempo or note-density control, and the tune itself is not selectable.
grades.lesson: Check that the defining event structure of the sound (here discrete plucked notes with clear gaps between them) is visible in the waveform at every setting, including extremes. Don't let decay lengths or sustain smear events into a continuous wash. Make sure each knob and toggle changes the picture noticeably.

flaws: Default render does not read as a slowing music box: note spacing stays almost uniform and the envelope decays smoothly like a single fade-out. The ritardando is barely visible, so the core 'wind-down' idea is weak.
Detune is not evident in the spectrogram; pitch lines look static and the 'detuning to a stop' character is missing at defaults.

Spectrogram shows a dense low-frequency smear (a pink band at the bottom with repeated vertical ticks) running through the whole clip, which sounds like a constant buzz or rumble rather than clean, tinkly comb tones. It is a poor fit for a bright tin comb.

Range extremes diverge. At minimum, notes blur into a continuous, nearly flat sustained wash with no discrete plucks, so it no longer reads as a music box. At maximum, 18% silence with big gaps and a few isolated late notes reads as sparse and broken rather than a controlled slowdown.
comb = brass has a lower centroid (1186 Hz) and a mushy, sustained texture instead of a distinct timbre. It reads as a muffled version of tin, not a different comb.

The tail = false render still has long decaying notes and ends much like the default, so the toggle has an unclear effect. The seed renders are very similar in detail, so variation is on the low side.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes a process over time (slowing, detuning, winding down), make sure that process is clearly visible in the default render's picture, and check that the extreme settings still keep discrete, recognisable events rather than collapsing into a wash or leaving sparse gaps.

flaws: The brief is a tune slowing down to a stop, but at defaults the note spacing looks almost constant. The waveform is a steady run of equal-height bursts with a decay at the end. The slowdown is barely visible, so it reads as a short tune fading out rather than a winding-down mechanism.
