The comb = brass render is a dense, sustained wash with long overlapping notes and a smeared spectrogram. It loses the plucked, tine-like transient of a music box and sounds like a pad or organ, not a comb. The tin/brass choice changes the character too much to read as the same sound.

At maximum range the picture splits into a few isolated notes with long gaps and 18% silence. The last notes are stranded in dead air, so it no longer reads as a continuous wind-down. At minimum range everything is dense and even with no visible deceleration, so the slowdown knob does not produce a clear difference.
The detune effect cannot be seen in the spectrogram. Pitch lines look like flat, steady horizontal bars with no visible sag or wobble, so the 'detuning to a stop' half of the brief is weak.

The tune choices (minor waltz, descending) change the note pattern but not the wind-down shape, so they act as presets rather than a designer's controls. Knobs for the final stop time or pitch-sag curve, and for tine brightness, are missing.
Seed variation is mostly the same pattern with small differences in note height and density. That is acceptable, but the takes are close to identical in timing.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes a process over time (slowing, detuning, decaying), make that change obvious in the default render and check that the extremes of its knob show a clear trajectory. A flat sound with a fade-out at the end does not count as the process.

brief: Loopable 3s stopped-at-lights bed with muffled outside traffic and HVAC; knobs: traffic density 0..1, HVAC fan level 0..1, window (closed/cracked), distant horns 0..1

flaws: Defaults read as a flat band of low-mid noise with no identifiable HVAC tone, engine idle or distinct muffled traffic passes. It sounds like generic brown noise rather than a car interior at a stoplight.

The spectrogram shows almost all energy in a thin strip at the bottom, with a nearly empty, uniformly pale upper band. There is little spectral structure to suggest muffling through glass or distant vehicles.
The traffic and fan layers are not distinguishable. The waveform has a constant, dense envelope with no pass-by swells, so the traffic density knob has little to work with.

Range extremes diverge too much. The minimum setting drops the centroid to 209 Hz and shows only two broad low blobs, while the maximum shows distinct pulsing swells and tonal horn lines. They no longer feel like the same bed. The minimum is a rumble with almost no HVAC or air character.
The window cracked setting mostly raises the centroid and adds a brighter wash. It does not change the character in a convincing way.

Loopability is doubtful. The waveform has a different amplitude profile at the start and end, with a quiet start and a swell at the end, so a loop point could be audible. Horn events look like faint horizontal lines that are barely perceptible at the defaults.
The window knob is binary, and no engine idle or vibration knob is offered, though the title says 'idling'.
grades.lesson: Make each layer named in the brief (e.g. HVAC tone, traffic passes, horns) individually identifiable in the spectrogram at defaults, with distinct spectral and temporal signatures. Check that the knob extremes keep the same character instead of collapsing to one noise band or changing into a different sound.

flaws: Spectrogram shows almost all energy in a thin band at the very bottom, with the rest nearly empty. It reads as a low rumble or noise bed, not a car interior with muffled traffic, HVAC hiss and an engine idle. Mid and high content for HVAC air and traffic texture is missing.

Waveform has a strong amplitude swell and dip across the 3 s, for example the minimum-range render, which has a pronounced bulge in the middle and quiet edges. This is not a steady bed, and it makes a loop audibly pulse. The start and end levels also differ between renders, so the loop seam is questionable.

The window closed/cracked knob changes the centroid from 444 to 773 Hz, but the spectrogram shows little visible change. The 'cracked' state looks nearly identical to the default, so the knob is weak.

The minimum and maximum extremes look like different sounds. The minimum is a bass-heavy, sparse, impulsive texture with a pulsing look. The maximum is a broader, busier wash. Distant horns are not visible as tonal events in any render, so that knob reads as nothing.
The seeds vary in overall envelope. Seed 2 swells to a bulge and seed 3 is flat with a hard start. They look like different structures rather than two takes of the same bed.
No discernible discrete traffic passes (whooshes, Doppler) at the default settings, so the 'stopped at lights' scene is not conveyed.
grades.lesson: Check that every knob produces a visible, distinct feature in the spectrogram (tonal events for horns, a band shift for filters), and that a loop bed holds a steady level, with matching start and end, across seeds and extremes.

flaws: The waveform is a continuous, even noise-like swell with no discernible individual vehicle passes. It reads as a generic noise wash, not a stopped-at-lights scene with muffled traffic and HVAC.

The spectrogram energy is concentrated at the very bottom and in a few narrow horizontal bands. The mid and high bands look like uniform speckle. There is no clear low-frequency engine or HVAC rumble with the shaped muffling the brief describes.

The distant horns show up as short, regular, pillar-like blocks of stacked harmonic lines. They look synthetic and tonal, and at maximum they repeat in an evenly spaced pattern that sounds like a mechanical pulse, not random horns.

The extremes do not differ much. The minimum and maximum renders share a similar level and spectral shape (RMS 0.176 vs 0.169, centroid 629 vs 920 Hz). The minimum is not a sparse bed and the maximum is not a dense one. The envelope amplitude swells at maximum look like a slow tremolo.

A 3 s loopable bed that ends with a different amplitude shape than it starts with is likely to produce an audible seam when looped. Seed 2 and seed 3 end with a swell and a decay respectively, with no sign of crossfading or matched endpoints.

The window closed/cracked knob changes the centroid only modestly (784 to 1116 Hz) and has no clearly visible filtering effect in the spectrogram, so it is a weak control. Nothing in the knob set covers the engine idle rumble that defines the scene.
grades.lesson: Check that the render shows the distinctive, recognisable events and spectral layers the brief names (for example separate vehicle passes, an idle rumble, a fan tone) rather than one generic noise bed. Make each knob produce a visible, large change in its own layer, and make loop endpoints match.

brief: Reverse clap riser into crash hit; knobs: space (plate|hall|spring), rise-length 0..1, hit-weight 0..1, brightness 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The reverse riser is short and weak at defaults. It reads as a small swell before the hit rather than a convincing reverse-clap build.

Hit weight is concentrated in a low band below roughly 150 Hz and shows as a sustained red patch. It sounds more like a thump than a crash, and the broadband crash energy decays quickly into a thin tail.
The space options (plate, hall, spring) look similar. Hall differs mainly through a longer, denser tail, and plate and spring are nearly identical in the spectrogram.
The tail-off render is cut off cleanly, but 54% silence in a fixed 3.4 s file means a lot of dead space. Total length does not change with the knobs, so the sound cannot be trimmed to fit a scene.
At the extremes the hit moves later in time as rise-length grows. This is expected, but the file length stays fixed and the max tail leaves little room after the hit.
grades.lesson: Make the file length follow the main time-based knobs (rise, tail) so users get a trimmed asset. Check that each choice option (such as the reverb types) is visibly and audibly distinct, not just labelled differently.

brief: Desk stapler punched hard through a stack; knobs: stapler size (mini/desk/heavy-duty), force 0..1, paper thickness 0..1, metal ring 0..1, desk thump toggle, room tail toggle

flaws: The default render is a roughly 0.12 s noisy burst followed by sparse isolated blips (echo or room-tail ticks) across the remaining 0.4 s. A real stapler slam is one sharp crunch-and-clack transient with a short ring, so this reads as a flutter or ricochet, not a single punch.

The tail is not a smooth decay. It is a series of discrete spaced-out ticks with long silence between them (47% silence), which sounds like a distant echo of repeated hits and not a room tail or metal ring.
The waveform opens with a cluster of two or three bursts. The staple punch, clinch and desk impact are not distinct in the picture, so the mechanical sequence is smeared into noise.

The spectrogram shows strong low-frequency energy at the very start of the default, which is the desk thump. Most of the body is broadband noise with little defined metallic ring, so the stapler character is weak.

The max-range render is a long, dense 0.5 s wash with a sustained noise body and little transient shape. This is not a stapler slam and differs in kind from the minimum render, where the sound is a faint, thin tick.
The size choices differ mainly in centroid. Mini and heavy-duty look like the same burst-plus-ticks pattern, so they do not read as clearly different mechanisms.
Seeds keep the same overall shape, but the positions of the late blips shift noticeably. They read as random echo placement and not as distinct takes of one hit.
grades.lesson: Build the sound from the physical event sequence, with one clear transient and a smoothly decaying tail. Do not add sparse random late events that read as echoes, and check that the extremes of the knobs still sound like the same single event.

flaws: The default render looks like a burst of noise about 0.1 s long, followed by several small decaying blips. A stapler punch should be one sharp click or crunch, then a short clack of the anvil. The repeated echo-like pulses read as a bouncing or ricocheting object, not a stapler.

The pulses decay unevenly into sparse tail blips out to about 0.5 s. In the spectrogram they show up as isolated horizontal lines, which sound like discrete pings, not a natural metal ring or room tail. The tail looks like a few sparse resonators, not a real decay.

The 'every range at max' render turns into a long, dense wash of about 0.4 s with a continuous noisy body. That is not a stapler any more. It sounds like a rumble or crash, and the sharp transient is lost, so the extremes do not read as the same sound.

With thump off the sound is still mostly broadband noise at 2.5 kHz, and the repeated pulses are still there. It does not read as a clean stapler click, so the toggle changes the tone without fixing the core shape problem.

Silence is 47% at the defaults, so about half the file is empty tail. That is wasteful for a one-shot. The waveform shows the energy confined to the first 0.15 s, followed by sparse isolated blips that make the file feel gappy.
grades.lesson: Check that the transient and decay structure matches the physical event: one impact should give one clear attack and a smooth decay. Discrete repeated pulses or isolated resonator blips read as echoes or bounces, so use them only when the real object makes them.

flaws: Every render is 0.40 s with the same shape, a slow swell and a long decay (about 0.1 s to peak, then tailing out). A stapler punch should be a sharp click or crack with an almost instant attack, then a short metallic ring. This reads as a soft thud or a bloomed burst, not a hard staple through paper.
The envelope has no distinct two-stage event. A stapler should have a press or crunch through the paper followed by a clinch snap, but the waveform is one blob with no separate transients.

The max-range render sustains a fat, nearly flat body for about 0.3 s. It sounds like a sustained buzz or tone rather than a stapler, and the 'metal ring' knob appears to produce horizontal sustained lines, which is a tonal drone and not a metallic ping.

The size presets change the character more than the type of object. Heavy-duty is a wobbly low rumble with a centroid of 849 Hz, which is more like a thump than a heavier stapler. Mini has a similar swell and just sits higher.
The spectrogram shows long horizontal banding, which implies static resonant partials. These make the sound read as synthetic and tonal rather than a short impact.
The 'room tail' toggle was not demonstrated, and a 0.40 s total length leaves little room for a tail anyway.
grades.lesson: Check the attack time against the real-world event: impact sounds need a near-instant onset and a fast decay, so a waveform that swells before it peaks reads as a different sound, whatever the spectrum or knob set looks like.

brief: Loopable 4s highway tire roar and wind inside cabin; knobs: road surface (asphalt/concrete/gravel), speed 0..1, wind hiss 0..1, insulation 0..1, low rumble 0..1

flaws: The spectrogram is nearly all low-contrast blue noise with the energy squeezed into a thin strip at the very bottom. A real cabin roar has a clear low-frequency rumble bed with a smooth spectral slope. This looks like flat broadband noise with a small low-end smear, so it reads as generic noise rather than a car interior.

The waveform has a dense, uniform block envelope with sharp vertical spikes. These look like random crackle or impulses, and they would sound like a gravelly texture instead of a steady tire drone. Surface choice and wind hiss are not visually distinct from this.

Range is weak. Defaults, concrete, gravel and both extremes all look almost identical: same envelope, same 4 s block, same strip of low energy. Centroids move only between about 600 and 1016 Hz, and the extreme-max render is not clearly different from the default. Speed, insulation and rumble do not produce the expected tonal or spectral shifts, such as a lowpass from insulation or a rising pitch and level from speed.
Surface differences are subtle. Asphalt, concrete and gravel should differ in texture, brightness and grain, but they read as the same noise with slightly different level.
The brief asks for a loopable sound, but the waveform shows no evidence of a seamless loop, and the seed 3 end tapers visibly. Loop continuity is a risk.

Seeds differ in RMS (0.169 to 0.215) and in the crackle pattern. They share the same overall shape, which is acceptable, but the level swing between takes is larger than a designer would want from a seed change.
grades.lesson: Check that each knob moves the spectrogram in the way the real-world control would, such as insulation acting as a lowpass or speed raising level and brightness. If the extreme renders look the same as the default, the knobs are only changing noise level and need to be re-engineered to change spectral shape.

flaws: The spectrogram is almost entirely low-frequency energy with a thin band of noise. It looks like generic filtered noise, not a cabin with broadband tire roar plus wind hiss. Nothing suggests road texture or cabin resonances.
Range is weak. Concrete, gravel and asphalt differ by only about 750 to 980 Hz in centroid and look almost identical in the pictures. A designer would not hear three distinct surfaces.

Every knob at minimum versus maximum gives centroid 506 Hz versus 727 Hz and nearly the same picture and RMS (0.226 vs 0.232). Speed, insulation, wind and rumble do not change the character much. Maximum should be clearly louder and brighter, and minimum clearly quieter and darker.
The waveform is a flat, dense slab with a constant level, which suits a loop. But there is no slow movement from gusts, bumps or road joints, so it sounds static and synthetic over 4 s.
The loop seam is not shown to be clean. The waveform has small irregular spikes near the end that could cause a click or an audible repeat.
Seeds are similar in overall shape, but the detail differences are small. That is fine for variation but does not make up for the weak range.
grades.lesson: Make sure each knob visibly changes the spectrogram (band balance, level, texture) across its full range, so extremes and categorical choices look and sound clearly different, not just measurably different.

flaws: Spectrograms show energy concentrated at the very bottom with a flat, nearly empty field above. The wind hiss and tire-roar mid band do not show up. The sound reads as low-passed noise, not a cabin with road and wind.

Surface choices are barely distinguishable. Concrete (centroid 933 Hz) and gravel (1207 Hz) look almost identical to the default asphalt in both waveform and spectrogram. Gravel should have visible crunchy texture and a brighter spectrum, and it does not.

Range extremes are weak. The minimum render (centroid 542 Hz) is a smaller, duller version of the same noise, and the maximum is the same noise louder. Speed, insulation and wind do not change the spectral character in a way a designer would hear as different driving conditions.
Waveform envelopes show a slow swell and an obvious amplitude fade toward the end of some renders. For a 4 s loopable bed, this puts the loop seam at risk.

Seeds 2 and 3 have identical stats (peak 0.693, rms 0.155, centroid 996 Hz), and the waveforms look nearly identical. That suggests the seed has little effect on the output, so the variation is minimal.
The brief lists five knobs. The renders give no evidence that wind hiss and low rumble are separable layers, because the spectrograms show no distinct high-frequency band or sub-bass band.
grades.lesson: Build each knob as a distinct, visible spectral layer (e.g. a separate sub-bass band, a mid roar band, a high hiss band). Then check the spectrogram to confirm that every choice option and every extreme shows up as a clear change in band energy and texture, not only in level or overall brightness.

brief: Loopable 2-4 s bed of market crowd murmur and haggling. Knobs: crowd size (sparse/busy/packed), excitement 0..1, distance 0..1, laughter density 0..1, loop-crossfade toggle.

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.80); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: The spectrogram is mostly broadband noise with a few low-frequency blobs (energy below roughly 1 kHz). There are no formant-like bands or syllabic structure and no individual voices. It reads as amplitude-modulated pink noise or surf, not market murmur or haggling.
No laughter or haggling events are visible at defaults. There are no bright, pitched bursts, so the laughter density knob has nothing to show and the brief's 'haggling' content is missing.

Crowd size changes level and modulation depth, not density. Sparse, default and packed all have a similar centroid (935–971 Hz) and a similar noisy texture. Sparse is just a quieter, swelling version of the same noise, and packed does not read as many overlapping voices.

The seeds differ too much in loudness and envelope (rms 0.121–0.183), with swells and dips of different shape. They are only loosely the same kind of take. Slow level dips of around 3 dB inside a 3 s bed make it hard to use as a steady loop bed.

Loop seam: the crossfade toggle changes almost nothing visually (rms 0.18 vs 0.183, near-identical image). The sparse variant has a loud start and end with a dip in the middle, which would pump when looped.
The all-max extreme is a dense, flat, noise-like wash with a lower centroid (752 Hz). It loses all murmur character, so the extremes do not hold the sound's identity.
grades.lesson: Make the signature content of a sound (here voices, with formants, syllable rhythm and laughter bursts) visible as distinct structure in the spectrogram. Filtered noise with a slow amplitude wobble reads as a generic texture, and density knobs should change the number of events, not just level.

flaws: Spectrogram is a flat broadband noise wash with a centroid of about 1 kHz. It shows no formant or syllabic structure, no pitch contours, and no voice-like banding, so it reads as filtered noise rather than a murmuring crowd.
Nothing in the picture suggests haggling or laughter. There are no distinct voices, bursts or rising exclamations, and no laughter-like energy pulses, so the brief's content is not delivered.

The size choices are weakly differentiated: the centroid is about 1030 Hz for sparse, packed and default alike, and only the RMS and envelope wobble change. Sparse looks like a slightly lower-level version of the same noise rather than fewer individual voices.

The range extremes barely differ. All-min has a centroid of 973 Hz and all-max has 793 Hz, and both have nearly the same texture. Distance and excitement do not produce a clearly different spectral tilt or character.

The loop is not demonstrably seamless. The crossfade=false render looks nearly identical to the default, and the default waveform starts and ends at different amplitudes, so the crossfade toggle has little visible effect.

The seeds are inconsistent in level and envelope. Seed 3 has a large opening burst, then a flat, lower-energy body with an RMS of 0.114 against 0.167 for seed 2, so the takes do not feel like the same sound.
grades.lesson: A texture built from a noise source needs structure that identifies it, such as formant-like bands, syllabic modulation or discrete events, and each knob must visibly change that structure rather than just level or tilt. Check that the extremes of a knob look different on the spectrogram, not only in the numbers.

flaws: Default render does not read as a crowd bed. The waveform swells and dips like a slow breathing envelope, with a large burst near 2 s. A walla bed should be a dense, steady wash, and this has audible lumps that would pulse when looped.
The spectrogram is a diffuse noise smear with no visible voice formant structure or syllabic rhythm, and no distinct laughter events. It reads as filtered noise rather than murmur and haggling.
The 'sparse' size is not a bed. It has a loud cluster of bursts at the start, then a near-empty trough, then a quieter patch. It reads as a few isolated voices and is not usable as loopable ambience.

The loop boundary is a problem. The default starts and ends near silence with a large mid-clip peak, so a loop would have an obvious pulse. The crossfade toggle barely changes the picture (rms 0.108 vs 0.107), so it does little to fix the shape. Seed 2 has a loud swell at the very end that would clash with the start on a loop.

At the range extremes the sound loses its character. The max setting is flat, uniform noise with centroid 717 Hz and no crowd detail. The min setting is a smooth modulated hum. These do not read as clearly different crowd states.

The seeds differ mostly in where the big bursts fall, so the overall energy shape changes between takes. That is inconsistent for a bed. Loudness also varies a lot (rms 0.094 to 0.151) across sizes and seeds with the peak normalized to 0.8.
Knob set is thin. Laughter density and distance are sensible, but there is no control over language or voice-pitch mix, no haggling or shout accents, and no way to control how steady the bed is.
grades.lesson: For loopable ambience beds, check that the envelope is statistically stationary across the whole clip, with no big swells, troughs or isolated bursts near the edges. Build density from many overlapping small events instead of a few loud ones, and verify that the loop seam is inaudible.

brief: Pages flipped in a document, notebook, or binder; knobs: binding (stapled/spiral/ring binder), flip rate, page count 0..1, snap 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 2.21); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: Each page flip is a flat, broadband noise burst (centroid ~4 kHz) with a hard vertical attack. Real paper has a swish, a riffle and a soft body, so this reads as a stuttering machine-gun or ratchet rather than pages.

The spectrogram is almost identical across bindings: vertical stripes with no tonal or resonant movement. Only the ring binder shows low-mid horizontal bands, and spiral shows faint ones. Stapled and spiral are hard to tell apart, so the binding choice does little to change the character.

The pulses are too regular, with no cascade or accelerating riffle and no page-to-page level and spacing variation. At the maximum setting the result is a dense buzz that no longer reads as individual pages.
With the tail off, the sound stops abruptly and leaves 62% silence between the pulses. The pulses look like short isolated clicks.
The 2 s default length with a long decaying tail is odd for a page flip, which is usually a short gesture. The tail is a noise wash rather than paper settling or a binder rattle.
The seeds share one shape but differ little beyond pulse timing. The spectral content is identical.
grades.lesson: Model the physical gesture, not just a train of noise bursts. Give each event its own spectral shape, soft attack and decay, and per-event variation in level, timing and tone. Make the categorical choices (such as the binding) differ audibly in spectrum and resonance, not only in timing or density.

flaws: Defaults read as a dense burst of broadband noise clicks (centroid ~2.5 kHz), more like a card shuffle or rapid ratchet than paper pages. There is no soft paper rustle or swish body between the transients, and the transients are uniform in shape.

Each flip is a hard vertical stripe across the full spectrum, so it sounds like a train of identical clicks. Paper should have a gradual fan or riffle with varied page-to-page amplitude and brightness.
The trailing tail after the main burst is a few isolated tiny blips with a gap, which reads as stray clicks rather than a natural settle. The 25-37% silence comes mostly from this.

The ring binder variant adds sustained horizontal tonal lines in the spectrogram (ring resonance). These sound metallic and ring-like for the whole duration, so it reads as a different sound and not a binder with rings rattling.

At minimum range the flips become four widely spaced loud thumps followed by sparse fading ticks. This is no longer a page flip, it is a few knocks with irregular gaps, and it is clearly a different kind of sound.
Seed variation is mostly in loudness (rms 0.095 to 0.128) and hit placement. The overall shape is consistent, but the takes are similar enough that they would feel repetitive across a project.

Knobs: the binding choice is useful, but 'snap' and 'page count' do not map clearly to what a designer wants (paper stiffness, flip speed, number of pages). The tail toggle just chops the sound abruptly, ending on a hard cut with no decay.
grades.lesson: Check that a sound has the continuous body that defines its material (e.g. rustle between transients), not just a train of identical impulses, and confirm that every knob extreme still reads as the same object rather than a different event.

flaws: Default render reads as a generic swell of broadband noise, not discrete page flips. The waveform is a smooth lens-shaped envelope with no clear individual transients, and the spectrogram shows vertical hash with no separated events.
Page flutter is a rapid series of sharp, bright paper-edge transients with gaps between them. Here the events overlap into one continuous wash, so it could pass as a whoosh or a breath.

The 'binding' choice barely changes the sound. Spiral and ring binder have the same envelope and noise texture as the default. The ring binder has only a few low-frequency blips, and nothing audibly reads as a metal ring or a staple.
The range extremes are weak. Minimum shows 4-5 soft lumps and maximum shows one burst, and neither reads as a clearly different flip speed or page count.
About 1.6-2 s of low-level noise with a long fade is too long and smeared for a page flip. The tail looks like noise decay, not paper settling.
Seeds differ mainly in overall envelope shape and level (rms 0.098 vs 0.152), so they feel less like two takes of one sound. Seed 3 has a gap and a trailing blip near the end.
grades.lesson: Build impact-like sounds from discrete, individually shaped transients with audible gaps between them, and make sure each categorical option changes the transient character (timbre, resonance) so it is distinguishable, not just the overall noise envelope.

brief: Motorboat passing across the harbour mouth; knobs: hull size (dinghy|trawler|ferry), speed 0..1, wake splash 0..1, distance 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Spectrograms show energy almost entirely in a thin band below ~300 Hz, with very little mid or high content. A motorboat pass should show engine harmonics, prop cavitation, and wake splash/hiss. This reads as a low rumble with a swell, not a boat.

The 'pass' is just a symmetric amplitude swell. There is no visible Doppler pitch glide, no change in spectral tilt as the boat approaches and recedes, and no stereo or distance filtering cue. The envelope is a mirror-image triangle, which sounds like a fade in/out.

The waveform shows regular, comb-like amplitude pulsing across the whole clip, like a tremolo or sine-modulated drone. It sounds artificial and mechanical rather than like an engine with irregular firing and water noise.

The hull sizes differ mainly in centroid (430, 565, 761 Hz). The ferry is higher in centroid than the dinghy, which is counterintuitive, since a big hull should be lower and heavier. Three hulls look nearly the same in shape.
The range extremes barely change the picture. Min and max look like the same swell with slightly different pulse density, so speed, wake and distance do not give clearly different sounds.

The wake splash and distance knobs show no visible effect on the spectrogram's upper bands. Splash should add broadband noise and distance should roll off highs, but the high region stays almost empty in every render.
The seeds share one shape but differ little beyond the pulse pattern, and the tail toggle is a minor change that does not add a convincing wash or wake slap.
grades.lesson: When you build a moving-source sound, check that the picture shows the cues that make it move (pitch glide, spectral tilt change, asymmetric approach and recede), and that every texture layer the knobs promise (splash, hiss, wash) puts visible energy in its own frequency band, not just a symmetric volume swell on one low drone.

flaws: Every render is 4.00 s with the same symmetric triangular swell: it rises, peaks mid-clip, then falls. It reads as a generic amplitude-modulated noise burst, not a motorboat. A pass-by needs a Doppler pitch glide (falling engine tone), which no spectrogram shows.

The spectrum is almost all low-frequency mush, with a hot band at the bottom and sparse speckle above. There are no visible engine harmonics, no propeller or cavitation texture, and no bow-wave or water noise. Centroids of 450-600 Hz are plausible for a boat but the picture reads as filtered noise.
The 'tail = false' render is nearly identical to the default (centroid 443 vs 478 Hz, same length and envelope). The toggle has little audible or visible effect, so it is not a useful control.

Hull size changes the picture very little: dinghy, trawler and ferry look like the same noise burst with slightly different brightness. They are not clearly different boats, with no lower fundamental or heavier diesel throb for the ferry.
The range extremes are weak. The minimum is a dark, thin blob with barely any content above 300 Hz. The maximum is only slightly busier, and neither sounds like a different speed or distance.

Pass duration is fixed at 4 s, and speed does not seem to change the timing of the pass. A fast boat should give a short, sharp pass and a slow one a long, gentle pass. A designer cannot fit this to a scene.
grades.lesson: For a moving source, make the motion itself visible in the spectrogram (Doppler pitch glide, filtering that changes with distance, and a pass time tied to speed). A plain amplitude swell on noise reads as a generic whoosh, not the named object. Check that each categorical choice and toggle changes the picture in a way you can see.

flaws: Spectrogram is almost entirely low-frequency energy (centroid ~560 Hz) with no visible engine harmonics, firing-rate lines, or prop cavitation. It reads as a generic low rumble swell, not a motorboat.

The pass is a symmetric rise and fall in amplitude with no Doppler pitch shift, so there is no visible falling line across the pass. Without that, the pass doesn't read as a boat moving across the harbour mouth.
The wake splash is not identifiable as a separate element. Splash and slap should be bright, irregular broadband bursts, but the spectrogram shows only a faint noisy texture at the top.

The hull choices differ mainly in level and centroid (791, 561, 641 Hz). The ordering is odd, with the dinghy brighter than the ferry. They are not clearly three different engines, and a trawler diesel should have a distinct low chug.

The 'every range at maximum' render has the same centroid (561 Hz) as the default, which suggests some knobs have little effect on the spectrum. The 'minimum' render is only a darker version of the same shape.
The tail toggle only shortens the file (3.52 s vs 4.00 s). The envelope barely changes, so it is a weak control.
The 4 s file starts and ends at a fairly high level. The ending is not a clean fade, which could cut off abruptly when looped or layered.
grades.lesson: When the brief describes motion (a pass, a fly-by), make sure the render shows the physical cues of that motion, such as Doppler pitch glide, a filter that changes with distance, and a source-specific harmonic structure. An amplitude swell over filtered noise reads as generic rumble, not the named object.

brief: Empty rocking chair creaking back and forth; knobs: wood (oak|wicker), creak amount 0..1, floor contact 0..1, rock rate, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the waveform is a slow crescendo that builds across the full 3 s to a peak at the very end and then stops. This is a ramp, not rocking. A rocking chair should show a periodic back-and-forth with repeated creak and floor-contact events, and none are visible.

The spectrogram at defaults and at every range setting is a smeared wash of low-mid noise with no discrete creak events. There are no pitch-glide squeaks, which are what make a chair creak. It reads as a rising rumble or noise swell, not wood stressing.
The ending is abrupt: the envelope is at its loudest on the last sample and cuts off. That is a defect for a sound described as having a tail.

The tail=false render is the only one that shows distinct periodic events, four thumps with silence between them (48% silence). This suggests the rocking rhythm exists only in that mode, and the 'tail' knob is actually the thing that hides a continuous noise bed. The default therefore buries the rock cycle under sustained noise.
Rock rate and the other ranges barely change the picture. Min and max look like the same ramp with a different slope and centroid (156 vs 322 Hz), so the extremes are not clearly different sounds.
The oak/wicker choice changes mostly the brightness (293 vs 645 Hz). It does not change the creak character, so it is a weak choice.
The seeds share the same crescendo shape, which is acceptable, but that shape is the wrong one for the brief.
grades.lesson: Check that the defining event structure of the sound (here, discrete periodic creaks and thumps) is visible at the default settings. Do not let a continuous noise bed or a global envelope ramp cover it, and do not leave it visible only in an alternate toggle state.

flaws: At defaults the waveform is a slow crescendo that peaks at the very end of the 3 s and then stops. It looks like a swell, not a chair rocking back and forth. There are no discrete rock cycles and no periodic creak events.

The tail=false render is the only one that shows rocking: four distinct floor-contact thumps with silence between them. That is the shape the brief describes, but the default hides it, and the tail toggle seems to change the whole structure rather than just the decay.

The default spectrogram is a continuous dense smear in the low and mid bands. It reads as sustained noise or rumble. A creak should be tonal, with stick-slip pulses and a wobbling pitch, and none of that is visible.

The default centroid is 293 Hz, and the minimum-range centroid is 156 Hz. A creaking wooden chair should have more mid and high-mid content. At minimum settings the sound is mostly low rumble, which is unconvincing.
The max-range render ends on a hard peak at the final sample with no decay, so it ends abruptly. A sound editor would have to trim it or fade it out.
The seeds share the same crescendo shape but vary only slightly. They are acceptable as takes of one sound, but the shared shape is the wrong one.

The rock rate knob does not appear to produce visible periodicity at the defaults, so the main control for this sound does not do what its name says. The creak and floor-contact knobs are sensible in concept, but their results are muddled in the renders.
grades.lesson: Check that the default render shows the defining temporal structure of the sound, such as repeated cycles, discrete events or an envelope with a natural ending. Do not let a smooth noise swell stand in for it. A toggle should only change a detail like the tail, never remove the structure that makes the sound recognisable.

flaws: Default render reads as a series of low thump/knock transients (centroid ~390 Hz, energy concentrated at the bottom) rather than a creaking chair. A creak is a sustained, pitch-wobbling friction squeal with harmonic or resonant structure, and the spectrogram shows no such tonal, gliding content.

The five events at the defaults are about 0.6 s apart and look like decaying impacts or footsteps. There is no continuous rocking motion, no swell as the chair moves, and no creak that rises and falls with the rock direction. The brief says 'creaking back and forth', but what is shown is thumps.
The rocker-floor contact sounds dominate and the creak layer is barely visible. The spectrogram has no gliding tonal lines, so the sound reads as the wrong thing.
The minimum range gives only 3 sparse, low-pitched thumps (centroid 139 Hz) with 50% silence. That is a different sound with almost no creak and is not usable as a rocking chair.
The 'wicker' choice is mostly a brighter, noisier version of the same thumps and does not add a distinct creak character such as fibre crackle.
The 'tail = false' toggle only trims the ring-out, and silence jumps to 51%, so the effect is small and it leaves a gappy result.
Seed variation is mainly in event timing and amplitude, and the character stays the same. That is acceptable, but the decay shapes are nearly identical, so it adds little.
grades.lesson: Check that the defining feature of the sound named in the brief (here, a pitch-gliding friction creak) is actually visible in the spectrogram at defaults. Don't let an easy-to-synthesise impact layer stand in for it and dominate the render.

brief: Candle flame snuffed by a sudden breath; knobs: candle size (taper|pillar), breath strength 0..1, sizzle 0..1, smoke hiss 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: sizzle

flaws: Default render does not match a snuffed candle: a 2.2 s symmetric swell-and-decay of broadband noise, with a slow ~0.5 s attack. A real breath-snuff is an abrupt puff and a fast extinguish, followed by a brief sizzle and a thin smoke hiss. This reads as a wind gust or a noise swell.

The spectrogram is a diffuse, even broadband wash centred around 3 kHz, with no distinct puff, sizzle crackle or hiss layers. The elements named in the knobs (breath, sizzle, smoke) cannot be told apart.

With the tail toggled off, the sound becomes a short ~0.4 s noise burst followed by near-silence and a stray click. This is a much better snuff shape than the default, which suggests the default envelope is wrong and the tail is badly designed.
Range extremes (minimum and maximum) are just the same swell with a slightly different centroid and rise time. They do not give distinct character, e.g. a gentle puff versus a hard blow.
The candle-size toggle changes mostly loudness (RMS 0.107 vs 0.141) and little else, so it adds little sonic character. The tail toggle changes the sound far more than any continuous knob.
The two seeds are very similar in envelope. That is acceptable, but they share the same wrong shape.
grades.lesson: Before tuning knobs, check that the default envelope matches the real event's time structure (e.g. sharp onset then decay for an impulsive event). A smooth swell-and-decay noise wash reads as generic whoosh, not the named sound. Make each named layer (puff, sizzle, hiss) spectrally and temporally distinct so its knob has a recognisable effect.

flaws: The default render reads as a generic broadband noise burst with a decaying tail, not a candle snuff. A real snuff is a short puff of breath followed by a brief sizzle and a faint smoke hiss, and it is quiet and mostly mid-high.

The spectrogram is a flat wash of energy from the bottom to the top of the spectrum, with a centroid around 4 kHz. There is no distinct breath shape (a fast noise swell) and no separate sizzle crackle or hiss layer, so the layers don't read as separate elements.
The 2 s tail is long and smooth for a snuff, which is normally about 0.5–1 s. Roughly 30% of the file is silent or very quiet, so the sound feels padded.
There is a low-frequency pre-roll before the onset in the defaults. The sound begins with rumble before the hit, which makes no sense for a breath hitting a flame.

At the minimum range settings the sound has a noisy, low pre-hit section with a sparse, ragged shape that looks unnatural. The maximum settings only make it brighter and denser, so the extremes differ by brightness rather than by character.
With the tail off, the render is mostly a click with a few isolated tonal spikes (vertical lines in the spectrogram), which look like artifacts. The sound ends up as a thin pop rather than a snuff.
The candle size options (taper|pillar) change the result only subtly, and the seeds mostly differ by a small shift in rms. The knobs do not clearly map to distinct audible elements.
grades.lesson: Make each named element of the sound (e.g. breath, sizzle, hiss) a distinct, visible layer with its own spectral and temporal shape, and size the overall duration to the real event instead of padding it with a long smooth tail or a pre-roll.

flaws: The render is a broadband noise burst with a smooth exponential decay and a centroid around 4.5 kHz. It reads as a generic noise puff or hiss, not a candle snuff. A snuff should have a breath whoosh, then a brief sizzle or pinch, then a faint smoke hiss. Those stages are not distinct in the picture.
The defaults have no clear sequence of events. The spectrogram shows one wash of noise with a tail fading out, with no separate sizzle crackle and no rising or falling breath shape.
The 'tail = false' variant has a visible gap and an isolated thin vertical line in the spectrogram. That looks like a stray click or artifact, and the sound drops out unnaturally.

The taper and pillar choices are almost identical in the picture (same envelope and spectrum), so the size knob adds little. The minimum range setting is dull and low-passed, with a centroid of 2.2 kHz, which is a different character from the default.
The 1.2 s length with a smooth fade is the same at every setting, so the breath strength knob cannot change the duration or the attack. A designer would expect more control over the onset.
Seeds look like the same shape with different noise detail, which is fine, but the underlying shape is too generic to be a useful candle sound.
grades.lesson: Build a sound from its distinct, recognisable stages (for example onset, event, aftermath) so each stage shows up as its own feature in the render, and check that choice knobs change the picture noticeably. A single shaped noise burst with a decay reads as generic.

brief: Lighthouse foghorn blast; knobs: horn (diaphone|electric|ship-whistle), length 0..1, growl 0..1, distance 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

errors: random combination 3: 73% of the buffer is silent
random combination 3: 73% of the buffer is silent

brief: Idle drum machine hum and transformer buzz, loopable 3 s; knobs: mains (50Hz|60Hz), hum 0..1, hiss 0..1, crackle 0..1

Minimum range gives peak 0.076, almost inaudible, with 4% silence. The maximum shifts the centroid to 863 Hz and adds tall spikes. The extremes differ mainly in loudness and spike count, not in character.
No evidence of a drum-machine element (e.g. a clock tick or fan/motor flutter), so the 'idle drum machine' part of the brief is missing. It is basically generic hum and noise.

grades.lesson: When a knob selects between discrete variants (like 50 Hz vs 60 Hz), check that the spectrogram of each setting shows a clearly different structure, and make sure the characteristic harmonic content of the source is visible, not just broadband noise and a low band. flaws: The waveform is a dense, near-constant block with a comb-like pulsing texture. It reads as a harsh buzz or square-wave train, not a warm transformer hum with a drum machine's idle character.

The brief names a drum machine hum, but there is no sign of any machine-specific element such as a fan, a low-level whir or clock whine. It is only a generic buzz.
grades.lesson: Check that each knob's extremes produce a clearly visible and audible change in the spectrogram (for example, discrete crackle ticks or a broadband hiss floor). Build the sound from a physically plausible spectrum, such as a harmonic stack with a natural rolloff, rather than a raw pulse or square wave.

flaws: The waveform is a dense, flat-topped block with a comb-like picket-fence envelope. It looks like a clipped or harsh buzz, not a soft transformer hum. The envelope shows regular periodic pulses at the top, which suggests a pulse-train artifact rather than a sine-plus-harmonics hum.

The spectrogram has a very thin hot line at the very bottom plus a faint, evenly textured wash above it. There is little visible harmonic structure (100/120 Hz, 200/240 Hz and so on) that would identify transformer buzz. Idle drum machine character (motor, fan, fluctuating tone) is not visible.

brief: Power window motor lowering glass with seal squeal and wind rush; knobs: motor strain 0..1, seal squeal 0..1, outside wind 0..1, travel speed, end-stop thunk tail toggle

flaws: Defaults: the sound occupies only about the first 1.2 s of a 2.5 s file, then 38% is dead silence. A window-down move is a continuous motor whirr, and the dead tail makes it look like a short burst rather than a travel.

Waveform at default is a dense, noisy blob with no clear motor tone. The spectrogram shows broadband noise and no visible harmonic line or pitch change as the motor strains or the glass reaches the end of its travel. It reads as a noise burst, not a motor.
Seal squeal is not visible as a distinct tonal component in the spectrogram. It shows only faint scattered specks.

Range minimum: the file is full-length with about 6% silence and a 164 Hz centroid, so it is a low rumble with no motor character, and it is the only setting that fills the 2.5 s. Range maximum: it is only about 1.2 s long and has 58% silence. The same knob sweep changes the event length from full to under half, so the extremes do not read as the same sound.

Travel speed changes the duration of the event, but the file length stays fixed at 2.5 s, so faster settings leave long dead tails instead of a trimmed file. This is a design flaw, since a designer needs the clip to end when the glass stops.

Thunk toggle off: the waveform loses its tail and the silence rises to 49%. The end-stop thunk is not visible as a distinct low-frequency transient at the end in either state, so the toggle's effect is unclear.
Seeds are consistent in length and envelope, but they differ little, mainly in fine detail. This is acceptable but not strong.
grades.lesson: Make the rendered file length follow the event's actual duration as set by the speed or length knobs, rather than padding to a fixed length with silence. Check that each named component (a tonal motor whine, a squeal, an end-stop thump) is visibly distinct in the spectrogram, not just noise.

flaws: At defaults the spectrogram is mostly a diffuse noise wash with only faint wavering lines. The motor whine is not a clear, steady tone with a gliding pitch, and the seal squeal is not distinct, so it reads as generic noise rather than a power window.
The envelope is a slow swell and fade that stays dense through the whole body. A window motion has a clear start click or relay, a steady run and a defined stop, and none of these are obvious here.

The end-stop thunk is barely visible at defaults, only a small blip near the end. With thunk off, the sound is a flat, uniform block that stops abruptly with no motor spin-down. The tail toggle therefore adds little and the plain version sounds unfinished.

The range minimum is a very low-centroid hum (253 Hz) with strong horizontal bands, close to a mains or drone sound. It is 3.5 s long and has lost the squeal and wind, so it does not read as the same sound as the max setting.
The max setting is short (1.66 s) and a bit noisy and hissy, so the motor character is lost in broadband noise.
grades.lesson: Make each component of a composite sound (tone, squeal, wind, thunk) visibly distinct in the spectrogram at defaults, with a clear start, body and end, so the result reads as the specific object rather than generic filtered noise.

flaws: The motor body is a sustained buzz with a fairly flat envelope. It has little of the spin-up and load change a real window motor has, so it reads a bit synthetic.
The squeal is drawn as thin wandering lines in the upper spectrogram. It may sound like a whistle or a tonal artifact rather than rubber on glass.
The end-stop thunk is a single sharp spike at the very end. It is useful, but it looks more like a click than a dull thud with low-frequency body.
Minimum settings give a 3.69 s render with a low 245 Hz centroid, which is dull and long. The sound is mostly a bare motor hum there, so the range ends are quite different in length and character.
The silence fraction is 16% at defaults, which looks like the tail after the thunk and is slightly wasteful.
grades.lesson: Give a mechanical sound a time-varying envelope and pitch (spin-up, load change, wind-down) rather than a flat sustained buzz, and make the impact event carry low-frequency body, not just a transient spike.

brief: Small studio room tone with monitors idling, loopable 4 s; knobs: room (booth|control|live), air 0..1, monitor-hiss 0..1, distant-hvac 0..1

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: air

Defaults, the booth/live variants and the all-max render look nearly identical, with centroids of 1079, 1146, 1066 and 1112 Hz. The room choice (booth/control/live) barely changes the character; a booth should sound much deader and a live room more reverberant.

All-min differs from the others only in being darker and lower (centroid 506 Hz), and it still looks like the same noise. Knob extremes mostly shift brightness and level, so air, hiss and hvac are not clearly distinct layers.

A centroid around 1 kHz with energy spread broadly across the spectrum is too bright and full for a quiet idle room, where most energy should sit low with a faint high hiss. The waveform is also fairly loud and dense (rms 0.166), which is not a subtle room tone.
The brief asks for a loopable 4 s clip, but the waveform has an envelope that is not shown to be seamless, and the all-min render has visible spikes. Loopability is not evident.
Seeds look like the same texture with small differences. That is acceptable, but the sound is too generic for variation to be meaningful.
grades.lesson: Make each knob control a layer with its own visible spectral signature (e.g. a narrow hum, a high hiss band, a low rumble) and make categorical choices change that signature strongly, so the sound reads as its specific source rather than generic filtered noise.

The room choice (booth/control/live) changes the centroid only slightly (603 vs 521 Hz) and the pictures are nearly identical. The three rooms are not clearly different, so the choice is weak.

grades.lesson: Make each knob move a distinct, visible spectral feature (a hiss band, a hum with harmonics, a low rumble), and make categorical choices differ clearly in the spectrogram. Avoid isolated clicks in beds that must loop, and do not normalise every render to the same peak.

flaws: The spectrogram shows a flat broadband noise bed with a hot band at the very bottom. There is no visible monitor-hiss HF character, no low HVAC rumble structure, and no mains hum tones, so it reads as generic noise rather than an idle studio room.
The room choice (booth/control/live) barely differs: centroid 1080 vs 1056 vs 1072 Hz and near-identical pictures. A designer would struggle to hear a clear difference between rooms.
At the minimum extreme the waveform shows a regular periodic pulsing pattern, which is a rhythmic artifact in a room tone and would be noticeable when looped.
The 4 s loop is stated, but the start and end envelopes are not clearly seamless in the pictures, so loop quality is unverified.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob is meant to change the character of a sound (such as room size), make each option visibly different in the spectrum and envelope. Test that the options are distinguishable at a glance, not only that they are technically different.

brief: Halyards slapping a mast in the wind; knobs: mast (aluminium|wood), wind 0..1, slap density 0..1, ring 0..1, rate

brief: Automatic selector moved through P-R-N-D detents; knobs: lever type (stalk/console/rotary), detent click 0..1, travel smoothness 0..1, transmission clunk 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the waveform is a dense, near-continuous wash with only 7% silence. A gear selector moving through P-R-N-D should be four distinct, crisp detent clicks with clear gaps, plus a low clunk. Here the clicks smear into each other and the sustained mid-band energy reads as a rattly buzz rather than a mechanical detent.
The four events are evenly spaced like a metronome, with no variation in timing or weight. A person moving a lever would hesitate and vary the pace, so this reads as a loop and not a gesture.

The minimum-range render is the only one that clearly reads as four discrete hits (sharp transient, short decay), and it is the cleanest of all the renders. The defaults and the maximum are much muddier. The default sits too far toward the smeared end of the range, and the maximum loses the click definition entirely.

The three lever types are barely distinguishable: centroids of 781, 903 and 987 Hz, with near-identical envelopes in the pictures. The 'choice' knob does not give a designer clearly different mechanisms (stalk vs console vs rotary).

With tail=false the sound is cut by a hard, blocky low-frequency block at the end of each event and 30% silence. This looks like an abrupt gate and not a natural decay, and the clunk reads as a slab of low-frequency energy.

Total length is fixed at 2.20 s with four events regardless of settings. There is no control over which gears are traversed (for example P to D only) or over the pacing, which limits use as a game asset.
The seed variation is acceptable (same structure, different detail), but the seed 2 and seed 3 renders differ noticeably in loudness, with RMS 0.152 vs 0.159 and peaks landing in different places.
grades.lesson: For a sequence of discrete mechanical events, make each event a sharp, short transient with a clear gap before the next, and add human-like timing and weight variation. Check that the default render shows separate hits and not a continuous wash. Make each choice option audibly distinct in the spectrum and envelope, not just a small shift in centroid.

flaws: At defaults the render reads as a dense, continuous buzz, not four discrete detent clicks. The waveform is a near-constant ~0.4 amplitude with little decay between events, and it only breaks into four events at the extremes. The detents are smeared together, so this does not sound like a P-R-N-D shift.

The pitched energy is wrong for a mechanical selector. The spectrogram shows a sustained horizontal low band under each event and wide hot low-frequency blocks. That reads as a hum or motor drone, not a plastic or metal click.
The 'transmission clunk' is the dominant element, a wide heavy low-end block at default and max. It swamps the detent click, which should be the main event. The default balance is wrong.
The lever types are barely distinguishable. Stalk, console and rotary have near-identical envelopes and differ only slightly in centroid (903 vs 987 Hz), so the choice knob adds little.

The range is inconsistent. The minimum render is four clean transient clicks with decays, while the maximum is a sustained, nearly gapless texture. Both are meant to be the same kind of sound, but they read as different things.
With tail=false, 30% of the render is silent, and each event ends in a hard rectangular block at the bottom of the spectrogram. This reads as an abrupt cutoff or gate artifact.
Four evenly spaced events with an identical rhythm in every seed give a mechanical, metronomic feel. The seeds differ in detail but not in timing.
grades.lesson: Check that the default render's envelope matches the brief's discrete events: transients must decay to near silence between hits. Keep a layer such as a clunk or rumble from smearing the events into a continuous texture, and make sure the primary character layer dominates at defaults.

flaws: The 'every range at minimum' render collapses to a single click over 0.91 s, so it no longer reads as a P-R-N-D sweep through four detents.
The rotary lever has 3 visible events and 1.9 s, which is not clearly the same four-step gesture as stalk and console.
The detent clicks are very sparse, with about 48% silence and a small RMS of 0.043, so the sound feels thin and mechanical rather than a physical lever with weight.
The transmission clunk is a low-frequency thud that is hard to tell apart from the detent click in the picture.
The 'tail = false' render still has a visible low-frequency spike after each click, so the toggle does not fully remove the tail.
grades.lesson: Make sure each knob's minimum still produces the full event structure of the sound (the same number of events), scaling intensity rather than removing events, so extremes read as the same kind of sound.

brief: Bare bulb buzzing and flickering out; knobs: bulb (filament|fluorescent), buzz 0..1, flicker chaos 0..1, pop 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The default is mostly a low hum (centroid ~780 Hz) with strong energy at the very bottom. A real filament bulb buzz is mains-harmonic and brighter, so it reads a bit like a generic drone.
The final pop and its ringing decay (~0.8 s) are the same in every render. They look like a bang with a reverb tail rather than a bulb dying. The tail toggle off still ends on a click.

At the range minimum the buzz is almost a continuous blob with a few isolated ticks, which reads as flicker-free hum, not a dying bulb. The gaps are the most characteristic feature, and they vary a lot between settings.
Silence runs from 14% to 33%. The gaps in the fluorescent render are long and empty, so the sound would not work as a loop or a sustained ambience.
The fluorescent render has a clearly different spectrum, but the buzz section is short and sits next to a long dead gap. It is less convincing than the filament.
grades.lesson: Build the signature event (here, the flicker dropouts and the final death) so it is shaped by the knobs and the seed. If one fixed gesture such as a ringing pop appears identically in every render, the sound reads as a template. Check the extremes of every range to confirm the defining character is still present.

brief: Mechanical handbrake ratchet pull or electronic parking brake whir; knobs: brake type (lever/electric), ratchet speed 0..1, click density 0..1, motor whine 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The default lever pull is a dense, noisy buzz: the ratchet clicks blur into a continuous wash, so it reads more like a generic swell than distinct pawl clicks.
The envelope crescendos and then decays smoothly, which fits a motor better than a lever. A real handbrake pull has discrete clicks that speed up or slow down but stay separate.

The minimum-range render is sparse, widely spaced clicks that run about 2 s, which is slow. The maximum range collapses into noise with almost no click definition, so the two extremes barely read as the same sound.
The electric type has a visible whine line, which is good, but it is weak and sits under broadband noise. It is less distinct than a real EPB motor tone.
With the tail off, the sound ends abruptly with a flat 23% silence gap. That is acceptable for a toggle, but it is not clean.
grades.lesson: Make sure the rhythmic, discrete events in a sound (clicks, steps, ticks) stay individually audible at the default and at the extremes of the density or speed knobs, and don't let them smear into broadband noise. Check that the extremes still read as the same kind of sound, not just that they sound different from each other.
grades.scores_note: Passes with average about 6.25 only if rounded; judged as a usable first pass.

brief: Grandfather clock ticking then abruptly halting; knobs: clock (mantel|grandfather), tick level 0..1, mechanism rattle 0..1, tick rate, tail toggle

flaws: Ticks at defaults read as soft low thumps (centroid ~228 Hz) with long decaying tails. A grandfather clock tick should be a short, dry, bright click with some wood/escapement resonance, and this is muffled and boomy.

The brief says the clock halts abruptly, but the final event is a louder, longer, broadband thump with a decaying tail, so it sounds like a big hit or a gong rather than a mechanism seizing. The ticks do not stop dead on a clear clunk.
At the default the ticks are almost continuously connected by their tails (only 6% silence). That reads as a pulsing drone and not discrete ticks. The tick-tock alternation is weak.

The mantel variant gives distinct ticks but they look like tonal low-frequency blips with a ringing line, not mechanical clicks. Its 46% silence suggests ticks that are too sparse or too short for a mantel clock.

At minimum range only 3 ticks fall in the whole 3.2 s, so it barely reads as a ticking clock. At maximum the ticks blur into a continuous rumble and the stop is lost in the wash, so the extremes do not hold together.
The tail toggle only changes decay, and tail=false still leaves a large thump at the stop. The 'stop dead' moment is not controlled by any dedicated knob such as stop time or stop type.
Seeds differ only in tiny detail, which is acceptable, but the timing is identical, so they sound like the same take.
grades.lesson: Check that the defining transient of the sound (here a crisp tick and a clear mechanical stop) has the right spectrum and decay length. Do not let tails smear discrete events into a drone, and do not let the closing event be a bigger version of the same thing.

flaws: The default grandfather ticks read as soft, low, rounded thumps (centroid ~228 Hz) with no sharp escapement click. They sound more like a heartbeat or muffled knocks than a clock tick, and the spectrogram has almost no high-frequency transient.

The brief says it ticks and then halts abruptly, but the final event is a large, loud 'clunk' with a long ringing tail. The stop is a noisy bang rather than a clean halt, and the ticks die off before the stop.
The tail=false render still has a long decay on the last event, so it does not halt abruptly. The toggle changes little, and the ticks themselves keep long rounded decays.
The mantel preset has a higher centroid and sharper ticks, but it is 46% silence and the ticks are thin and sparse. It does not read as a clear grandfather/mantel pair of the same mechanism.
At minimum range, only 3 ticks fit before the stop, with large gaps, so the sound no longer reads as a ticking clock. At maximum, the ticks are blurred into a continuous wash with rattle noise.

The two seeds are nearly identical in layout and shape, with only slight amplitude differences in the ticks. This is little real variation, and the tick spacing and the stop are the same on every take.
grades.lesson: Build the defining transient of a sound (for a clock, the sharp tick click with bright content and a short decay) first and check it in the spectrogram. Don't let low-frequency body and long decays blur it into a generic thump, and make 'abrupt' events actually cut off.

flaws: Defaults read as a muffled thump, not a clock. The centroid is 228 Hz and the spectrogram shows low-frequency energy with almost no bright, sharp tick transient. A grandfather clock tick should have a crisp click with a wooden or metallic top end.
Ticks are heavy low-frequency pulses with a slow decay, closer to soft heartbeat or thud pulses than escapement ticks. They lack the tick-tock alternation of pitch that gives a clock its character.

The 'stops dead' ending is unconvincing. The final event is a much larger broadband thump followed by a long decaying tail, and it reads as a crash or slam rather than the mechanism halting. The brief says the ticking halts abruptly, but nothing in the sound makes that clear.
The tick-rate minimum leaves only 3 ticks in 3.2 s with large gaps, then the same big final hit. Ticks are too sparse to read as a clock, and the pacing looks broken.

The tail-off version has overlapping ticks with long bodies, so the ticking does not clearly stop. The max-range render has a messy, blurry tick stream, so the extremes are not clean variations of the same sound.
The mantel setting is the most clock-like, but its centroid of 551 Hz is still low and it has 46% silence. Mantel and grandfather differ mainly in pitch and decay, so the choice feels thin.
grades.lesson: Check the defining transient of the sound against the brief. For mechanical, rhythmic sounds the sharp, bright attack must be clearly visible in the spectrogram, not buried in a low-frequency body. A closing event that is meant to signal an ending must read as that ending, not as a louder, different hit.

brief: Loopable 2-4 s full market square bed: distant hammering, carts, animals, chatter. Knobs: time of day (dawn/noon/dusk), activity 0..1, animal amount 0..1, reverb 0..1, loop-crossfade toggle.

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 2.16); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: Defaults read as a dense, continuous noise wash with a mostly flat envelope. Distant hammering, carts, animals and chatter are not separable as layers. It sounds like generic broadband noise, not a market square.

The hammering layer is only faint, evenly spaced vertical ticks near the top of the spectrogram. It is metronomic and very quiet. At the minimum-range setting the hits become a regular pulse, which reads as a clock or machine rather than a blacksmith.

There is no visible animal or voice structure, such as formant-like chatter or bird and animal calls. A few thin horizontal lines are the only pitched content, and they look like steady tones rather than calls.

The tail of the default render has a bright, red-hot burst at the bottom right of the spectrogram, and the waveform ends with a different energy than it starts. This is a loop-seam risk for a bed that must loop. The crossfade=false render looks nearly identical to the default, so the toggle does little to fix or reveal the seam.

The dawn, dusk and noon variants differ mostly in level and a bit of modulation, with centroids of 977, 844 and 951 Hz. The time-of-day change is subtle and does not clearly change the character, for example more birds at dawn or fewer carts at dusk.

The seeds share the same broad noise texture, but the hammer ticks and swells are placed differently enough that they do not read as the same sound with a different take. Only the overall noise floor is consistent.
grades.lesson: When a brief lists distinct layers (hammering, carts, animals, chatter), make each layer spectrally and temporally distinctive and irregular. Check that each can be picked out in the render, rather than relying on a broadband noise bed with faint periodic ticks. Verify that the loop seam is clean, since a loop toggle that changes nothing visible means the seam was never designed.

flaws: Spectrogram shows mostly horizontal tonal lines and sparse blips rather than a dense, layered crowd bed. Chatter, carts and animals are not identifiable, so it reads as a synthetic drone with clicks, not a market square.
Minimum-range render is a sparse, regular series of loud transient pulses with gaps between them. It is a different kind of sound from the default and no longer reads as an ambience bed.
Maximum-range render is a flat, saturated wall of noise with almost no event structure. The hammering, carts and animals vanish, so extremes do not read as the same sound.
Dawn and dusk renders have large amplitude swells and dips, which makes the bed uneven. A 3 s loop with such pronounced peaks will sound like an obvious pulsing repeat.
Crossfade=false shows a visible start/end discontinuity, and the default's final spike near the end suggests the loop point is not seamless. For a loopable bed this is a weakness.
Time-of-day settings differ mainly in envelope shape rather than in believable content (fewer crowds at dawn, more animals at noon), so the choice knob feels arbitrary.
grades.lesson: For ambience beds, build recognizable layered source events (distinct voices, impacts, animals) at consistent density, and verify that both knob extremes keep the same event density and character instead of collapsing into either sparse pulses or a flat noise wall.

flaws: The spectrogram reads as a dense, broadband noise wash with faint horizontal lines and vertical ticks. There are no recognisable hammer strikes, cart rumble, animal calls or chatter formants. It reads as filtered noise, not a market square.
The 'distant hammering' brief calls for discrete transients with a decaying tail. The waveform shows only a smooth, undulating noise envelope with no distinct hits.

The animal and chatter layers are not visible as separate events. There are no tonal calls (bleats, clucks, crows) and no syllabic modulation in the 300-3000 Hz band, so the knobs probably change the noise texture more than the content.

The time-of-day variants (dawn/dusk/noon) differ mostly in loudness modulation and slight centroid shift. They do not read as clearly different scenes, such as sparse early activity versus a busy midday.

The min and max range renders are the same texture at different density and brightness, so extremes are only mildly distinct. The max render looks like a flat, saturated wall with no foreground detail.

Loop crossfade off shows a fade-in and fade-out at the edges (3% silence), as expected. The default rendering has a full-level start and end, so the loop seam risk is only partly handled. Loop integrity is hard to confirm from the picture.

Seeds share the same noise-bed character, but each appears to rely on random amplitude wobble. The hits are not clearly structured events, so the variation is in noise detail rather than in market content.
grades.lesson: When a brief names specific sound events (hammering, carts, animal calls, chatter), build each one as a distinct, identifiable event layer with its own envelope and spectrum, and check that it is visible in the spectrogram. Do not substitute a shaped noise bed, because a designer can't use a texture that doesn't contain the named sounds.

brief: Filing cabinet or desk drawer shut hard; knobs: material (steel cabinet/wood desk/plastic pedestal), drawer size (small/file), force 0..1, contents rattle 0..1, latch click 0..1, room tail toggle

errors: random combination 3: 77% of the buffer is silent

flaws: Default render lasts 1.4 s with a long, thin tail of low ringing. A drawer slam should be a sharp bang with a short decay, then a brief rattle. This reads as a resonant thud ringing out, closer to a struck tank than a drawer.

The spectrogram shows horizontal lines at a few fixed low frequencies, which are static modal tones. They sound like a pitched hum or ring instead of the broadband thump and metallic or wood clatter a drawer makes. The centroid of about 540 Hz and the lack of high-frequency content mean there is no latch click or impact crack visible.
The waveform has almost no secondary events. Contents rattle and the latch click are not visible as distinct transients after the main hit, so the slam-then-rattle structure is missing.

Material variants are not distinct enough. Wood, plastic and steel all show the same hit shape and the same low ringing lines, differing mainly in length and slight centroid shifts. Plastic shows a bit more mid energy, but none of them clearly reads as its material.

The 'room = false' variant still has a ringing tail with 27% silence, and the dry version looks no more like a slam. The drawer size 'small' option is longer than the plastic one, which is inconsistent.
The range minimum has a lower peak and the same ringing wash, so extremes do not change the character. Force mostly acts as a level change.
grades.lesson: Check that a sound's time structure matches the real event (sharp transient, correct decay length, secondary events) and that the spectrum is broadband where the source is noisy; fixed-frequency resonances alone make everything read as the same pitched ring regardless of material.

flaws: Defaults read as a generic decaying thud/noise burst, not a slam. There is no distinct two-stage event (slide, then latch or impact), and the latch click is not visible as a separate bright transient.

The spectrogram is dominated by low-frequency energy with a smeared, noisy body. A steel cabinet should have a metallic ring and a wood desk a dull knock, yet the material renders look very similar in envelope. Centroids of 865-1303 Hz do not separate them convincingly.

The tail does not read as a clean, intentional decay. Defaults show a long low-level wiggly tail out to 0.66 s, while the 'room = false' version is a very different sound with a stretched, comb-like low-frequency structure. The room toggle changes the character of the sound, not just the reverb.

The extreme range settings do not stay the same kind of sound. At minimum the hit is late, weak and soft, with a delayed onset that looks like dead air at the start. At maximum it is a long, dense wash. Neither extreme is clearly a drawer slam.
The harness reports 14-25% silence, but the waveforms mostly show a quiet tail. The dry version is short and stubby, and nothing in the renders suggests a sustained rattle of contents.

The knob list is reasonable, but the size knob shows only 'small' and 'file' with little visible difference in the renders. Material differences are subtle, so a sound designer could not tell the three options apart.
grades.lesson: Check that each categorical knob (material, size) produces a visibly different spectrum and envelope, and that each distinct event in the brief (slide, impact, latch, rattle) appears as its own identifiable feature in the render, not blended into one decaying noise burst.

flaws: The default steel render is a dense burst that rises over about 0.1 s and decays smoothly. A real slam has a sharper impact followed by a separate latch click, and here the rattle and latch events are not clearly separated from the main body.
The steel default shows strong horizontal lines at the bottom, which suggests pitched ringing. That reads as a tonal metal ring or a bell, not a dull cabinet thud, so it is somewhat musical.

The wood and plastic variants are more convincing, with a distinct transient followed by scattered rattle hits. Steel is the least believable of the three and the main material difference rests on it.

The minimum-range render starts later, at about 0.15 s after a soft pre-swell. This reads as a drawer sliding in, which is fine, but the lead-in is a little long. The maximum render has a slightly smeared envelope.
Seeds differ mainly in fine detail and in the amount of rattle. They share the same overall envelope, which is acceptable.
grades.lesson: Make the impact transient, the resonant body and the secondary events (latch, rattle) separate layers with their own timing and level. Check that a pitched modal ring does not dominate so much that a dull, noisy object sounds like a tuned one.

brief: Heavy binder or stack of documents dropped flat on a desk; knobs: object (binder/ream/folder stack), weight size (light/heavy), drop height 0..1, slap brightness 0..1, desk boom 0..1, room tail toggle

errors: knob size: too quiet (peak 0.277)
knobs with no audible effect: height
knob size: too quiet (peak 0.215)
random combination 3: too quiet (peak 0.227)

flaws: Defaults show a single sharp transient followed by a long, thin 1 s tail that decays slowly and stays visible to the end. A paper binder landing flat on a desk should be a short slap with a quick thump, not a lingering ringing decay. It reads as a resonant drum or box hit rather than paper.

The spectrogram is concentrated in the lowest band with little broadband slap or paper-crack energy. The 'slap brightness' texture is weak, so the object does not read as a binder or documents. The top of the spectrum is nearly empty.
Object variants (binder, ream, folder stack) look nearly identical in envelope and spectrum. The centroid shifts only 743 to 1185 Hz, so they are not clearly different objects.
Even with the tail off, the sound still has a ringing, pitched low-frequency decay that reads as boomy resonance. There is no layered secondary impact such as a paper settle or scatter.

Maximum range gives a long, strong ringing decay of about 0.3 s with large amplitude lobes. This reads as a boomy drum hit rather than a heavy book, so the extremes drift away from the intended sound.
grades.lesson: Check the spectrogram against the real material of the object, not just the envelope shape. A transient followed by a long resonant decay reads as a drum or box, so give soft or dry objects a fast damped tail and broadband noise content, and make the object choices differ audibly in spectrum and decay.

flaws: Default render is a 1 s sound with a ~23% silent tail, which reads as a thin, ringing decay rather than a paper or binder slap. The waveform shows a sharp transient followed by a long, low-level sustained sine-like ring. A dropped stack of paper should be a short thud with a quick, damped decay, not a resonant tone.

The spectrogram shows a persistent low-frequency band (the desk boom) running the full length, with tonal streaks. It sounds like a pitched hum or resonant box rather than a paper-on-wood impact, and the slap/paper noise component is weak and sparse.

The three object choices (binder, ream, folder stack) look nearly identical in envelope and spectrum, differing mainly in centroid (743, 824 and 1185 Hz). A designer would not hear them as three clearly different objects.

With 'tail = false' the sound is cut to 0.6 s and the waveform appears to end abruptly. The spectrogram shows a hard vertical edge at the cut, which would click or sound truncated, so the toggle is not production-ready.
