flaws: The waveform is a dense wash of low-frequency energy with a single heavy band at the bottom of the spectrogram. Kick, snare and hat are not visibly separate, so it does not read as a drum pattern.
There are no visible hat or snare bands, so the top of the spectrogram is almost empty. A 909 should have bright hats and a snappy snare, but the centroid sits at only 672-958 Hz.
The circuits barely differ. 808, 909 and cr78 show nearly the same hit layout and envelopes, with only small centroid shifts, so the choice knob does not give three distinct kits.

At minimum range (80 bpm, 3.00 s) there are large gaps in the middle with few hits, so it no longer reads as a groove. At maximum range the pattern collapses into a continuous dense wash with no clear transients.
The kick has no visible falling pitch line, and sustained low energy smears between hits, which muddies the groove.
The seeds mostly repeat the same hit positions with only small detail changes, and seeds 2 and 3 are nearly identical in rms and centroid. The loop ends mid-hit, so it will not loop cleanly.
The fill toggle changes only the tail, and the effect is subtle.
grades.lesson: When a sound is a mix of distinct components, such as drum voices, make each component occupy its own clearly visible frequency band and envelope. Check that every choice option changes the timbre noticeably, and that the extremes of every range still sound like the same thing, not a gap or a wash.

flaws: The waveform shows no distinct kick/snare/hat pattern. It is a continuous wash of low-frequency energy with a few decaying hits, so it does not read as a one-bar drum loop.

The spectrogram is dominated by a bright low band along the bottom, with no visible kick pitch-drop lines. Hi-hats and snare noise bursts are barely visible, so the kit lacks separation across the spectrum.
The 808, 909 and CR-78 circuits look very similar in the picture (centroids 672, 958 and 714 Hz, same hit positions). They do not read as clearly different machines.

The maximum range setting turns the loop into a dense, nearly constant wall of sound at 1.71 s, with no gaps between hits. The minimum setting leaves a large hole of about 1 s mid-bar and runs 3 s. Both extremes stop reading as a groove.
With fill off, the end of the loop decays into a tail, so it may not loop seamlessly. Seeds 2 and 3 are nearly identical to each other and to the default, so variation is weak.
grades.lesson: Make each voice of a multi-instrument pattern occupy its own clearly visible frequency band and transient shape (low kick with pitch drop, mid snare noise burst, high hat tick). Check that the extremes of density and tempo still leave audible gaps between hits and loop cleanly, rather than turning into a continuous wash.

flaws: The brief is a one-bar drum loop, but the renders read as a low, mushy wash: the centroid sits around 670 Hz and almost all the energy is a hot band at the bottom. There are no distinct hi-hats or snares in the spectrogram and no bright top end, so it is hard to tell a kit from a bass-heavy decaying noise.
Only about 4-5 broad low-frequency hits are visible per bar, with very similar decay shapes. The pattern does not show the kick/snare/hat layering that makes it a groove.
The circuits do not differ enough: 808, 909 and cr78 have similar spectrograms and centroids of 672, 958 and 714 Hz. A designer would expect clearly different kit character.

At maximum range the waveform becomes a dense, continuous block with almost no gaps between hits (rms 0.277, 1.71 s). The rhythm is lost and it no longer reads as a drum pattern. At minimum range there are long dead stretches inside the bar (3.0 s, with a big hole in the middle), so it reads as sparse and broken rather than a slow groove.

Loop integrity is doubtful. The default ends with the waveform still at high level, and fill=false ends on a tail that trails off, so the bar is unlikely to loop seamlessly. Seeds 2 and 3 are nearly identical in rhythm, so variation is weak.
The knobs are reasonable (circuit, tempo, swing, density, accent, fill). However, there is no per-instrument level or tone control, and the density and tempo extremes break the sound.
grades.lesson: When a sound is made of several distinct layers (kick, snare, hat), check that each layer occupies its own visible spectral region and that the preset or variant choice changes the spectrum clearly. Also make sure the range extremes keep the rhythmic or structural identity instead of smearing into a wash or leaving dead gaps.

brief: Metal gangway plate slamming onto the quay; knobs: material (steel|aluminium|wood), force 0..1, rattle 0..1, ring 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: rattle

flaws: Default steel slam reads as a low thud with a thin tail. The centroid is ~395 Hz and almost all energy sits below ~500 Hz, so it lacks the bright metallic clang or plate-impact transient the brief describes.

The default has 32% silence, meaning the waveform drops to near nothing for about the last 60% of its length. A metal plate slam should keep a decaying ring or rattle, so this reads as cut off or empty.
The wood option is not a metal gangway at all. It is a short, sparse tick with 51% silence and almost no sustain. It contradicts the brief, and it is a different sound from the other two materials.
At minimum range settings the sound is 65% silence with a weak, dull body (rms 0.038). At maximum it becomes a long, droopy 2 s ring, so the extremes behave like different kinds of sound.

Spectrograms show energy confined to the lowest band plus a few thin horizontal ring lines. There is little mid or high content for the impact, rattle or chain-and-plate jangle a sound editor expects.
Aluminium and the max-range version have long, smooth, almost pure decays, which sound like a sustained tonal hum rather than a slammed plate. Ring modes appear to be too few and too stable.
grades.lesson: Check that the default render actually has the spectral content and the envelope of the real-world object in the brief, such as a bright impact transient and a plausible decay. Make sure every choice option (e.g. a material) still belongs to that object instead of turning into a different sound.

flaws: The brief is a metal gangway plate, yet the material choice includes wood. Wood gives a short, dull, 47% silent render that reads as a wooden thunk, not a metal slam. It is a plausible option but off-brief.
The minimum-range render is 55% silent and has weak energy. It is mostly a short tick followed by a long empty tail, so it reads as a different, much smaller event than the slam.
The default is mostly a decaying ring with a thin transient. It could use more low-end thud to convey the weight of a plate hitting the quay.
The 'rattle' component is hard to see in the spectrogram. It shows as scattered sparse clicks, not a clear secondary chatter after the impact.
The aluminium render sustains longer and sounds more like a ringing bar than a plate, with a slow, smooth decay.
The seeds share the same overall shape with different detail, which is good, but their peaks vary noticeably (0.50 to 0.64), so the level is slightly inconsistent between takes.
grades.lesson: Keep every choice option within the brief's subject, and check that the minimum of each range still reads as a weaker version of the same event rather than a near-empty render with a long silent tail.

brief: Horse hooves walking or trotting on cobbles. Knobs: gait (walk/trot/canter), rate, horseshoe ring 0..1, weight 0..1, surface wetness 0..1, tail toggle.

flaws: The default is meant to be a walk, but the waveform shows about 8 evenly spaced hits in 3 s. That is a brisk trot, not a four-beat walk, and the walk gait never shows its characteristic four-beat pattern.

Gait differentiation is weak. Walk and trot look nearly identical: evenly spaced, similar-amplitude hits. Canter groups into triplets, but the grouping is subtle, so the choice knob barely changes the character.

Each hoof strike is a plain decaying thump with broadband noise. There is no clear clop/ring structure, no visible horseshoe metallic ring on the cobbles, and no stone click transient, so it reads more like a generic knock than hooves on cobbles.
A single hit per step: a real hoof gives a double impact (toe/heel, or shoe plus stone) and the front and hind hooves differ. Here every strike is the same, so it sounds mechanical, like a metronome.

The tail is a long, noisy wash that sits at a constant level beneath the hits. It looks like a reverb/noise bed rather than a natural cobble-street decay, and with the tail off the hits become isolated, near-identical pulses with 51% silence.

At minimum ranges the hits become sparse thin clicks with a high centroid (1813 Hz), which sounds like ticking rather than hooves, and at maximum they smear into a dense blur; the extremes don't hold together as the same sound.
The seeds look very similar in timing and amplitude pattern, so variation is mostly in level, not in the feel of the take.
grades.lesson: Make the default of a choice knob an accurate, recognisable example of that choice (e.g. a real four-beat walk), and make each choice differ in rhythmic structure rather than just speed. Then build each event from several distinct layers (transient, body, resonance) with per-event variation, so it does not sound like a repeated sample.

flaws: Defaults are labelled as a walk but show about 7 near-uniform impacts in 3 s with no clear four-beat pattern. A walk should be slower, with four evenly spaced hoof falls per stride.

Trot and canter do not match their real rhythms. Trot should be a two-beat diagonal pair, but it shows evenly spaced single hits. Canter should be a three-beat gallop with a gap, but it shows a clumped pattern that looks like irregular walking.
Each hit is a smeared blob rather than a sharp transient. The envelopes decay slowly and the spectrogram is a wide band of smear, so it reads as a thud with a long tail, not a hoof clack on stone.

Maximum range turns the hits into a dense, continuous rumble of about 12+ overlapping impacts with no individual hoof strikes. This reads as a different sound, closer to a drumroll or machinery than a horse.
With tail off, the hits have clean boxy cut-off ends, so the envelope sounds artificial. The effect is weak too, since only the decay is removed.
Horseshoe ring shows as thin horizontal ticks at fixed pitches in the spectrogram. It sounds like a tonal ping rather than the metallic clink of a shoe on cobble, and it repeats identically each hit.
Gait changes feel like only a rate change, not a change in hoof pattern. Rate and gait overlap as controls, and gait should set the pattern while rate sets the tempo.
grades.lesson: When a sound is defined by a rhythmic pattern (gait, footsteps, machinery), check that each mode produces the real event pattern and grouping, not just a different speed. Keep each event a sharp transient with a clean decay, so that range extremes never fuse into a continuous rumble.

flaws: Default gait does not read as a horse walk: about 7 evenly spaced single hits, with no four-beat pattern and no paired hoof-fall structure. It looks like a metronomic trot, and the 'trot' option looks almost identical.
Walk, trot and canter are not clearly distinct. Canter should have a three-beat rhythm with a gap, but it only shows uneven clustering, and the waveform is mostly a continuous busy wash.
Each hit has a long, smeared decay with a wide, noisy low-mid body. The result is closer to a muffled thud than a sharp cobble clack, with little of the ringing of a horseshoe striking stone.
At maximum settings, hits merge into a dense continuous wash with no individual hoof strikes, and the centroid drops to 565 Hz. This reads as a rumble, not hooves.
The 'tail' toggle does very little beyond changing the end. With the tail off, hits are blocky, with a flat rectangular spectrogram look that suggests an artificial cutoff.
Seed variation is low: the hit pattern and timing are nearly the same across seeds, with only small amplitude differences, so the takes sound like the same loop.
grades.lesson: Make sure the rhythmic structure that defines each category (e.g. gait footfall pattern) is clearly different and recognisable, and verify that the extreme settings keep individual events distinct instead of merging into a wash.

brief: Loopable 3 s empty-room air with faint settling creaks; knobs: room size (closet|bedroom|hall), air level 0..1, creak density 0..1, hum 0..1, loop toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: creaks

flaws: The brief asks for 'faint settling creaks', but at defaults the waveform and spectrogram show only a flat noise bed. No discrete creak transients are visible, so it reads as generic noise rather than a room tone.

The spectrogram is dominated by a bright red line at the very bottom, a constant low-frequency hum or rumble that stays loud. The hum is meant to be one optional knob but sits prominently at defaults, so the sound reads as a drone, not air.

The room choice changes little. Closet (721 Hz centroid) and hall (248 Hz) look almost the same as default: a stationary noise wash with a different tilt. There is no audible reverb, tail or space character, so the three sizes are mostly EQ differences.

At the minimum setting a single isolated creak shows up as a spike at about 2/3 of the way through, while at default and maximum no creaks appear. Creak density therefore does not behave consistently, and the maximum has none visible.

The loop=false render shows a fade in and out, which is fine. But the looped version starts and ends at full level with a visible hard edge at the start, so loop seam quality is doubtful for an ambience that has to loop.
The seeds are all the same flat-noise texture with only small RMS and centroid differences. This is consistent, but with no distinguishing events there is nothing to vary between takes.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a distinctive event (creaks, drips, clicks), make sure it is clearly visible and audible at default settings and across the whole range of its density knob. A steady noise bed with the feature missing will read as generic noise, not the described sound.

flaws: Default render doesn't read as room air: the bed is nearly absent and the waveform is a series of loud, bursty noise events with quiet gaps, so it sounds like a rustle or scratching, not a steady room tone with faint creaks.
The creaks are not faint. They are broadband noise bursts with no tonal or resonant wood character, and they dominate the picture, which contradicts the brief.

room = hall shows a loud burst at the start, a decay to near silence, then a long swell to the end. This is a reverb-like envelope that is not an even room tone, and it cannot loop without an audible jump.
The maximum-range render is a dense, loud, constant noise (rms 0.239, centroid 304 Hz) with no creaks visible. It is a different sound, more like a rumble or wind, not an empty room.
The minimum-range render is mostly silent (17%) with two isolated bursts. That is not usable room air, and the quiet gaps break the loop and the ambience feel.

Loopability is doubtful: with loop=false the waveform fades in and out at the edges, but with loop=true the default shows bursts at the very start and end, so the loop seam is not controlled. The room-size choice also changes the event pattern and loudness instead of only the acoustics.
grades.lesson: For an ambience, build a continuous, steady bed first and keep the events (creaks, clicks) clearly quieter and sparser than it. Make sure every choice and range extreme still has the bed and keeps a loop-safe start and end level.

flaws: The waveform is a dense, flat noise band for the full 3 s. The brief asks for faint settling creaks, but there are no discrete transients or low-frequency creak events in the waveform or the spectrogram.
The spectrogram is broadband noise with a small low-frequency concentration and no visible hum line or tonal structure. It reads as generic noise, not room tone.
Room size changes only the centroid (closet 1410 Hz, default 885 Hz, hall 527 Hz). It reads as a filter tilt, not a change in space, and there are no visible differences in decay or reverb character.
The range extremes for air, creak and hum look almost identical to the default. Min and max are nearly the same picture, so those controls barely change the character.
The loop=false render fades in and out over its full length, so it isn't a useful one-shot. The looping version also has a visible dip and burst near the end, so the loop seam is uncertain.
The 'air' is a loud, constant wash (RMS 0.15–0.19) for something that should be quiet and subtle.
grades.lesson: When the brief names specific sparse events (creaks, hum), make sure they are clearly visible in the render at defaults and that their knobs produce obvious differences. Don't let a broadband noise bed stand in for the whole sound.

brief: Anchor dropping and chain rattling out; knobs: anchor size (small|medium|heavy), chain length 0..1, splash 0..1, clank 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: tail

flaws: No clear anchor-splash event. The waveform builds gradually to a peak around 1.7 s, so it reads as a swelling rattle, not a drop followed by chain pay-out. A sound editor would expect a distinct entry impact or splash.
About 35% of the render is silent at defaults, and 56% at minimum settings. The sound is only about 2.5 s of content in a 3.5 s file, with a long dead tail. This is wasteful and sounds unfinished.

The size knob changes the sound very little. Small, medium and heavy have almost identical envelopes and spectrograms, with only a centroid shift. Heavy does not produce a convincing low-end thud or weight.
Chain rattle is visible as sparse, discrete, horizontal tonal streaks. These look like pitched ringing and not metallic clanks with a broadband transient, so the chain may sound like a tonal tinkle.
The tail toggle does almost nothing: its waveform and spectrogram are nearly the same as the default, so the knob is of little value.

Extremes are inconsistent. At minimum settings the sound is a short burst with a different shape and 56% silence. At maximum it is a long, swelling wash, which loses the 'drop then rattle' structure. These read as different sounds.
grades.lesson: Make sure the defining event of the brief (here the impact or splash) is a clear, distinct feature in the render, and that each categorical or toggle knob produces a visibly different result. Also trim dead silence from the file so the length matches the content.

flaws: The defaults do not read as an anchor drop. There is a roughly 0.6 s run-up of small blips, then one dense, near-continuous block of broadband noise with a flat-topped, square-ish envelope. A heavy chain rattling out should show discrete clanks with a speed-up, then a hard stop. This reads as a noise burst or rumble instead.

The splash and the chain rattle are not separable. The splash should be a distinct transient with a bright wash as the anchor hits the water, but there is no clear impact event. The low red band at the bottom reads as a steady drone and not a thud with a pitch drop.

The tail is mostly empty. About 45% of the render is near-silent, with a few sparse blips trailing after the main event, and the waveform fades into near-nothing. That is dead weight for a 3.2 s asset and feels like an abrupt, unnatural fall-off.

Range extremes change duration a lot (2.5 s to 4.0 s). At the maximum setting the chain events smear into a vertical-line comb pattern. At the minimum setting the sound is a short, boxy, low block (centroid 303 Hz) with no splash character, so it no longer reads as the same sound.
Seed variation is mostly timing and onset shift. Seed 3 starts the event at t=0, with no run-up, while the others have a lead-in, so the takes differ in structure instead of just detail.

The size knob mainly shifts the centroid and changes the block's width. It does not change the chain's character (link size, clank pitch), so 'heavy' sounds like a lower-passed version of the same sound.
grades.lesson: Make each sub-event in a composite sound (impact, splash, rattle, tail) a distinct, audible element with its own envelope and timing. Check that the default render shows those events as separate shapes, not one continuous noise block, and trim dead air in the tail.

flaws: Waveform reads as a long sustained, dense buzz at constant amplitude for about 1 s after the onset, then a smooth decay. It looks like a rattle or noise burst, not a heavy anchor hitting water followed by chain links paying out. There is no distinct splash transient and no sense of the chain speeding up and slowing down.

Spectrogram energy is mostly a bright red band at the very bottom plus vertical comb-like striations. This looks like a low drone with periodic clicks, not individual metallic clanks. There is little mid/high-frequency metal ring or splash noise, so centroids of 400-1300 Hz are too dull for chain and splash.

Small and heavy differ mainly by brightness and level, with nearly the same timing and shape. Small still has the same long 3 s structure, and an anchor that is small should be shorter with a quicker chain run. Size does not change the physical behaviour.

Every range at minimum (chain length 0, etc.) still produces a long rattle of about 1 s, so the chain-length knob changes less than it should. At the minimum setting the sound is still dense, which suggests the chain control is not scaling event count properly.
tail=false cuts the file to 2.3 s with 31% trailing silence, so the file has dead air after the sound. The tail toggle should trim or fade the render rather than pad it.
The first 0.3 s has small isolated ticks before the main hit, which reads as odd pre-impact artifacts rather than the anchor falling through air.
grades.lesson: Check that each knob changes the physical structure of the sound (event count, timing, spectrum), not just its level or brightness, and that the main event shows distinct, recognizable layers (impact, splash, metal ring) in the spectrogram rather than one undifferentiated noise band.

brief: Loopable 4 s wind around the house exterior; knobs: exposure (sheltered|open), gust strength 0..1, whistle 0..1, rain 0..1, loop toggle

errors: too slow: 2791 ms worst render in the sandbox
warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 2.01); takes should stay the same sound
seeds change the sound a lot (distance 2.04); takes should stay the same sound
slow: 1328 ms worst render

flaws: The spectrum is low-heavy with a centroid of about 670 Hz. The wind reads as a rumbly noise bed with little mid or high air, so it is not very house-like.
The whistle shows as thin, nearly static horizontal lines, close to steady tones. It lacks the pitch wandering and gust-coupled modulation that make a haunted whistle convincing.

The gust envelope is a single swell, and at the seed 3 default it is a large burst at the end. A 4 s loop with one big event will sound obviously repetitive when looped. With loop=false the file fades in and out, which is expected.
The sheltered and open settings differ mostly in level and modulation depth, not in character. Sheltered has higher RMS and a flatter envelope, which is counterintuitive.
The brief names the 'rain' knob, but there is no clear sign of rain texture in the spectrogram, which has no dense high-frequency content.
grades.lesson: Make every named knob produce a visible, characteristic change in the spectrogram, such as tonal motion, high-frequency texture or envelope shape. Check that a loopable sound has no single dominant event that makes the repeat obvious.

brief: Loopable 2-4 s busy open-plan bed with distant typing, murmur and occasional phones; knobs: occupancy (quiet/busy/crunch), chatter level 0..1, keyboard density 0..1, phone ring chance 0..1, HVAC under-bed 0..1, loop crossfade toggle

errors: knobs with no audible effect: crossfade

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: crossfade

flaws: At defaults the render reads as a dense, uniform band of noise with an even envelope. The spectrogram shows no distinct typing clicks, no phone-ring tonal lines, and no voice formant structure. It sounds like generic filtered noise, not an open-plan office.
Typing and phones, the two elements the brief names, are not visible at defaults. A designer would hear a hiss bed with no identifiable office content.

The occupancy choices (quiet, crunch) look almost the same as the default. Centroid moves only 1187-1364 Hz and the waveform shape is nearly identical, so the choice does not change the character of the scene.

The range minimum shows isolated sharp vertical clicks (keyboard) with a thin bed, which looks like the right idea. The default and maximum do not look like this, and the maximum collapses into a dense noise wall. The element that should make the sound recognisable is only audible at one extreme.
The crossfade toggle makes almost no visible difference. The waveform edges at default and with crossfade off look alike, so the loop seam cannot be judged and the knob looks nearly inert.
The waveform has a swelling macro-envelope that rises and falls over the 4 s, which may cause a level dip or bump at the loop point. That undermines a bed meant to loop seamlessly.
Seeds differ mostly in fine detail and share an identical macro shape. That is acceptable, but it suggests the structure is deterministic and only the noise texture changes.
grades.lesson: Make the defining events of the sound (clicks, rings, voices) clearly distinct from the bed at default settings. If they only emerge at one knob extreme, the default reads as generic noise. Check the spectrogram for the discrete features the brief names before shipping.

flaws: At defaults the render is a dense, uniform band of mid-frequency noise with a flat envelope. No individual keyboard clicks, phone rings or murmur formant structure are visible, so it reads as generic noise or a filtered wash, not an open-plan office.

The spectrogram has no clear phone-ring tonal lines (steady horizontal partials) or discrete typing transients at default settings. The 'distant typing, murmur and occasional phones' elements the brief names do not read as separate layers.

The occupancy choices quiet, default and crunch look almost the same (centroid 1364, 1253, 1187 Hz, similar texture). They do not read as clearly different crowd densities, and 'crunch' is not a distinct state.

The minimum-range render collapses into sparse, regular vertical spikes (centroid 483 Hz, 3% silence) that look like a ticking machine, not a bed. It has the wrong character and a dip in the middle, which breaks the no-gaps ambience requirement.

The loop crossfade toggle makes almost no visible difference (rms 0.148 vs 0.15), and the waveform shows a swell and taper at the edges rather than a seamless even bed. Loopability is not convincingly demonstrated.
Seeds look nearly identical in overall shape and spectrum, with only small detail differences. That is acceptable for variation, but it also points to a texture dominated by one noise source.
grades.lesson: Make each layer named in the brief (e.g. typing, phones, murmur) a distinct, visible event type in the render at defaults, and check that the extreme settings keep the same character instead of collapsing into a different sound. A generic noise bed with the right centroid still reads as the wrong thing.

flaws: The bed does not read as an open-plan office. The spectrogram is mostly broadband noise with no visible formant or syllabic structure for murmur and no clear key-click texture for typing. It sounds like modulated noise.

The phone rings show up as isolated horizontal bars, such as the red tone burst around 1 kHz. They are loud, stick out from the bed, and are not 'occasional distant'. This works against an ambience that is meant to sit under a scene.

The amplitude envelope swells and dips by large amounts, for example a loud block at 1.5-2.5 s in the quiet and seed renders. A loopable bed should be even, and these swells will make the loop pulse audibly.
With crossfade off, the end looks faded or ragged compared with the start (the waveform tapers on the right). The loop-point behaviour is hard to judge, and the default may not loop seamlessly.

Seeds differ in where the loud events land, so they look like different takes, but the dominant phone or burst block is much stronger than the bed in every take. The takes feel event-driven rather than like a steady ambience.
At minimum, the 'every range' render is sparse and spiky, with isolated transients and a thin low-frequency bed. It reads as a different sound from the dense bed at the defaults.
The 'busy' occupancy value is never shown, and 'crunch' looks flatter and denser than quiet, so the occupancy steps do not clearly map to busier crowds.
grades.lesson: For an ambience bed, keep the level even so it loops, and build each layer (voices, keys, phones) from believable component structure. Keep sparse events, such as phone rings, well below the bed so they do not dominate the take.
